# 💡 Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- Enterprise network segmentation separates workloads according to trust, purpose, environment and data sensitivity.
- Secure VPC design uses multiple Availability Zones, non-overlapping CIDRs and separate public, private and isolated subnets.
- Route tables, Security Groups and Network ACLs must work together to permit only required communication.
- Security Groups provide stateful resource-level filtering, while Network ACLs provide stateless subnet-level controls.
- VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink reduce internet exposure and enable private access to AWS and internal services.
- AWS Transit Gateway simplifies large-scale connectivity and supports separate routing domains for production, development, shared services and inspection.
- Centralised inspection using AWS Network Firewall can enforce consistent east-west and outbound network policies.
- Hybrid connections using VPN and Direct Connect must use restricted routing, redundancy, monitoring and tested failover.
- DNS is a critical security layer and should include central governance, query logging and malicious-domain filtering.
- Zero Trust architecture does not grant access merely because a workload or user is inside a trusted network.
- Network telemetry, change governance and Infrastructure as Code are essential for maintaining a secure enterprise network.
- Every permitted connection should have a documented business purpose, owner and security control.

💼 Business Scenario

Section titled “💼 Business Scenario”

CloudNova Technologies is expanding its SecurePay platform across multiple AWS accounts and Regions.

The current environment includes:

  • Production AWS accounts
  • Development AWS accounts
  • Shared services
  • Centralised security tooling
  • Hybrid connectivity to on-premises data centres
  • Internet-facing applications
  • Internal business applications
  • Amazon EKS workloads
  • Amazon ECS services
  • AWS Lambda functions
  • Amazon RDS databases
  • Partner API integrations

A recent architecture assessment identifies several network-security weaknesses:

  • Production and development workloads share the same VPC.
  • Databases are deployed in public subnets.
  • Security Groups allow inbound access from 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Administrators connect directly through public IP addresses.
  • All private workloads use a shared NAT gateway.
  • VPC peering connections have grown without central governance.
  • DNS queries are not centrally logged.
  • East-west traffic is not inspected.
  • On-premises networks have broad access to AWS workloads.
  • Workloads access AWS services through public endpoints.
  • Route tables are poorly documented.
  • No formal network-flow approval process exists.

The CISO asks:

Section titled “What Is Network Segmentation?”

Network segmentation divides an environment into smaller security zones.

Each zone contains systems with similar:

  • Business purpose
  • Trust level
  • Data sensitivity
  • Exposure requirements
  • Compliance obligations
  • Operational ownership

Segmentation limits unnecessary communication between systems.

Isolation

  • Log important network activity.
  • Automate network configuration.
  • Document every permitted flow.
  • Design for future growth.

🏢 Enterprise Best Practices

Section titled “🏢 Enterprise Best Practices”

CloudNova’s network standards include:

  • Use separate AWS accounts and VPCs for major trust boundaries.
  • Design a non-overlapping enterprise IP-address plan.
  • Deploy critical workloads across multiple Availability Zones.
  • Place only approved edge resources in public subnets.
  • Place application workloads in private subnets.
  • Place databases in isolated subnets.
  • Minimise public IP addresses.
  • Use Security Group references instead of broad CIDRs.
  • Restrict management access.
  • Use Systems Manager Session Manager where possible.
  • Use VPC endpoints for private AWS service access.
  • Centralise routing using Transit Gateway where appropriate.
  • Separate production and non-production routing domains.
  • Inspect egress and sensitive east-west traffic.
  • Preserve symmetric routing through stateful appliances.
  • Log VPC, Transit Gateway, DNS and firewall activity.
  • Use DNS filtering to block known malicious destinations.
  • Automate networking through Infrastructure as Code.
  • Review public exposure continuously.
  • Document every approved network flow.
  • Test network failover and incident-isolation procedures.

🚫 Common Mistakes

Section titled “🚫 Common Mistakes”

❌ Using overlapping VPC CIDR ranges.

❌ Placing databases in public subnets.

❌ Assigning public IP addresses to private workloads.

❌ Allowing SSH or RDP from 0.0.0.0/0.

❌ Using one Security Group for every tier.

❌ Allowing unrestricted outbound traffic without review.

❌ Using one route table for every subnet.

❌ Assuming NAT gateways provide security inspection.

❌ Creating large numbers of unmanaged VPC peering connections.

❌ Allowing development networks to access production.

❌ Bypassing central inspection routes.

❌ Ignoring asymmetric routing.

❌ Using only network location as proof of trust.

❌ Failing to enable VPC Flow Logs.

❌ Sending DNS queries directly to unapproved public resolvers.

❌ Giving partner networks broad access.

❌ Using public AWS service endpoints when private endpoints are available and required.

❌ Making manual routing changes outside approved pipelines.

💡 Key Takeaways

Section titled “💡 Key Takeaways”

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

  • Enterprise network segmentation separates workloads according to trust, purpose, environment and data sensitivity.
  • Secure VPC design uses multiple Availability Zones, non-overlapping CIDRs and separate public, private and isolated subnets.
  • Route tables, Security Groups and Network ACLs must work together to permit only required communication.
  • Security Groups provide stateful resource-level filtering, while Network ACLs provide stateless subnet-level controls.
  • VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink reduce internet exposure and enable private access to AWS and internal services.
  • AWS Transit Gateway simplifies large-scale connectivity and supports separate routing domains for production, development, shared services and inspection.
  • Centralised inspection using AWS Network Firewall can enforce consistent east-west and outbound network policies.
  • Hybrid connections using VPN and Direct Connect must use restricted routing, redundancy, monitoring and tested failover.
  • DNS is a critical security layer and should include central governance, query logging and malicious-domain filtering.
  • Zero Trust architecture does not grant access merely because a workload or user is inside a trusted network.
  • Network telemetry, change governance and Infrastructure as Code are essential for maintaining a secure enterprise network.
  • Every permitted connection should have a documented business purpose, owner and security control.

# Identity Is the New Security Perimeter

Traditional security architectures relied heavily on network boundaries.

```text
Inside Corporate Network

↓

Trusted

Outside Corporate Network

↓

Untrusted
```

Modern cloud environments cannot rely on network location alone.

Users and workloads may connect from:

- Corporate offices
- Home networks
- Mobile devices
- CI/CD platforms
- SaaS services
- Partner networks
- Multiple AWS accounts
- Multiple Regions

The modern security decision becomes:

```text
Who is requesting access?

↓

How was the identity verified?

↓

What resource is being requested?

↓

What action is required?

↓

What context applies?

↓

How long should access remain active?

↓

How will the activity be monitored?
```

Identity therefore becomes a primary security control.

```text
↓

↓
```

# Human vs Machine Identities

| Area | Human Identity | Machine Identity |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Example | Developer | Lambda function |
| Authentication | MFA and federation | Role or workload identity |
| Session | Interactive | Programmatic |
| Credentials | Temporary user session | Temporary role credentials |
| Lifecycle | HR-driven | Deployment-driven |
| Monitoring | Sign-ins and privileged actions | API activity and behavioural patterns |
| Common Risk | Account takeover | Credential theft or excessive permissions |

Human and machine identities require separate governance processes.

# Identity Federation

Identity federation allows users authenticated by an external identity system to access AWS without maintaining separate IAM-user credentials.

```text

↓

↓

AWS

↓
```

- Central identity lifecycle
- Single sign-on
- Central MFA
- Temporary credentials
- Faster access revocation
- Better auditability
- Reduced IAM-user usage
- Consistent access policies

# Identity Lifecycle Management

Identity lifecycle includes:

```text

↓

Employee or Contractor Created

↓

Mover

↓

↓

↓
```

CloudNova integrates access lifecycle with:

- Human Resources
- Contractor management
- Identity provider
- IAM Identity Center
- Access-review processes

# Joiner Process

When a new employee joins:

1. HR creates an approved employee record.
2. The identity provider creates the identity.
3. The employee is assigned to approved groups.
4. IAM Identity Center receives the identity and group membership.
5. Approved permission sets become available.
6. MFA registration is completed.
7. Access is validated.
8. Activity is monitored.

# Mover Process

When an employee changes role:

1. Old group memberships are reviewed.
2. Unnecessary access is removed.
3. New access requires approval.
4. Conflicting permissions are checked.
5. Privileged access is reassessed.
6. Access changes are logged.

Access must not simply accumulate throughout an employee’s career.

# Leaver Process

When a person leaves:

1. Identity-provider access is disabled.
2. Active sessions are revoked where possible.
3. Group membership is removed.
4. Application assignments are removed.
5. API keys and tokens are reviewed.
6. Owned resources are transferred.
7. Privileged activity is reviewed.
8. Evidence is retained.

# SAML 2.0 Federation

Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 is commonly used for browser-based enterprise federation.

```text
User

↓

↓

SAML Assertion

↓

AWS Federation Service

↓

AssumeRoleWithSAML

↓

Temporary AWS Credentials
```

A SAML assertion may include:

- User identity
- Group membership
- Role mapping
- Session attributes
- Authentication context

# SAML Federation Flow

```text
1. User authenticates to Identity Provider
2. Identity Provider verifies MFA and policy
3. Identity Provider generates signed SAML assertion
4. AWS validates assertion
5. AWS role is selected
6. AWS STS issues temporary credentials
7. User accesses authorised AWS resources
```

# OpenID Connect

OpenID Connect is an identity layer built on OAuth 2.0.

OIDC is commonly used for:

- Web applications
- Mobile applications
- CI/CD platforms
- Kubernetes workloads
- External automation

```text
External Workload

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

Signed Token

↓

AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity

↓

Temporary AWS Credentials
```

# SAML vs OIDC

| Area | SAML 2.0 | OpenID Connect |
|------|----------|----------------|
| Common Use | Enterprise workforce federation | Modern applications and workloads |
| Token Format | XML assertion | JSON Web Token |
| Typical Access | Browser-based enterprise SSO | Applications, APIs and automation |
| AWS STS Operation | AssumeRoleWithSAML | AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity |
| Example | Employee access | GitHub Actions deployment |

# AWS Security Token Service

AWS Security Token Service issues temporary security credentials.

Temporary credentials include:

- Access key ID
- Secret access key
- Session token
- Expiration time

```text
Trusted Identity

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

Authorised AWS API Access

↓

Automatic Expiration
```

# Why Temporary Credentials Are Safer

Temporary credentials:

- Expire automatically
- Reduce long-term exposure
- Support role assumption
- Can use session policies
- Improve traceability
- Reduce credential-rotation burden
- Support federation
- Limit access duration

Long-term credentials remain valid until they are rotated, disabled or deleted.

# IAM Roles

An IAM role is an AWS identity with permissions that can be assumed by a trusted principal.

A role contains:

- Trust policy
- Permissions policies
- Optional permissions boundary
- Session-duration configuration
- Tags

# Trust Policy

The trust policy defines who or what can assume the role.

Example cross-account trust policy:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/CloudNovaFederationRole"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
```

This is safer than trusting an entire external account without additional restrictions.

# Permissions Policy

The permissions policy defines what the role can do after it is assumed.

Example read-only S3 policy:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::cloudnova-reports",
        "arn:aws:s3:::cloudnova-reports/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

# Trust vs Permissions

```text
Trust Policy

Who can assume the role?

↓

Role Session Created

↓

Permissions Policy

What can the role do?
```

Both must be secure.

A restrictive permissions policy cannot prevent an untrusted identity from attempting to assume a poorly configured role.

A restrictive trust policy cannot compensate for excessive permissions after assumption.

# Cross-Account Access

Cross-account access allows a principal in one AWS account to assume a role in another account.

```text
Security Engineer

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

Security Account Role

↓

Assume Cross-Account Role

↓

Production Account

↓

Temporary Read-Only Session
```

# Cross-Account Access Flow

```text
Source Principal

↓

sts:AssumeRole Permission

↓

Target Role Trust Policy

↓

AWS STS Evaluation

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

Target Account Access
```

Both sides must permit the action:

- The source identity must be permitted to call `sts:AssumeRole`.
- The target role must trust the source principal.

# Secure Cross-Account Trust

CloudNova restricts trust using:

- Exact principal ARNs
- Organisation ID conditions
- External IDs
- Source identity
- Session tags
- MFA conditions
- Short session duration
- Explicit role naming
- Access monitoring

# AWS Organisation Condition

A resource or trust policy can restrict access to principals from a specific AWS organisation.

Example:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "AWS": "*"
  },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-exampleorgid"
    }
  }
}
```

This condition should be combined with appropriate principal and authorisation controls.

# External ID

An external ID helps reduce the confused deputy risk when granting third-party access.

```text
CloudNova

↓

Creates Third-Party Role

↓

Requires Unique External ID

↓

Third Party Assumes Role

↓

AWS Verifies External ID
```

Example trust condition:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/PartnerAccessRole"
  },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "sts:ExternalId": "cloudnova-securepay-audit-2026"
    }
  }
}
```

The external ID is not a replacement for a securely designed principal relationship.

# Source Identity

Source identity allows an organisation to preserve the original identity across role sessions.

Example:

```text
Rohit.Mahajan

↓

Federated Session

↓

Assumes SecurityAuditRole

↓

CloudTrail Records Source Identity

↓

Investigation Links Activity to Original User
```

Source identity improves traceability across role chains.

# Role Chaining

Role chaining occurs when one assumed role is used to assume another role.

```text
Federated User

↓

Role A

↓

Role B
```

Role chaining can complicate:

- Session duration
- Identity traceability
- Permission analysis
- Troubleshooting
- Incident investigation

CloudNova minimises unnecessary role chaining.

# Permission Sets

A permission set in IAM Identity Center defines the permissions a user or group receives in assigned AWS accounts.

Examples:

- `CloudNova-Developer`
- `CloudNova-Production-ReadOnly`
- `CloudNova-Security-Auditor`
- `CloudNova-Billing-Viewer`
- `CloudNova-Network-Administrator`
- `CloudNova-Emergency-Administrator`

Permission sets can contain:

- AWS-managed policies
- Customer-managed policy references
- Inline policies
- Permissions boundaries
- Session-duration settings
- Relay-state configuration

# CloudNova Permission-Set Design

| Permission Set | Assigned Group | Accounts | Session Duration |
|----------------|----------------|----------|------------------|
| Developer | Development Teams | Development | 8 hours |
| Production ReadOnly | Engineering Leads | Production | 2 hours |
| Security Auditor | Security Team | All workload accounts | 4 hours |
| Network Administrator | Network Team | Network accounts | 1 hour |
| Incident Responder | Incident Response Team | Approved accounts | 1 hour |
| Emergency Administrator | Break-Glass Team | Restricted accounts | 30 minutes |

Session durations should reflect risk.

# Role-Based Access Control

Role-Based Access Control assigns access according to job function.

```text
User

↓

Job Role

↓

Group

↓

Permission Set

↓

AWS Account Access
```

Examples:

| Business Role | AWS Access |
|---------------|------------|
| Developer | Development deployment permissions |
| Security Analyst | Security findings and logs |
| Auditor | Read-only evidence access |
| Network Engineer | Network-management permissions |
| Finance Analyst | Billing and cost reports |

# RBAC Benefits

- Easy to understand
- Maps to job functions
- Supports access reviews
- Simplifies onboarding
- Supports separation of duties
- Reduces individual policy assignment

# RBAC Challenges

- Role explosion
- Excessive broad roles
- Difficult exception handling
- Access accumulation
- Static permission design

RBAC is often combined with ABAC.

# Attribute-Based Access Control

Attribute-Based Access Control uses attributes to make access decisions.

Attributes may include:

- Department
- Project
- Environment
- Cost centre
- Data classification
- Employment type
- Region
- Application name

```text
Principal Attribute

Project = SecurePay

↓

Resource Tag

Project = SecurePay

↓

Access Permitted
```

# ABAC Example

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:StartInstances",
        "ec2:StopInstances"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:ResourceTag/Project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/Project}"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

This allows users to manage resources matching their project attribute.

# Session Tags

Session tags can carry attributes into an assumed-role session.

Examples:

```text
Department = Security
Project = SecurePay
Environment = Production
EmploymentType = Employee
```

Session tags can support:

- ABAC
- Cost attribution
- Audit trails
- Conditional access
- Resource-policy decisions

# RBAC vs ABAC

| Area | RBAC | ABAC |
|------|------|------|
| Decision Basis | Job role | Attributes |
| Example | Security Analyst | Project equals SecurePay |
| Management | Group and role based | Tag and attribute based |
| Scalability | Can create many roles | Can reduce role count |
| Complexity | Easier initially | Requires strong attribute governance |
| Best Use | Stable job functions | Dynamic resource ownership |

# Permissions Boundaries

A permissions boundary defines the maximum identity-based permissions that an IAM user or role can receive.

```text
Identity Policy

Allows:
Create IAM roles

Permissions Boundary

Allows:
Create only approved application roles

Effective Permission

Intersection of both
```

A permissions boundary does not grant permissions by itself.

# Permissions-Boundary Use Case

CloudNova allows development teams to create workload roles.

Without a boundary:

```text
Developer

↓

Creates Administrator Role

↓

Privilege Escalation
```

With a boundary:

```text
Developer

↓

Creates Workload Role

↓

Mandatory Permissions Boundary

↓

Role Cannot Exceed Approved Limit
```

# Session Policies

A session policy can restrict permissions for a specific assumed-role session.

```text
Role Permission

Allows:
Read all approved production logs

Session Policy

Allows:
Read logs for Incident INC-204 only

Effective Session

Restricted to incident scope
```

Session policies cannot grant permissions beyond the role’s existing permissions.

# Effective Permissions

Effective access may be influenced by:

- Identity-based policy
- Resource-based policy
- Permissions boundary
- Session policy
- Service Control Policy
- Resource Control Policy where applicable
- Explicit deny
- AWS service-specific controls

Conceptually:

```text
Requested Action

↓

Identity Policy

↓

Resource Policy

↓

Permissions Boundary

↓

Session Policy

↓

SCP

↓

Explicit Deny Check

↓

Allow or Deny
```

An explicit deny generally overrides an allow.

# Service Control Policies and Identity

Service Control Policies define the maximum available permissions for identities in member accounts.

Example:

```text
IAM Role Allows:
Disable CloudTrail

SCP Denies:
cloudtrail:StopLogging
cloudtrail:DeleteTrail

Result:
Action Denied
```

SCPs do not grant permissions.

They define organisational boundaries.

# Zero Trust Identity Principles

CloudNova applies the following Zero Trust principles:

- Verify explicitly.
- Use least privilege.
- Assume compromise.
- Use temporary credentials.
- Evaluate context.
- Limit session duration.
- Require strong authentication.
- Record privileged activity.
- Continuously review access.
- Revoke access quickly.

# Zero Trust Access Decision

```text
Access Request

↓

Verify User or Workload Identity

↓

Validate MFA or Workload Token

↓

Check Device and Session Context

↓

Check Role and Attributes

↓

Check Organisation Guardrails

↓

Grant Minimum Required Session

↓

Monitor Behaviour

↓

Revoke When Risk Changes
```

# Context-Aware Access

Access decisions may consider:

- User identity
- Authentication strength
- Device compliance
- Geographic location
- Network source
- Time of request
- Requested AWS account
- Requested role
- Resource sensitivity
- Current threat intelligence
- Existing incident status

AWS policy conditions can support parts of this decision.

The external identity provider may enforce additional context before issuing federation access.

# Multi-Factor Authentication

MFA requires more than one authentication factor.

Factors may include:

- Something the user knows
- Something the user has
- Something the user is
- A cryptographic authenticator

CloudNova requires MFA for:

- Workforce authentication
- Privileged access
- Emergency access
- Sensitive application access
- High-risk changes

# MFA Strategy

CloudNova prioritises:

1. Hardware security keys for highly privileged users
2. Strong phishing-resistant authentication where supported
3. Authenticator applications for standard users
4. Controlled recovery procedures
5. No shared MFA devices
6. Regular MFA-registration reviews

# Root User Security

Every AWS account contains a root user.

The root user has unrestricted account-level authority.

CloudNova protects root users by:

- Using unique email addresses
- Enabling MFA
- Avoiding routine use
- Not creating root access keys
- Protecting recovery channels
- Monitoring root sign-in
- Testing emergency access procedures
- Storing credentials securely
- Restricting access to authorised custodians

# Root User Usage

Root access may be required for a limited number of account-specific tasks.

It must not be used for:

- Daily administration
- Application deployment
- Security monitoring
- Developer access
- Routine billing work
- API automation

# Privileged Access

Privileged access allows actions with significant security or operational impact.

Examples:

- Modifying IAM policies
- Changing SCPs
- Disabling logging
- Modifying KMS key policies
- Changing network routes
- Deleting backups
- Accessing restricted data
- Changing production infrastructure
- Disabling security services

# Privileged Access Management

Privileged Access Management controls how elevated access is:

- Requested
- Approved
- Granted
- Monitored
- Revoked
- Reviewed

```text
Access Request

↓

Business Justification

↓

Manager or System Owner Approval

↓

Security Approval Where Required

↓

Temporary Privileged Role

↓

Monitored Session

↓

Automatic Expiration

↓

Post-Access Review
```

# Standing vs Just-in-Time Access

## Standing Access

The user permanently holds privileged permissions.

```text
Administrator

↓

Administrator Access Available Every Day
```

Risk:

- Credentials may be compromised at any time.
- Privilege may be used accidentally.
- Access may remain after responsibilities change.

## Just-in-Time Access

Access is granted only when required.

```text
Engineer Requests Access

↓

Approval

↓

Temporary Role Assignment

↓

Short Session

↓

Automatic Expiration
```

# Just-in-Time Access Architecture

```text
Engineer

↓

Access Request Portal

↓

Ticket and Business Justification

↓

Approval Workflow

↓

Temporary Group or Role Assignment

↓

IAM Identity Center Permission Set

↓

Short-Lived AWS Session

↓

CloudTrail Monitoring

↓

Automatic Revocation
```

# Just-Enough Access

Just-enough access provides only the permissions required for the approved task.

Example:

Incorrect:

```text
Incident Responder

↓

AdministratorAccess
```

Preferred:

```text
Incident Responder

↓

View Logs
Isolate EC2 Instance
Revoke Role Session
Capture Evidence
```

# Privileged Role Categories

CloudNova separates privileged roles.

| Role | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| Identity Administrator | Manage identity configuration |
| Security Administrator | Manage security services |
| Network Administrator | Manage network controls |
| KMS Administrator | Manage encryption keys |
| Incident Responder | Contain and investigate incidents |
| Production Operator | Perform approved operational actions |
| Billing Administrator | Manage financial settings |
| Organisation Administrator | Manage AWS Organizations and SCPs |

No single routine role should control every security domain.

# Separation of Duties

Separation of duties prevents one individual from completing a sensitive process without oversight.

Example:

```text
Developer

Creates Change

↓

Reviewer

Approves Change

↓

Pipeline

Deploys Change

↓

Security Team

Monitors Result
```

Another example:

```text
KMS Administrator

Manages Key

But Cannot Decrypt Data

Data Operator

Uses Key

But Cannot Change Key Policy
```

# Toxic Permission Combinations

A toxic combination occurs when separate permissions together allow privilege escalation or control bypass.

Examples:

- Create role + attach policy + pass role
- Update Lambda code + privileged Lambda execution role
- Modify pipeline + production deployment role
- Create access key for another user
- Modify KMS key policy + access encrypted data
- Change CloudTrail configuration + delete audit logs
- Modify Security Group + access sensitive workload

Access reviews should evaluate combinations, not only individual permissions.

# IAM PassRole

`iam:PassRole` allows a principal to assign an IAM role to an AWS service.

Example:

```text
Developer

↓

Launches Lambda Function

↓

Passes Execution Role

↓

Lambda Receives Role Permissions
```

If `iam:PassRole` is too broad, a user may assign an overly privileged role to a service they control.

# Secure PassRole Policy

Restrict:

- Which roles may be passed
- Which services may receive the role
- Which resource path or naming convention is allowed

Example:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "iam:PassRole",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/application/securepay-*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "iam:PassedToService": "lambda.amazonaws.com"
    }
  }
}
```

# Break-Glass Access

Break-glass access provides emergency access when normal identity systems are unavailable.

Possible scenarios:

- Corporate identity provider outage
- IAM Identity Center outage or misconfiguration
- Federation failure
- Emergency security incident
- Locked administrative configuration

# Break-Glass Architecture

```text
Normal Access Unavailable

↓

Emergency Declared

↓

Authorised Custodians Approve

↓

Break-Glass Credential Retrieved

↓

MFA Required

↓

Emergency Role Used

↓

All Activity Logged and Alerted

↓

Credential Rotated After Use

↓

Formal Post-Incident Review
```

# Break-Glass Controls

CloudNova requires:

- Separate emergency identities
- Strong MFA
- No daily use
- Secure credential storage
- Dual control where practical
- Immediate alerting
- Short session duration
- Restricted permissions
- Regular testing
- Credential rotation after use
- Formal incident documentation

# Break-Glass Anti-Patterns

❌ Shared administrator password in a document.

❌ No MFA.

❌ Permanent access keys.

❌ No monitoring.

❌ No named owner.

❌ Never testing the process.

❌ Using the emergency identity for normal operations.

# AWS Account Root vs Break-Glass Role

These are not always the same.

```text
Root User

Account-Level Ultimate Authority

Break-Glass Role

Emergency Administrative Access for Defined Tasks
```

A break-glass role should be designed with only the required emergency permissions.

Root access should remain protected separately.

# Workload Identity for Amazon EC2

EC2 applications should use IAM roles through instance profiles.

```text
EC2 Instance

↓

Instance Profile

↓

IAM Role

↓

Temporary Credentials from Instance Metadata

↓

AWS API
```

Applications should not store access keys on the instance.

# EC2 Metadata Security

CloudNova requires:

- Instance Metadata Service Version 2
- Restricted metadata access where possible
- Least-privilege instance roles
- No credentials in user data
- Monitoring of metadata-related attacks
- Regular role reviews

# Workload Identity for AWS Lambda

Lambda functions use execution roles.

```text
Lambda Function

↓

Execution Role

↓

Temporary AWS Credentials

↓

Approved AWS Services
```

Each function or tightly related function group should use a purpose-specific role.

Avoid one shared Lambda role with broad access.

# Workload Identity for Amazon ECS

ECS separates:

- Task execution role
- Task role

## Task Execution Role

Used by ECS for actions such as:

- Pulling container images
- Sending logs
- Retrieving deployment-time configuration

## Task Role

Used by the application running inside the container.

```text
ECS Service

├── Execution Role
│   └── Platform Operations
│
└── Task Role
    └── Application Permissions
```

# Workload Identity for Amazon EKS

EKS workloads should not rely on broad worker-node permissions.

Preferred patterns provide workload-specific identity.

```text
Kubernetes Service Account

↓

Workload Identity Association

↓

IAM Role

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

AWS Service
```

Benefits include:

- Pod-level permissions
- Reduced node-role privileges
- Better isolation
- Better auditability
- Least privilege

# Workload Identity for CI/CD

CI/CD systems should use federation rather than stored AWS access keys.

Example:

```text
GitHub Actions

↓

GitHub OIDC Token

↓

AWS IAM OIDC Provider

↓

Deployment Role

↓

Temporary STS Credentials

↓

Approved Deployment
```

# Secure CI/CD Trust Policy

The role trust policy should restrict:

- Repository
- Branch
- Environment
- Organisation
- Audience
- Workflow context

Conceptual example:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
  },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
    },
    "StringLike": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:cloudnova/securepay:ref:refs/heads/main"
    }
  }
}
```

IAM Roles Anywhere allows workloads outside AWS to obtain temporary AWS credentials using trusted X.509 certificates.

# Service Roles

A service role is assumed by an AWS service to perform actions on behalf of the customer.

Examples:

- CloudFormation execution role
- CodeBuild service role
- Lambda execution role

- Purpose-specific

# Service-Linked Roles

A service-linked role is associated with a specific AWS service and includes permissions required by that service.

CloudNova should:

- Understand why each role exists.
- Monitor role creation.
- Avoid unnecessary manual modification.
- Review service dependencies before deletion.

# Long-Term Access Keys

CloudNova prohibits routine long-term access keys for human users.

Where legacy access keys still exist:

- Assign an owner.
- Document the business justification.
- Restrict permissions.
- Store securely.
- Monitor usage.
- Rotate regularly.
- Set an expiry and migration plan.
- Remove unused keys.

# 🔍 Troubleshooting

## Problem — User Cannot Access an AWS Account Through IAM Identity Center

Review:

- User status in the identity provider
- User provisioning
- Group membership
- IAM Identity Center identity source
- Permission-set assignment
- AWS account assignment
- Permission-set provisioning status
- Session expiration
- Browser or cached session

## Problem — AssumeRole Returns Access Denied

Review both sides of the relationship.

### Source Side

Confirm that the source principal can call:

```text
sts:AssumeRole
```

against the target role ARN.

### Target Side

Confirm that the role trust policy trusts the source principal.

Also review:

- SCPs
- Permissions boundaries
- Session policies
- MFA conditions
- External ID
- Organisation ID
- Source identity requirements
- Role ARN
- AWS account ID

Run:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity
```

## Problem — Access Is Allowed Despite Restrictive Identity Policy

Review:

- Resource-based policy
- Role session
- Group policies
- Managed policies
- Inline policies
- Permission-set policies
- Resource ownership
- Service-specific authorisation behaviour

Do not assume that only one policy affects the request.

## Problem — Access Is Denied Despite an Allow Policy

Review:

- Explicit deny
- SCP
- Permissions boundary
- Session policy
- Resource policy
- KMS key policy
- VPC endpoint policy
- AWS service-specific controls
- Region restrictions
- Requested resource ARN

## Problem — Federated User Has the Wrong Permissions

Review:

- Identity-provider group
- Group-to-permission-set mapping
- Account assignment
- Permission-set policy
- Attribute mapping
- Session tags
- Provisioning status
- Cached session

The user may need to start a new session after access changes.

## Problem — OIDC Workload Cannot Assume Role

Review:

- OIDC provider ARN
- Token issuer
- Token audience
- Subject claim
- Repository or branch condition
- Trust-policy syntax
- Token expiration
- STS action
- AWS Region
- Role ARN

## Problem — Access Analyzer Reports External Access

Review:

- External principal
- Resource policy
- Trust boundary
- Organisation ID
- Public access
- Business justification
- Existing compensating controls

Do not archive the finding without recording why the access is expected.

## Problem — Permission Boundary Blocks a Required Action

Review:

- Identity policy
- Permissions boundary
- Resource policy
- Required action
- Resource ARN
- Condition keys

Do not remove the boundary simply to resolve the issue.

Update the approved boundary only after security review.

## Problem — Break-Glass Access Does Not Work

Review:

- Credential availability
- MFA device
- Role trust policy
- SCP restrictions
- Account recovery process
- Session duration
- Emergency documentation
- Responsible custodians

Break-glass access should be tested before an actual emergency.

# 🏢 Enterprise Best Practices

CloudNova’s identity standards include:

- Use a central corporate identity provider.
- Use IAM Identity Center for workforce access.
- Avoid IAM users for normal human access.
- Require MFA for all workforce access.
- Use phishing-resistant authentication for privileged users where supported.
- Use temporary credentials.
- Use exact principals in trust policies.
- Restrict external trust using conditions.
- Use external IDs for approved third-party access.
- Preserve source identity across role sessions.
- Use permission sets aligned with business roles.
- Apply RBAC for stable job functions.
- Apply ABAC for dynamic project and resource access.
- Govern principal and resource attributes.
- Use permissions boundaries for delegated role creation.
- Restrict session duration according to risk.
- Use just-in-time access for production.
- Use just-enough permissions for privileged tasks.
- Separate identity, security, network and key-management duties.
- Restrict `iam:PassRole`.
- Protect every AWS account root user.
- Maintain tested break-glass procedures.
- Use workload roles instead of embedded credentials.
- Use OIDC federation for CI/CD systems.
- Use workload-specific roles for containers and serverless functions.
- Review external and unused access continuously.
- Centralise identity logs.
- Monitor role assumptions and policy changes.
- Conduct regular access reviews.
- Remove dormant identities and credentials.
- Document every privileged-access exception.

❌ Creating IAM users in every AWS account.

❌ Sharing administrator accounts.

❌ Trusting an entire external AWS account unnecessarily.

❌ Using wildcard principals without restrictive conditions.

❌ Assigning `AdministratorAccess` for convenience.

❌ Using one permission set for all teams.

❌ Failing to remove access when users change roles.

❌ Allowing contractor access without an expiry date.

❌ Ignoring source identity.

❌ Using network location as proof of identity.

❌ Treating MFA as optional for administrators.

❌ Creating broad permissions boundaries.

❌ Assuming a permissions boundary grants access.

❌ Failing to restrict `iam:PassRole`.

❌ Storing CI/CD access keys in repository secrets.

❌ Failing to monitor trust-policy changes.

❌ Archiving Access Analyzer findings without investigation.

❌ Creating break-glass credentials but never testing them.

❌ Using the root user for daily administration.

# 💡 Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- Identity is a primary control plane for AWS security and must not depend solely on network location.
- Workforce, customer and workload identities require different authentication, authorisation and lifecycle controls.
- Enterprise workforce access should use a central identity provider, IAM Identity Center and temporary AWS sessions.
- Federation reduces the need for separate IAM users and long-term credentials across AWS accounts.
- IAM roles require both a secure trust policy and a least-privilege permissions policy.
- AWS STS provides temporary credentials for federated users, cross-account access and workload identities.
- Permission sets provide consistent workforce access across AWS Organizations.
- RBAC maps access to job functions, while ABAC uses governed attributes to make dynamic access decisions.
- Permissions boundaries, session policies and SCPs limit permissions but do not grant access independently.
- Zero Trust access verifies identity explicitly, evaluates context and provides minimum required access for a limited duration.
- Privileged access should use just-in-time and just-enough access rather than permanent administrator permissions.
- Break-glass access must be separate, strongly protected, monitored, tested and reviewed after use.
- Workloads should use purpose-specific roles instead of embedded AWS access keys.
- OIDC federation allows CI/CD platforms and external workloads to obtain temporary AWS credentials.
- IAM Access Analyzer, CloudTrail and access reviews are essential for identifying external, excessive and unused access.
- Identity architecture must include strong lifecycle management so that access is adjusted when people join, change roles or leave.
- Every privileged identity, role, permission set, trust relationship and exception must have a named owner and documented business purpose.

💼 Business Scenario

Section titled “💼 Business Scenario”

CloudNova Technologies now operates:

  • 150 AWS accounts
  • Multiple AWS Regions
  • 5,000 employees
  • 900 software developers
  • 150 platform engineers
  • 80 security professionals
  • External contractors
  • Business partners
  • Automated CI/CD pipelines
  • Amazon EC2 workloads
  • Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS platforms
  • AWS Lambda applications
  • Hybrid workloads outside AWS

CloudNova uses Microsoft Entra ID as its corporate identity provider.

The current AWS access model has several weaknesses:

  • IAM users exist in individual AWS accounts.
  • Developers maintain long-term access keys.
  • Shared administrator accounts are still used.
  • Contractors retain access after projects end.
  • Production access is granted permanently.
  • Users have different permissions in different accounts.
  • Some application roles have wildcard permissions.
  • Cross-account trust policies are overly broad.
  • Emergency accounts are not regularly tested.
  • Privileged sessions are not consistently monitored.
  • Access reviews are performed manually.
  • Workloads outside AWS use stored access keys.
  • No formal privileged access management process exists.

A recent internal investigation discovers that a former contractor still has active access to a development account.

The contractor cannot directly access production, but the development account contains a role that trusts an entire external AWS account.

The CISO asks:

“How can CloudNova ensure that every person and workload receives only the correct access, for the correct reason, for the minimum required time?”

As the AWS Security Architect, you must design CloudNova’s enterprise identity, federation and privileged-access architecture.

Identity Types

Section titled “Identity Types”

CloudNova separates identities into three major categories:

  1. Workforce identities
  2. Customer identities
  3. Workload identities

Workforce Identities

Section titled “Workforce Identities”

Workforce identities represent people working for or supporting the organisation.

Examples:

  • Employees
  • Administrators
  • Developers
  • Security analysts
  • Auditors
  • Contractors
  • Support engineers
  • Business partners

Workforce identities should normally originate from a central identity provider.

Customer Identities

Section titled “Customer Identities”

Customer identities represent users of CloudNova applications.

Examples:

  • SecurePay customers
  • Retail users
  • Mobile application users
  • External application users
  • Partner-portal users

Customer identities should not normally be created as IAM users.

Possible customer-identity services include:

  • Amazon Cognito
  • External customer identity platforms
  • OpenID Connect providers
  • SAML identity providers
  • Custom identity systems

Workload Identities

Section titled “Workload Identities”

Workload identities represent software, services and machines.

Examples:

  • EC2 instances
  • Lambda functions
  • ECS tasks
  • EKS workloads
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • External servers
  • Automation tools
  • SaaS platforms

Workloads should use roles and short-lived credentials wherever possible.

Joiner Process

Section titled “Joiner Process”

When a new employee joins:

  1. HR creates an approved employee record.
  2. The identity provider creates the identity.
  3. The employee is assigned to approved groups.
  4. IAM Identity Center receives the identity and group membership.
  5. Approved permission sets become available.
  6. MFA registration is completed.
  7. Access is validated.
  8. Activity is monitored.

Mover Process

Section titled “Mover Process”

When an employee changes role:

  1. Old group memberships are reviewed.
  2. Unnecessary access is removed.
  3. New access requires approval.
  4. Conflicting permissions are checked.
  5. Privileged access is reassessed.
  6. Access changes are logged.

Access must not simply accumulate throughout an employee’s career.

Leaver Process

Section titled “Leaver Process”

When a person leaves:

  1. Identity-provider access is disabled.
  2. Active sessions are revoked where possible.
  3. Group membership is removed.
  4. Application assignments are removed.
  5. API keys and tokens are reviewed.
  6. Owned resources are transferred.
  7. Privileged activity is reviewed.
  8. Evidence is retained.

Zero Trust Identity Principles

Section titled “Zero Trust Identity Principles”

CloudNova applies the following Zero Trust principles:

  • Verify explicitly.
  • Use least privilege.
  • Assume compromise.
  • Use temporary credentials.
  • Evaluate context.
  • Limit session duration.
  • Require strong authentication.
  • Record privileged activity.
  • Continuously review access.
  • Revoke access quickly.

Multi-Factor Authentication

Factors may include:

MFA Strategy

Section titled “MFA Strategy”

CloudNova prioritises:

  5. No shared MFA devices

Root User Security

Section titled “Root User Security”

Every AWS account contains a root user.

The root user has unrestricted account-level authority.

CloudNova protects root users by:

  • Using unique email addresses
  • Enabling MFA
  • Avoiding routine use
  • Not creating root access keys
  • Protecting recovery channels
  • Monitoring root sign-in
  • Testing emergency access procedures
  • Storing credentials securely
  • Restricting access to authorised custodians

Root User Usage

Section titled “Root User Usage”

  • Application deployment
  • Security monitoring
  • Developer access
  • Routine billing work
  • API automation

Toxic Permission Combinations

Section titled “Toxic Permission Combinations”

A toxic combination occurs when separate permissions together allow privilege escalation or control bypass.

Examples:

  • Create role + attach policy + pass role
  • Update Lambda code + privileged Lambda execution role
  • Modify pipeline + production deployment role
  • Create access key for another user
  • Modify KMS key policy + access encrypted data
  • Change CloudTrail configuration + delete audit logs
  • Modify Security Group + access sensitive workload

Access reviews should evaluate combinations, not only individual permissions.

Break-Glass Anti-Patterns

Section titled “Break-Glass Anti-Patterns”

❌ Shared administrator password in a document.

❌ No MFA.

❌ Permanent access keys.

❌ No monitoring.

❌ No named owner.

❌ Never testing the process.

❌ Using the emergency identity for normal operations.

🏢 Enterprise Best Practices

Section titled “🏢 Enterprise Best Practices”

CloudNova’s identity standards include:

  • Use a central corporate identity provider.
  • Use IAM Identity Center for workforce access.
  • Avoid IAM users for normal human access.
  • Require MFA for all workforce access.
  • Use phishing-resistant authentication for privileged users where supported.
  • Use temporary credentials.
  • Use exact principals in trust policies.
  • Restrict external trust using conditions.
  • Use external IDs for approved third-party access.
  • Preserve source identity across role sessions.
  • Use permission sets aligned with business roles.
  • Apply RBAC for stable job functions.
  • Apply ABAC for dynamic project and resource access.
  • Govern principal and resource attributes.
  • Use permissions boundaries for delegated role creation.
  • Restrict session duration according to risk.
  • Use just-in-time access for production.
  • Use just-enough permissions for privileged tasks.
  • Separate identity, security, network and key-management duties.
  • Restrict iam:PassRole.
  • Protect every AWS account root user.
  • Maintain tested break-glass procedures.
  • Use workload roles instead of embedded credentials.
  • Use OIDC federation for CI/CD systems.
  • Use workload-specific roles for containers and serverless functions.
  • Review external and unused access continuously.
  • Centralise identity logs.
  • Monitor role assumptions and policy changes.
  • Conduct regular access reviews.
  • Remove dormant identities and credentials.
  • Document every privileged-access exception.

💡 Key Takeaways

Section titled “💡 Key Takeaways”

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

  • Identity is a primary control plane for AWS security and must not depend solely on network location.
  • Workforce, customer and workload identities require different authentication, authorisation and lifecycle controls.
  • Enterprise workforce access should use a central identity provider, IAM Identity Center and temporary AWS sessions.
  • Federation reduces the need for separate IAM users and long-term credentials across AWS accounts.
  • IAM roles require both a secure trust policy and a least-privilege permissions policy.
  • AWS STS provides temporary credentials for federated users, cross-account access and workload identities.
  • Permission sets provide consistent workforce access across AWS Organizations.
  • RBAC maps access to job functions, while ABAC uses governed attributes to make dynamic access decisions.
  • Permissions boundaries, session policies and SCPs limit permissions but do not grant access independently.
  • Zero Trust access verifies identity explicitly, evaluates context and provides minimum required access for a limited duration.
  • Privileged access should use just-in-time and just-enough access rather than permanent administrator permissions.
  • Break-glass access must be separate, strongly protected, monitored, tested and reviewed after use.
  • Workloads should use purpose-specific roles instead of embedded AWS access keys.
  • OIDC federation allows CI/CD platforms and external workloads to obtain temporary AWS credentials.
  • IAM Access Analyzer, CloudTrail and access reviews are essential for identifying external, excessive and unused access.
  • Identity architecture must include strong lifecycle management so that access is adjusted when people join, change roles or leave.
  • Every privileged identity, role, permission set, trust relationship and exception must have a named owner and documented business purpose.

# 🏢 Enterprise Best Practices

CloudNova standards include:

- Encrypt everything by default.
- Use customer managed KMS keys for sensitive workloads.
- Separate keys by application and environment.
- Enable automatic key rotation where supported.
- Apply least privilege to key policies.
- Store application secrets in AWS Secrets Manager instead of code or environment variables.
- Use envelope encryption for large-scale data protection.
- Centralize key management and monitoring.
- Use AWS Certificate Manager for TLS certificate lifecycle management.
- Log and review all cryptographic operations through CloudTrail.
- Separate key administrators from key users.
- Test backup and recovery of encrypted workloads.
- Document key ownership, rotation schedules, and destruction procedures.

---

# 🚫 Common Mistakes

❌ Sharing one KMS key across unrelated business units.

❌ Allowing developers unrestricted production decrypt permissions.

❌ Storing passwords or API keys in source code.

❌ Disabling key rotation without documented justification.

❌ Using wildcard principals in KMS key policies.

❌ Forgetting to monitor `kms:Decrypt` activity.

❌ Scheduling KMS key deletion without impact analysis.

❌ Manually managing public TLS certificates.

❌ Using default encryption settings without understanding ownership and governance.

❌ Treating secrets and encryption keys as the same asset.

# 💼 Business Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has completed the first phase of its AWS security architecture programme.

The organisation now operates:

- 500 AWS accounts
- 12 AWS Regions
- Production, development and sandbox environments
- A dedicated Security Tooling account
- A dedicated Log Archive account
- Amazon EC2, ECS, EKS and Lambda workloads
- Amazon S3 data lakes
- Amazon RDS and DynamoDB databases
- Internet-facing applications
- CI/CD pipelines
- Hybrid connectivity
- Third-party SaaS integrations
- Regulated financial and healthcare workloads

CloudNova has enabled several AWS security services, but its operational processes remain fragmented.

Current problems include:

- Each team monitors its own AWS accounts.
- Security findings are reviewed inconsistently.
- No central alert-severity model exists.
- Different teams classify the same event differently.
- GuardDuty findings are forwarded through email.
- CloudTrail logs are available but rarely investigated.
- AWS Config findings are treated as incidents.
- Security Hub contains thousands of unresolved findings.
- No formal alert-triage process exists.
- Analysts do not have standard investigation playbooks.
- Escalations depend on personal relationships.
- Development teams are contacted without sufficient evidence.
- High-confidence findings are not automatically contained.
- Repeated false positives are not tuned.
- Threat hunting is performed only after an incident.
- SOC performance is measured by the number of alerts closed.
- There is no formal relationship between cloud engineering and the SOC.
- Overnight security coverage is limited.
- Critical incidents may remain unreviewed for several hours.

During a weekend, Amazon GuardDuty generates a high-severity finding indicating unusual credential usage from a previously unseen country.

The finding is delivered to a shared mailbox.

No analyst reviews it for six hours.

During that period, the compromised identity:

1. Enumerates IAM roles.
2. Creates an access key.
3. Modifies a security group.
4. Launches cryptocurrency-mining instances.
5. Attempts to access sensitive S3 buckets.

The CISO asks:

> **“We have security tools, but do we have an effective security operation?”**

CloudNova must build an enterprise Security Operations Centre capable of continuously detecting, investigating, containing and learning from threats across its AWS environment.

# 1. What Is Enterprise Security Operations?

Enterprise security operations is the coordinated combination of:

- People
- Processes
- Technology
- Threat intelligence
- Governance
- Automation
- Measurement
- Continuous improvement

Its purpose is to identify and reduce cyber risk through continuous monitoring and response.

```text
Security Telemetry

↓

Detection

↓

Alert Triage

↓

Investigation

↓

Containment

↓

Recovery

↓

Lessons Learned

↓

Detection Improvement
```

Security operations is not a single AWS service.

It is an operational capability that uses multiple services, tools and teams.

# 2. Security Operations Objectives

An enterprise security-operations programme should:

- Maintain visibility across the environment.
- Detect malicious or unauthorised behaviour.
- Identify security-control failures.
- Prioritise risks using business context.
- Investigate suspicious activity.
- Contain active threats quickly.
- Preserve evidence.
- Coordinate incident response.
- Support regulatory obligations.
- Improve preventive controls.
- Reduce attacker dwell time.
- Measure security effectiveness.
- Provide leadership with reliable risk information.

# 3. Security Operations Is More Than Monitoring

Monitoring is one component of security operations.

```text
Monitoring

Observing systems and collecting telemetry

Detection

Identifying activity that may represent a threat

Triage

Determining whether the activity requires investigation

Investigation

Establishing what happened, how and to what extent

Response

Containing, eradicating and recovering

Improvement

Preventing or detecting similar activity more effectively
```

A team that only watches dashboards is not operating a complete SOC.

# 4. Security Operations Centre

A Security Operations Centre, commonly called a SOC, is the organisational function responsible for monitoring, detecting, investigating and coordinating responses to cybersecurity threats.

A SOC may be:

- A physical facility
- A virtual team
- A distributed global function
- An outsourced managed service
- A hybrid internal and external service

The effectiveness of a SOC depends more on its operating model than its physical location.

# 5. Cloud-Native Security Operations

Traditional SOCs often focused on:

- Firewalls
- Network traffic
- Endpoint antivirus
- Active Directory
- Physical data centres
- Static server infrastructure

A cloud-native SOC must additionally understand:

- AWS API activity
- IAM role sessions
- Temporary credentials
- AWS Organizations
- Service Control Policies
- Infrastructure as Code
- Serverless workloads
- Containers
- Control-plane events
- Resource policies
- Cross-account access
- Multi-Region activity
- Cloud service configurations
- Managed-service telemetry
- Short-lived infrastructure
- Shared-responsibility boundaries

# 6. Traditional SOC vs Cloud-Native SOC

| Area | Traditional SOC | Cloud-Native SOC |
|------|-----------------|------------------|
| Primary Visibility | Network and endpoints | API, identity, configuration, workload and network |
| Infrastructure | Long-lived servers | Dynamic and ephemeral resources |
| Identity | Users and service accounts | Federated users, roles, sessions and workload identities |
| Change Management | Manual or ticket-based | Infrastructure as Code and automated pipelines |
| Evidence | Disk, endpoint and firewall logs | CloudTrail, snapshots, service logs and API records |
| Containment | Isolate host or block IP | Revoke sessions, change policies, isolate resources and update controls |
| Scope | Data centre boundaries | Multiple accounts, Regions and cloud services |
| Automation | Often limited | Core operational requirement |
| Ownership | Central IT | Shared across security, cloud, DevOps and application teams |

# 7. CloudNova SOC Mission

CloudNova defines its SOC mission as:

> Protect CloudNova’s customers, workforce, data and cloud services by continuously detecting, investigating and coordinating the response to security threats across all AWS environments.

The mission is supported by five operational goals:

1. Achieve complete security visibility.
2. Detect high-impact threats quickly.
3. Prioritise alerts using business risk.
4. Contain confirmed threats safely.
5. Continuously improve detection and response.

# 8. SOC Scope

The SOC scope must be formally documented.

CloudNova’s SOC monitors:

- AWS management-plane activity
- Identity and access activity
- Network activity
- Endpoint and workload activity
- Container activity
- Data-access activity
- Security-control configuration
- Vulnerability findings
- Malware findings
- CI/CD security activity
- SaaS security events
- On-premises security events
- Third-party access
- Business-critical application events

Without a defined scope, teams may incorrectly assume that another team is monitoring a service.

# 9. Security Operations Operating Model

A SOC operating model defines:

- What the SOC is responsible for
- What it monitors
- How it receives events
- How alerts are prioritised
- Who investigates alerts
- When incidents are declared
- Who can perform containment
- How teams communicate
- How evidence is managed
- How performance is measured
- How the operation improves

```text
Governance

↓

People + Process + Technology

↓

Security Monitoring

↓

Detection and Investigation

↓

Response Coordination

↓

Measurement and Improvement
```

# 11. SOC Organisational Models

Common SOC models include:

1. Centralised SOC
2. Distributed SOC
3. Hybrid SOC
4. Virtual SOC
5. Managed SOC
6. Follow-the-sun SOC

# 12. Centralised SOC

A centralised SOC performs monitoring and investigation from one central team.

```text
Business Units

↓

Central SOC

↓

Enterprise Investigation and Response
```

## Benefits

- Consistent processes
- Centralised expertise
- Unified tooling
- Easier governance
- Standard reporting
- Central threat visibility

## Challenges

- May lack application context
- Can become a bottleneck
- May struggle with regional requirements
- Business teams may feel disconnected

# 13. Distributed SOC

A distributed model allows business units or regions to operate their own security-monitoring teams.

```text
Business Unit A SOC

Business Unit B SOC

Regional SOC

Cloud SOC
```

## Benefits

- Strong local context
- Faster contact with system owners
- Regional knowledge
- Support for local regulations

## Challenges

- Inconsistent standards
- Duplicate tooling
- Fragmented visibility
- Difficult enterprise reporting
- Uneven maturity

# 14. Hybrid SOC

A hybrid model combines central governance with distributed operational support.

```text
                         Enterprise SOC

                Standards, SIEM and Coordination

                              │

          ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
          │                   │                   │
      Cloud SOC          Regional SOC       Product Security
          │                   │                   │
          └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                              │
                     Shared Incident Process
```

CloudNova chooses a hybrid model.

The central SOC manages:

- Enterprise monitoring standards
- SIEM and Security Lake
- Incident coordination
- Detection engineering
- Threat intelligence
- Executive reporting
- Major-incident management

Cloud-specialist teams provide:

- AWS technical investigation
- Cloud containment
- IAM analysis
- Infrastructure-as-Code review
- Service-specific expertise

Application teams provide:

- Business context
- Application ownership
- Remediation
- Recovery validation

# 15. Follow-the-Sun Security Operations

A follow-the-sun model transfers active monitoring between global teams.

Example:

```text
India SOC

08:00–16:00 IST

↓

Europe SOC

08:00–16:00 GMT

↓

Americas SOC

08:00–16:00 Local Time

↓

India SOC
```

Benefits include:

- Continuous coverage
- Reduced overnight staffing
- Better regional expertise
- Improved analyst wellbeing

Risks include:

- Poor shift handovers
- Inconsistent processes
- Ownership confusion
- Delayed escalation
- Loss of investigation context

A standard handover process is essential.

# 17. Tier 1 SOC Analyst

Tier 1 analysts typically:

- Monitor alert queues.
- Validate alert completeness.
- Review basic contextual information.
- Eliminate known benign activity.
- Follow triage procedures.
- Collect initial evidence.
- Enrich alerts.
- Assign severity and priority.
- Escalate suspicious cases.
- Document actions.

Tier 1 analysts should not simply close alerts to reduce queue size.

# 18. Tier 2 SOC Analyst

Tier 2 analysts typically:

- Investigate escalated alerts.
- Correlate activity across data sources.
- Review AWS identity and API events.
- Analyse affected resources.
- Determine potential attack scope.
- Recommend containment actions.
- Contact system owners.
- Create incident cases.
- Preserve relevant evidence.
- Support remediation.

# 19. Tier 3 Analyst

Tier 3 analysts handle:

- Advanced persistent threats
- Complex identity compromises
- Cross-account attack paths
- Malware analysis
- Cloud privilege escalation
- Threat hunting
- Detection gaps
- Forensic analysis
- High-impact incident support
- New attacker techniques

Tier 3 may include specialists rather than a single team.

# 20. Detection Engineer

A detection engineer converts threats and attack techniques into monitorable logic.

Responsibilities include:

- Identifying detection requirements
- Defining telemetry dependencies
- Writing detection rules
- Testing detections
- Mapping rules to MITRE ATT&CK
- Measuring detection performance
- Tuning false positives
- Maintaining rule documentation
- Retiring obsolete detections
- Conducting detection gap assessments

# 21. Threat Hunter

A threat hunter searches for malicious activity that has not generated a reliable alert.

Threat hunting is:

- Hypothesis-driven
- Evidence-based
- Repeatable
- Documented
- Intelligence-informed

Example hypothesis:

> An attacker using compromised developer credentials may enumerate IAM roles before attempting privilege escalation.

The hunter searches for:

- Unusual `ListRoles` activity
- `GetRole` across many roles
- `SimulatePrincipalPolicy`
- Unexpected `AssumeRole`
- New access keys
- Changes to trust policies

# 22. Incident Responder

Incident responders coordinate:

- Incident declaration
- Containment
- Evidence preservation
- Technical investigation
- Stakeholder communication
- Eradication
- Recovery
- Post-incident review

Not every SOC alert becomes an incident.

The incident responder becomes involved when the event meets the incident-declaration criteria.

# 24. Security Event Terminology

A mature SOC uses consistent terminology.

# Security Event

A security event is an observable occurrence relevant to security.

Examples:

- IAM role assumed
- Security group changed
- S3 object accessed
- GuardDuty finding generated
- KMS key disabled

An event does not automatically indicate malicious activity.

# Security Alert

An alert is a notification generated because an event or group of events matches a detection condition.

Example:

```text
Event:
An IAM role was assumed.

Alert:
The role was assumed from an unusual country and immediately created an access key.
```

# Security Finding

A finding is a structured observation generated by a security service or assessment tool.

Examples:

- GuardDuty finding
- Security Hub finding
- Inspector vulnerability
- IAM Access Analyzer finding
- AWS Config non-compliance result

A finding may represent:

- A threat
- A vulnerability
- A misconfiguration
- External access
- Compliance failure

# Security Case

A case is the investigation record used to document:

- Alert details
- Evidence
- Analyst actions
- Timeline
- Decisions
- Communication
- Resolution

# Security Incident

A security incident is a confirmed or reasonably suspected event that threatens:

- Confidentiality
- Integrity
- Availability
- Business operations
- Regulatory obligations
- Customer trust

```text
Event

↓

Alert or Finding

↓

Triage

↓

Investigation

↓

Confirmed Security Impact

↓

Incident
```

# 26. Alert Triage

# 27. Triage Questions

An analyst should ask:

1. What generated the alert?
2. Which account and Region are involved?
3. Which identity performed the activity?
4. Was the identity federated, human or workload-based?
5. What source IP address was used?
6. Is the source expected?
7. What resource was affected?
8. Is the resource production or development?
9. Is sensitive data involved?
10. Is the activity part of an approved change?
11. Has similar activity occurred before?
12. Are other alerts related?

# 29. Severity vs Priority

Severity and priority are related but different.

## Severity

Severity represents the potential or actual technical impact.

## Priority

Priority represents how urgently the organisation must respond.

Example:

A technically severe finding in an unused sandbox account may receive a lower response priority than a medium-severity finding affecting a production payment system.

# 30. CloudNova Alert-Severity Model

| Severity | Description | Example |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| Critical | Confirmed or imminent major compromise | Root credential compromise |
| High | Strong evidence of malicious activity or major control failure | Privileged credential used from a hostile location |
| Medium | Suspicious activity requiring investigation | Unusual API enumeration |
| Low | Limited-risk anomaly or policy deviation | Non-sensitive configuration change |
| Informational | Security-relevant activity with no immediate risk | Approved administrative role assumption |

# 31. CloudNova Incident-Priority Model

| Priority | Business Meaning | Initial Response Target |
|----------|------------------|-------------------------|
| P1 | Critical business or security impact | Immediate |
| P2 | Major impact or credible active threat | Within 30 minutes |
| P3 | Moderate impact requiring investigation | Within 4 hours |
| P4 | Low impact or routine security issue | Within 1 business day |
| P5 | Informational or improvement activity | Planned backlog |

The organisation must define response targets that reflect its staffing and business obligations.

# 32. Risk-Based Prioritisation

CloudNova evaluates:

```text
Alert Confidence

×

Asset Criticality

×

Potential Impact

×

Threat Activity

×

Exposure

=

Operational Priority
```

This is a conceptual model rather than a universal mathematical formula.

Factors include:

- Is the alert high confidence?
- Is the affected asset internet-facing?
- Does the resource contain restricted data?
- Is a privileged identity involved?
- Is the activity ongoing?
- Is the account production?
- Is an attacker known to exploit this behaviour?
- Can the activity spread across accounts?
- Are preventive controls disabled?

# 33. False Positive, Benign Positive and True Positive

## False Positive

The detection fired, but the activity did not meet the intended detection condition.

Example:

A parser incorrectly identified an AWS service IP as malicious.

## Benign Positive

The detection correctly identified the behaviour, but the behaviour was authorised.

Example:

An approved penetration test generated reconnaissance alerts.

## True Positive

The detection correctly identified suspicious or malicious activity.

Example:

A compromised role created an unauthorised access key.

These classifications support detection tuning.

# 34. False Negative

A false negative occurs when malicious activity is not detected.

False negatives are especially dangerous because they may remain invisible.

Causes include:

- Missing telemetry
- Disabled logging
- Incorrect detection logic
- Unsupported service
- Evasion technique
- Excessive threshold
- Parsing failure
- Detection disabled
- Analyst oversight

# 35. Alert Fatigue

Alert fatigue occurs when analysts receive more alerts than they can effectively review.

Symptoms include:

- Large alert backlogs
- Rapid alert closure
- Missed critical alerts
- Low analyst morale
- Inconsistent investigations
- Excessive false positives
- Reliance on severity labels without context

Alert fatigue is not solved by hiring analysts alone.

It requires:

- Better detections
- Better enrichment
- Risk-based prioritisation
- Automation
- Rule tuning
- Alert suppression
- Ownership
- Telemetry quality

# 56. Indicator-Based Detection

Indicator-based detection looks for known malicious values.

Examples:

- Malicious IP address
- Known malware hash
- Suspicious domain
- Known attacker user agent

Benefits:

- High confidence when current
- Easy to implement

Limitations:

- Indicators change quickly
- Attackers can rotate infrastructure
- May detect only known threats

# 57. Behaviour-Based Detection

Behaviour-based detection identifies suspicious actions or patterns.

Example:

```text
Normal Developer Behaviour

Uses approved Region
Assumes development role
Works during normal hours

Suspicious Behaviour

Signs in from new country
Enumerates IAM roles
Assumes production role
Creates access key
Disables logging
```

Behavioural detections can identify attacks without relying on a known malicious IP address.

# 58. Sequence-Based Detection

Some attacks become visible only when events are correlated.

Example sequence:

```text
ConsoleLogin

↓

ListRoles

↓

AssumeRole

↓

CreateAccessKey

↓

PutRolePolicy
```

Each individual event may be legitimate.

The sequence may indicate privilege escalation and persistence.

# 81. Why Alert Count Is a Weak Metric

Closing a large number of alerts does not necessarily indicate effective security.

- Did the SOC detect important threats?
- Were critical incidents contained quickly?
- Did alerts include sufficient context?
- Are repeat incidents decreasing?
- Is detection coverage improving?
- Are business-critical assets monitored?
- Are false negatives being identified?

# 🔍 Troubleshooting

## Problem — Too Many Security Alerts

Review:

- Duplicate findings
- Repeated low-value detections
- Missing suppression rules
- Missing business context
- Broad detection conditions
- Test or development activity
- Vulnerability findings treated as active incidents
- Findings duplicated across tools
- Poor severity mapping

Do not disable a detection simply because it creates many alerts.

Determine whether:

- The environment has a real control problem.
- The detection needs tuning.
- The activity should be prevented.
- The alerts should be grouped into one case.

## Problem — Analysts Are Missing Critical Alerts

Review:

- Queue prioritisation
- On-call notifications
- Severity mapping
- Alert enrichment
- Staffing
- Shift coverage
- Alert backlog
- Case assignment
- Dashboard design
- Escalation rules
- Tool availability

## Problem — Findings Are Not Reaching the Central SOC

Review:

- Delegated administrator configuration
- Member-account enrolment
- Region enablement
- Security Hub integrations
- EventBridge rule
- Event-bus permissions
- Cross-account role
- Encryption permissions
- SIEM ingestion
- Network connectivity
- Log-delivery status

## Problem — The SOC Cannot Determine Resource Ownership

Review:

- Resource tags
- Account metadata
- Application catalogue
- Configuration-management database
- Infrastructure-as-Code repository
- Organisational Unit
- Cost-centre mapping
- Deployment-pipeline metadata

Resource ownership should be established before an incident occurs.

## Problem — Every Alert Is Marked High Severity

Review:

- Severity criteria
- Vendor default severity
- Business context
- Asset criticality
- Confidence level
- Exposure
- Data sensitivity
- Threat activity

Severity must support prioritisation rather than eliminate it.

## Problem — Security Automation Causes Business Disruption

Review:

- Detection confidence
- Approval workflow
- Resource criticality
- Testing
- Rollback
- Exception handling
- Change management
- Automation permissions
- Idempotency
- Failure state

Move high-impact actions to analyst-assisted automation until confidence improves.

## Problem — Shift Handover Loses Investigation Context

Review:

- Case documentation
- Handover template
- Assigned owner
- Timeline quality
- Evidence references
- Pending decisions
- Communication log
- Next required action

## Problem — Analysts Close Alerts Without Investigation Notes

Review:

- Case-management requirements
- Quality reviews
- Analyst training
- Queue pressure
- Performance metrics
- Closure-reason options
- Manager oversight

Do not reward analysts only for closure volume.

## Problem — Threat Hunting Produces No Findings

No findings does not automatically mean the hunt failed.

Review:

- Hypothesis quality
- Telemetry coverage
- Query accuracy
- Search period
- Data retention
- Time-zone handling
- Identity mapping
- Region coverage

A hunt may still identify:

- Telemetry gaps
- Detection opportunities
- Logging failures
- Required control improvements

# 🏢 Enterprise Best Practices

CloudNova establishes the following standards:

- Define a formal SOC mission and scope.
- Document security-operations authority.
- Monitor every production AWS account and approved Region.
- Centralise security findings and investigation workflows.
- Use a consistent event, alert, finding and incident vocabulary.
- Separate severity from response priority.
- Enrich alerts with identity, asset and business context.
- Use risk-based alert prioritisation.
- Maintain documented triage and escalation procedures.
- Assign named owners to active cases.
- Maintain 24×7 coverage for critical environments.
- Use structured shift handovers.
- Develop playbooks for high-risk AWS scenarios.
- Maintain technical runbooks for containment actions.
- Preserve evidence in protected storage.
- Record chain-of-custody information where required.
- Establish a formal detection-engineering lifecycle.
- Map detections to known attacker techniques.
- Manage detections through version control.
- Test detections before and after deployment.
- Tune detections without hiding genuine risk.
- Conduct regular threat-hunting exercises.
- Automate enrichment before automating containment.
- Require approval for high-impact response actions.
- Test automation rollback procedures.
- Monitor the health of security telemetry.
- Measure security outcomes, not only alert volume.
- Conduct case-quality reviews.
- Train analysts in AWS architecture and identity.
- Review SOC maturity at least annually.
- Feed incident lessons into architecture and detection improvements.

# 🚫 Common Mistakes

❌ Purchasing a SIEM and assuming the SOC is complete.

❌ Sending all security findings to email.

❌ Treating every finding as an incident.

❌ Using vendor severity without business context.

❌ Measuring analysts only by alerts closed.

❌ Ignoring telemetry health.

❌ Monitoring only the primary AWS Region.

❌ Failing to monitor sandbox and development accounts.

❌ Allowing alert backlogs to grow without risk-based review.

❌ Closing benign positives without tuning detections.

❌ Suppressing alerts without documented justification.

❌ Escalating alerts without sufficient evidence.

❌ Contacting application teams without a clear request.

❌ Automating destructive containment too early.

❌ Failing to test playbooks.

❌ Maintaining outdated contact lists.

❌ Performing threat hunting only after an incident.

❌ Failing to preserve cloud evidence.

❌ Losing investigation context during shift changes.

❌ Treating AWS Config non-compliance as proof of compromise.

❌ Ignoring identity and control-plane activity.

❌ Failing to involve cloud specialists in investigations.

❌ Using one investigation process for every alert type.

❌ Reporting alert volume as the primary security outcome.
