# Lesson 04 — Kubernetes Worker Nodes

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand the purpose of Kubernetes Worker Nodes
- Identify the components running on every Worker Node
- Explain how workloads are executed
- Understand the interaction between Worker Nodes and the Control Plane
- Identify common security risks affecting Worker Nodes
- Apply enterprise best practices for securing Worker Nodes

---

# Why This Matters

The Control Plane makes decisions.

Worker Nodes perform the actual work.

Every application, microservice, API, and container running inside Kubernetes executes on a Worker Node.

If an attacker compromises a Worker Node, they may gain access to:

- Running containers
- Kubernetes Secrets
- Service Account tokens
- Customer workloads
- Sensitive application data
- Cloud credentials

This is why Worker Node security is one of the most critical responsibilities of a Kubernetes Security Engineer.

---

# What is a Worker Node?

A Worker Node is a server—physical or virtual—that runs containerised applications.

Worker Nodes receive instructions from the Control Plane and execute workloads.

A Kubernetes cluster typically contains multiple Worker Nodes to provide:

- High availability
- Scalability
- Load balancing
- Fault tolerance
- Resource optimisation

---

# Kubernetes Cluster Architecture

```text
                Control Plane
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        │            │            │
        ▼            ▼            ▼
   Worker 1     Worker 2     Worker 3
        │            │            │
      Pods         Pods         Pods
```

Applications run only on Worker Nodes.

---

# Components of a Worker Node

Every Worker Node contains four primary components.

| Component | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| kubelet | Communicates with the Control Plane |
| kube-proxy | Manages networking |
| Container Runtime | Runs containers |
| Pods | Execute applications |

Together these components enable Kubernetes to run workloads efficiently.

---

# kubelet

The kubelet is the primary Kubernetes agent running on every Worker Node.

Its responsibilities include:

- Registering the node with the Control Plane
- Receiving instructions from the API Server
- Starting containers
- Monitoring Pod health
- Restarting failed workloads
- Reporting node status
- Managing resource utilisation

Without kubelet, a Worker Node cannot participate in the cluster.

---

# kubelet Communication

```text
API Server

↓

kubelet

↓

Container Runtime

↓

Pods
```

The kubelet continuously communicates with the API Server to ensure that the node matches the desired cluster state.

---

# Container Runtime

The Container Runtime is responsible for executing containers.

Modern Kubernetes environments commonly use:

- containerd
- CRI-O

Earlier Kubernetes versions frequently used Docker, but containerd is now the standard runtime for most enterprise deployments.

The Container Runtime:

- Downloads images
- Starts containers
- Stops containers
- Restarts containers
- Reports container status

---

# kube-proxy

kube-proxy manages networking on every Worker Node.

It is responsible for:

- Routing traffic
- Load balancing
- Service discovery
- Network forwarding
- Maintaining network rules

Without kube-proxy, Pods would not be able to communicate reliably.

---

# Pods on Worker Nodes

Worker Nodes execute Pods.

A Pod may contain:

- One application container
- Multiple tightly coupled containers

Example:

```text
Worker Node

│

├── Pod A
│     ├── Web Server
│     └── Logging Sidecar
│
├── Pod B
│     └── API
│
└── Pod C
      └── Database Agent
```

Pods share resources such as networking and storage within the same Pod.

---

# Worker Node Lifecycle

The lifecycle of a Worker Node follows these steps:

```text
Node Created

↓

Registers with Control Plane

↓

Receives Workloads

↓

Runs Containers

↓

Reports Health

↓

Handles Updates

↓

Removed or Replaced
```

Modern Kubernetes environments frequently replace Worker Nodes automatically rather than repairing them.

---

# Node Registration

When a Worker Node joins the cluster:

1. kubelet starts.
2. The node authenticates with the API Server.
3. The API Server validates the node.
4. The Scheduler begins assigning Pods.
5. Applications start running.

Only trusted Worker Nodes should be allowed to join the cluster.

---

# Managed Worker Nodes in Amazon EKS

In Amazon EKS, Worker Nodes can be managed in several ways.

### Managed Node Groups

AWS automatically manages:

- Operating system updates
- Node lifecycle
- Scaling
- Integration with EKS

---

### Self-Managed Nodes

The organisation manages:

- Operating system
- Patching
- Scaling
- Security configuration
- Maintenance

Managed Node Groups reduce operational overhead while still requiring workload-level security controls.

---

# How Workloads Reach a Worker Node

```text
Developer Deploys Application

↓

API Server

↓

Scheduler

↓

Worker Node Selected

↓

kubelet Receives Instructions

↓

Container Runtime Starts Pod

↓

Application Running
```

The Worker Node does not decide where Pods run—it only executes the assigned workload.

---

# Worker Node Security Risks

Common risks include:

- Unpatched operating systems
- Privileged containers
- Root access
- Weak SSH controls
- Container escape vulnerabilities
- Exposed kubelet APIs
- Excessive IAM permissions
- Malware infections
- Cryptomining attacks
- Unencrypted disks

Compromising a Worker Node can often lead to broader cluster compromise.

---

# Container Escape

One of the most serious threats is a container escape.

```text
Container

↓

Operating System

↓

Worker Node

↓

Other Containers

↓

Entire Cluster
```

If an attacker escapes from a container to the underlying host, they may gain control of other workloads running on the same node.

Preventing container escape is a key security objective.

---

# Worker Node Hardening

Enterprise security teams should:

- Keep operating systems patched
- Use hardened AMIs
- Remove unnecessary software
- Disable unused services
- Restrict SSH access
- Enable disk encryption
- Protect kubelet
- Apply least privilege IAM
- Enable secure boot where available
- Monitor system activity

Hardening significantly reduces the attack surface.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams continuously monitor Worker Nodes for:

- Unusual processes
- Cryptomining activity
- Container escapes
- High CPU utilisation
- Unexpected network connections
- Failed kubelet authentication
- Suspicious file changes
- Malware indicators
- Unauthorised software installations

Runtime monitoring enables early detection of attacks.

---

# Enterprise Example

A company hosts its online banking platform on Amazon EKS.

Each Worker Node runs:

- Payment services
- Customer APIs
- Authentication services
- Fraud detection applications

Security engineers implement:

- Managed Node Groups
- Encrypted EBS volumes
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- Runtime threat detection
- Vulnerability scanning
- Automated patching
- Continuous monitoring

These controls reduce the risk of compromise while maintaining availability.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use Managed Node Groups where appropriate
- Patch Worker Nodes regularly
- Disable unnecessary services
- Encrypt storage volumes
- Protect kubelet authentication
- Restrict administrative access
- Use least privilege IAM permissions
- Monitor runtime behaviour
- Scan workloads continuously
- Replace compromised nodes instead of repairing them

Treat Worker Nodes as critical production infrastructure.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- The purpose of Kubernetes Worker Nodes
- The role of kubelet
- The function of kube-proxy
- How the Container Runtime executes workloads
- How Worker Nodes communicate with the Control Plane
- Common Worker Node security risks
- Enterprise hardening and monitoring best practices

Understanding Worker Nodes provides the foundation for learning how Kubernetes schedules and secures workloads.

---

# Knowledge Check

### Question 1

Which component communicates directly with the Kubernetes API Server?

- A. kube-proxy
- B. kubelet
- C. Pod
- D. Deployment

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 2

Which component is responsible for running containers?

- A. Scheduler
- B. API Server
- C. Container Runtime
- D. Deployment

**Answer:** C

---

### Question 3

Which component manages networking on a Worker Node?

- A. kubelet
- B. kube-proxy
- C. etcd
- D. ReplicaSet

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 4

Which of the following is a common security risk for Worker Nodes?

- A. SQL Injection
- B. Container Escape
- C. DNS Spoofing
- D. Cross-Site Scripting

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 5

Which AWS feature simplifies the management of Kubernetes Worker Nodes?

- A. AWS Lambda
- B. Amazon RDS
- C. Amazon EKS Managed Node Groups
- D. Amazon CloudFront

**Answer:** C

---

# What's Next?

In the next lesson, you will learn about **Pods**, the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. You will explore Pod architecture, multi-container Pods, lifecycle management, and the security controls required to protect workloads running inside Pods.

Learn how Kubernetes Pods, ReplicaSets, and Deployments work together to run highly available, scalable, and secure applications in enterprise Kubernetes environments.

# Lesson 05 — Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what Pods are
- Explain the relationship between Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments
- Understand the lifecycle of a Pod
- Learn how Kubernetes provides high availability
- Identify common security risks affecting workloads
- Apply enterprise best practices for managing Kubernetes workloads securely

---

# Why This Matters

Applications running in Kubernetes are not deployed directly onto Worker Nodes.

Instead, Kubernetes deploys applications inside **Pods**, which are managed by **ReplicaSets**, which in turn are managed by **Deployments**.

This layered architecture enables Kubernetes to provide:

- High availability
- Automatic recovery
- Rolling updates
- Zero-downtime deployments
- Self-healing
- Easy scaling

Understanding these components is essential for designing secure and resilient Kubernetes environments.

---

# Kubernetes Workload Hierarchy

The relationship between these components can be visualised as:

```text
Deployment
      │
      ▼
ReplicaSet
      │
      ▼
Pods
      │
      ▼
Containers
      │
      ▼
Application
```

Each layer has a specific responsibility within Kubernetes.

---

# What is a Pod?

A **Pod** is the smallest deployable object in Kubernetes.

A Pod provides an isolated environment where one or more containers run together.

Pods share:

- Network namespace
- IP address
- Storage volumes
- Hostname
- Linux namespaces

A Pod represents a single running instance of an application.

---

# Pod Architecture

```text
Pod
│
├── Application Container
│
├── Sidecar Container
│
└── Shared Storage
```

Most Pods contain a single container.

However, enterprise applications often use multiple containers within the same Pod.

---

# Multi-Container Pods

Large organisations frequently deploy multiple containers inside a single Pod.

Example:

```text
Pod

├── Web Application

├── Log Collector

└── Monitoring Agent
```

Each container performs a dedicated role while sharing networking and storage resources.

---

# Pod Lifecycle

Every Pod progresses through a series of lifecycle phases.

```text
Pending

↓

Running

↓

Succeeded

↓

Failed

↓

Terminated
```

Pods are considered **ephemeral**, meaning they are temporary by design.

If a Pod fails, Kubernetes replaces it rather than repairing it.

---

# Pod States

| State | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Pending | Pod has been accepted but is not yet running |
| Running | Containers are executing successfully |
| Succeeded | Workload completed successfully |
| Failed | Workload terminated unexpectedly |
| Unknown | Kubernetes cannot determine the Pod status |

Monitoring Pod states helps identify application issues and security events.

---

# Pod Scheduling

When a Pod is created:

```text
Deployment

↓

ReplicaSet

↓

Scheduler

↓

Worker Node Selected

↓

Pod Created

↓

Container Started
```

The Kubernetes Scheduler selects the most suitable Worker Node based on available resources and scheduling policies.

---

# What is a ReplicaSet?

A **ReplicaSet** ensures that a specified number of identical Pods are always running.

Example:

Desired State:

```text
3 Pods
```

Current State:

```text
2 Pods
```

ReplicaSet automatically creates another Pod.

This enables Kubernetes' self-healing capability.

---

# ReplicaSet Example

```text
ReplicaSet

│

├── Pod 1

├── Pod 2

└── Pod 3
```

If Pod 2 fails:

```text
ReplicaSet

│

├── Pod 1

├── Pod 3

└── New Pod Created
```

The application remains available without administrator intervention.

---

# Scaling with ReplicaSets

ReplicaSets also provide horizontal scaling.

Example:

```text
Current Pods

3

↓

Traffic Increases

↓

Scale to

10 Pods
```

Kubernetes automatically distributes traffic across all running Pods.

---

# What is a Deployment?

A Deployment is the highest-level workload controller.

It manages ReplicaSets and provides enterprise deployment capabilities.

A Deployment enables:

- Rolling updates
- Rollbacks
- Scaling
- Self-healing
- Version control
- Declarative configuration

Enterprise applications are almost always deployed using Deployments.

---

# Deployment Architecture

```text
Deployment

│

▼

ReplicaSet

│

├── Pod

├── Pod

├── Pod

└── Pod
```

The Deployment monitors the ReplicaSet, which manages the Pods.

---

# Rolling Updates

Rolling updates allow applications to be upgraded without downtime.

Example:

```text
Version 1

↓

Update Initiated

↓

Pods Updated One by One

↓

Version 2 Running
```

Users continue accessing the application throughout the update process.

---

# Rollbacks

If a deployment introduces issues, Kubernetes allows administrators to revert to a previous version.

```text
Version 1

↓

Version 2

↓

Application Failure

↓

Rollback

↓

Version 1 Restored
```

Rollbacks minimise service disruption.

---

# High Availability

Deployments improve application availability by distributing Pods across multiple Worker Nodes.

```text
Worker Node 1

├── Pod A

├── Pod B

Worker Node 2

├── Pod C

├── Pod D

Worker Node 3

├── Pod E
```

If one Worker Node fails, Pods are recreated on healthy nodes.

---

# Enterprise Example

An online banking platform deploys:

- 12 Web Pods
- 8 Authentication Pods
- 6 Payment Pods

Each application is managed by a Deployment.

If a Worker Node fails:

- Pods are recreated automatically
- Customers continue accessing online banking
- No administrator intervention is required

This demonstrates Kubernetes' self-healing and high availability capabilities.

---

# Pod Security Risks

Common Pod security issues include:

- Running containers as root
- Privileged containers
- Exposed Secrets
- Untrusted container images
- Excessive Linux capabilities
- Insecure volume mounts
- HostPath usage
- Missing resource limits
- Outdated container images

These risks can increase the likelihood of workload compromise.

---

# Security Risks in Deployments

Poorly configured Deployments may:

- Use vulnerable container images
- Grant excessive permissions
- Expose internal services
- Deploy outdated software
- Allow unrestricted network access
- Store credentials insecurely

Security reviews should be part of every deployment pipeline.

---

# Enterprise Security Best Practices

Cloud Security Engineers should:

- Deploy trusted container images only
- Scan images before deployment
- Run containers as non-root
- Implement Pod Security Standards
- Configure resource requests and limits
- Restrict Linux capabilities
- Avoid privileged containers
- Use read-only root filesystems where possible
- Enable runtime monitoring
- Apply least privilege to Service Accounts

These practices reduce the attack surface while improving workload resilience.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should continuously monitor:

- Pod creation events
- Pod deletions
- CrashLoopBackOff errors
- Unexpected restarts
- Failed deployments
- Image changes
- ReplicaSet modifications
- Scaling events
- Resource consumption
- Runtime anomalies

Continuous monitoring enables early detection of operational and security issues.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What a Pod is
- How ReplicaSets maintain application availability
- How Deployments manage application lifecycle
- How rolling updates and rollbacks work
- The importance of self-healing and high availability
- Common workload security risks
- Enterprise best practices for securing Kubernetes workloads

These concepts form the foundation for managing secure and resilient applications in Kubernetes.

---

# Knowledge Check

### Question 1

What is the smallest deployable object in Kubernetes?

- A. Node
- B. ReplicaSet
- C. Pod
- D. Deployment

**Answer:** C

---

### Question 2

Which Kubernetes object ensures that a specified number of Pods are always running?

- A. Service
- B. ReplicaSet
- C. Namespace
- D. ConfigMap

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 3

Which Kubernetes object manages ReplicaSets and provides rolling updates?

- A. Deployment
- B. Scheduler
- C. kubelet
- D. Service

**Answer:** A

---

### Question 4

What happens if one Pod managed by a ReplicaSet fails?

- A. The application stops permanently.
- B. Kubernetes automatically creates a replacement Pod.
- C. The Worker Node shuts down.
- D. The Deployment is deleted.

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 5

Which of the following is considered a Pod security best practice?

- A. Run all containers as root.
- B. Use privileged containers by default.
- C. Deploy only trusted and scanned container images.
- D. Disable resource limits.

**Answer:** C

---

# What's Next?

In the next lesson, you will learn about **Kubernetes Services and Networking**, exploring how Pods communicate with each other, how applications are exposed internally and externally, and how networking is secured in enterprise Kubernetes environments.

# Lesson 06 — Services & Networking

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand Kubernetes networking fundamentals
- Explain how Pods communicate
- Understand the purpose of Kubernetes Services
- Differentiate between Service types
- Learn how traffic flows inside a Kubernetes cluster
- Identify networking security risks
- Apply enterprise networking best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Applications rarely consist of a single container.

Modern enterprise applications are built using dozens—or even hundreds—of microservices that must communicate securely and reliably.

For example:

- Web applications communicate with APIs.
- APIs communicate with databases.
- Authentication services communicate with identity providers.
- Payment services communicate with external gateways.

Kubernetes networking enables these services to communicate while maintaining scalability, reliability, and security.

Understanding Kubernetes networking is essential before learning Network Policies and Zero Trust networking in later modules.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Principles

Kubernetes networking is based on four key principles:

- Every Pod receives its own IP address.
- Pods can communicate with each other without Network Address Translation (NAT).
- Nodes can communicate with all Pods.
- Applications communicate using Services rather than Pod IP addresses.

These principles simplify application deployment and scaling.

---

# High-Level Networking Architecture

```text
                Internet
                    │
                    ▼
          Load Balancer / Ingress
                    │
                    ▼
              Kubernetes Service
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
       Pod A              Pod B
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
                Database
```

Traffic flows through Services before reaching application Pods.

---

# Pod Networking

Every Pod receives:

- Its own IP address
- A hostname
- Network namespace
- Shared networking within the Pod

Example:

```text
Worker Node

│

├── Pod A (10.0.1.10)

├── Pod B (10.0.1.11)

└── Pod C (10.0.1.12)
```

Pods communicate directly using their IP addresses.

However, Pod IPs are temporary.

---

# Why Pod IP Addresses Cannot Be Trusted

Pods are ephemeral.

When a Pod is deleted or recreated, its IP address changes.

Example:

```text
Old Pod

10.0.1.15

↓

Pod Deleted

↓

New Pod

10.0.2.34
```

Applications should never depend directly on Pod IP addresses.

This is why Kubernetes Services exist.

---

# What is a Kubernetes Service?

A Service provides a stable network endpoint for accessing one or more Pods.

Instead of connecting directly to a Pod, applications communicate through a Service.

Benefits include:

- Stable IP address
- DNS name
- Load balancing
- Automatic discovery
- High availability

---

# Service Architecture

```text
Application

↓

Service

↓

Pod 1

Pod 2

Pod 3
```

Even if Pods are replaced, the Service remains unchanged.

---

# Types of Kubernetes Services

Kubernetes provides four primary Service types.

| Service Type | Purpose |
|--------------|---------|
| ClusterIP | Internal communication within the cluster |
| NodePort | Exposes applications through Worker Node ports |
| LoadBalancer | Integrates with cloud load balancers |
| ExternalName | Maps a Service to an external DNS name |

Each type serves different networking requirements.

---

# ClusterIP

ClusterIP is the default Service type.

It allows applications inside the cluster to communicate securely.

Example:

```text
Frontend

↓

ClusterIP Service

↓

Backend API
```

ClusterIP is not accessible from the internet.

---

# NodePort

NodePort exposes an application using a port on every Worker Node.

Example:

```text
Internet

↓

Worker Node

Port 30080

↓

Application
```

NodePort is commonly used in development environments but is less common in enterprise production due to security considerations.

---

# LoadBalancer

In cloud environments such as Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, or Google GKE, a LoadBalancer Service provisions a cloud-native load balancer automatically.

```text
Internet

↓

AWS Load Balancer

↓

Kubernetes Service

↓

Pods
```

This is the preferred approach for exposing production applications.

---

# ExternalName

ExternalName allows Kubernetes Services to reference external resources.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

ExternalName Service

↓

database.company.com
```

No proxying occurs; Kubernetes returns the external DNS name.

---

# Kubernetes DNS

Every Service automatically receives a DNS name.

Example:

```text
payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local
```

Applications communicate using DNS rather than IP addresses.

Benefits include:

- Stable communication
- Easier application configuration
- Automatic service discovery

---

# kube-proxy

Every Worker Node runs kube-proxy.

Responsibilities include:

- Routing traffic
- Load balancing requests
- Managing Service rules
- Updating networking tables
- Forwarding requests to healthy Pods

kube-proxy ensures that traffic reaches the correct application.

---

# Container Network Interface (CNI)

The Container Network Interface (CNI) provides networking for Pods.

Popular CNI implementations include:

- Amazon VPC CNI
- Calico
- Cilium
- Flannel
- Weave Net

In Amazon EKS, the default option is the Amazon VPC CNI plugin.

---

# How Traffic Flows Through Kubernetes

```text
User

↓

Internet

↓

Load Balancer

↓

Service

↓

kube-proxy

↓

Pod

↓

Application

↓

Response
```

Each component contributes to delivering traffic securely and efficiently.

---

# Internal vs External Communication

Internal communication:

```text
Pod

↓

ClusterIP Service

↓

Pod
```

External communication:

```text
Internet

↓

Load Balancer

↓

Service

↓

Application
```

Separating internal and external traffic improves security.

---

# Enterprise Example

A banking application consists of:

- Web Frontend
- Authentication API
- Payments API
- Fraud Detection Service
- Customer Database

Communication occurs as follows:

```text
Customer

↓

Load Balancer

↓

Frontend Service

↓

Authentication Service

↓

Payment Service

↓

Database
```

Each component communicates through Kubernetes Services rather than directly to individual Pods.

---

# Common Networking Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently encounter:

- Publicly exposed Services
- Unrestricted NodePorts
- Missing Network Policies
- Weak DNS controls
- Insecure Ingress configurations
- Excessive east-west traffic
- Open cloud Security Groups
- Misconfigured load balancers
- Exposed internal APIs
- Lack of TLS encryption

These issues increase the cluster's attack surface.

---

# Enterprise Networking Best Practices

Security engineers should:

- Use ClusterIP for internal applications.
- Use LoadBalancer only when external access is required.
- Avoid unnecessary NodePort Services.
- Encrypt traffic with TLS.
- Implement Network Policies.
- Restrict ingress and egress traffic.
- Use DNS instead of Pod IP addresses.
- Enable logging and monitoring.
- Secure cloud load balancers.
- Apply Zero Trust networking principles.

These practices reduce the likelihood of unauthorised access.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Service creation
- Service deletion
- Load Balancer changes
- DNS failures
- Network latency
- Unusual east-west traffic
- NodePort usage
- Failed connections
- Traffic spikes
- External exposure of internal services

Monitoring provides visibility into networking behaviour and potential threats.

---

# Real-World Example

An attacker scans an organisation's public IP addresses and discovers a NodePort Service exposing an internal administration application.

Because authentication is weak, the attacker gains access to the application and moves laterally through the Kubernetes environment.

If the organisation had:

- Used a ClusterIP Service
- Restricted external exposure
- Implemented an Ingress Controller with authentication
- Applied Network Policies

the attack surface would have been significantly reduced.

---

# Best Practices Summary

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use Services instead of Pod IP addresses.
- Prefer ClusterIP for internal communication.
- Expose applications using secure Load Balancers.
- Limit NodePort usage.
- Protect DNS infrastructure.
- Enable TLS for all application traffic.
- Implement Network Policies.
- Monitor network traffic continuously.
- Review exposed Services regularly.
- Follow Zero Trust networking principles.

Secure networking is a foundational component of every production Kubernetes environment.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- How Kubernetes networking works
- Why Services are required
- The four Kubernetes Service types
- How Pods communicate
- The role of kube-proxy
- The importance of DNS and service discovery
- Enterprise networking best practices
- Common networking security risks

These concepts prepare you for implementing secure communication between workloads before moving on to Namespaces and network segmentation.

---

# Knowledge Check

### Question 1

Why should applications avoid communicating directly with Pod IP addresses?

- A. Pod IP addresses are encrypted
- B. Pod IP addresses change when Pods are recreated
- C. Pods cannot communicate over IP
- D. Services do not support IP addresses

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 2

Which Kubernetes Service type is used for internal cluster communication?

- A. LoadBalancer
- B. NodePort
- C. ClusterIP
- D. ExternalName

**Answer:** C

---

### Question 3

Which Service type automatically provisions a cloud load balancer in Amazon EKS?

- A. ClusterIP
- B. ExternalName
- C. NodePort
- D. LoadBalancer

**Answer:** D

---

### Question 4

Which component is responsible for routing Service traffic on Worker Nodes?

- A. kubelet
- B. Scheduler
- C. kube-proxy
- D. etcd

**Answer:** C

---

### Question 5

Which networking practice best reduces the attack surface of internal applications?

- A. Expose all applications using NodePort
- B. Use ClusterIP for internal services
- C. Disable DNS
- D. Assign static Pod IP addresses

**Answer:** B

---

# What's Next?

In the next lesson, you will explore **Kubernetes Namespaces**, learning how organisations logically separate workloads, implement multi-tenancy, enforce access controls, and prepare clusters for secure enterprise operations.

Why Pod IP Addresses Cannot Be Trusted

Pods are ephemeral.

When a Pod is deleted or recreated, its IP address changes.

Applications should never depend directly on Pod IP addresses.

This is why Kubernetes Services exist.

What is a Kubernetes Service?

Section titled “What is a Kubernetes Service?”

A Service provides a stable network endpoint for accessing one or more Pods.

Instead of connecting directly to a Pod, applications communicate through a Service.

Benefits include:

  • Stable IP address
  • DNS name
  • Load balancing
  • Automatic discovery

NodePort

  • Publicly exposed Services
  • Unrestricted NodePorts
  • Missing Network Policies
  • Weak DNS controls
  • Insecure Ingress configurations
  • Excessive east-west traffic
  • Open cloud Security Groups
  • Misconfigured load balancers
  • Exposed internal APIs
  • Lack of TLS encryption

These issues increase the cluster’s attack surface.

  • Use ClusterIP for internal applications.
  • Use LoadBalancer only when external access is required.

  • Encrypt traffic with TLS.
  • Implement Network Policies.

  • Use DNS instead of Pod IP addresses.

  • Implemented an Ingress Controller with authentication

  • Review exposed Services regularly.
  • Follow Zero Trust networking principles.

Secure networking is a foundational component of every production Kubernetes environment.

# Lesson 07 — Namespaces

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what Kubernetes Namespaces are
- Explain why Namespaces are used
- Create logical separation between workloads
- Understand multi-tenancy in Kubernetes
- Learn how RBAC integrates with Namespaces
- Identify common Namespace security risks
- Apply enterprise best practices for Namespace design

---

# Why This Matters

As Kubernetes clusters grow, organisations begin hosting hundreds—or even thousands—of applications on the same cluster.

Without logical separation:

- Developers could accidentally modify production workloads.
- Applications could interfere with each other.
- Security boundaries would become difficult to enforce.
- Managing permissions would become increasingly complex.

Namespaces solve these problems by providing logical isolation within a Kubernetes cluster.

Every enterprise Kubernetes deployment relies on Namespaces to organise workloads securely.

---

# What is a Namespace?

A **Namespace** is a logical partition within a Kubernetes cluster.

It allows multiple teams, applications, or environments to share the same cluster while remaining logically separated.

Think of a Namespace as a folder inside a file system.

Instead of placing every resource into one location, Kubernetes organises them into separate containers for easier management and improved security.

---

# Kubernetes Cluster Without Namespaces

Without Namespaces, everything exists together.

```text
Kubernetes Cluster

├── Pod
├── Pod
├── Service
├── Secret
├── Deployment
├── ConfigMap
├── Job
├── Ingress
└── ReplicaSet
```

Managing large environments quickly becomes difficult.

---

# Kubernetes Cluster With Namespaces

Using Namespaces provides logical separation.

```text
Kubernetes Cluster

├── Production
│     ├── Pods
│     ├── Services
│     └── Secrets
│
├── Development
│     ├── Pods
│     ├── Services
│     └── Secrets
│
├── Testing
│     ├── Pods
│     ├── Services
│     └── Secrets
│
└── Monitoring
      ├── Prometheus
      ├── Grafana
      └── Alertmanager
```

Each Namespace contains its own resources.

---

# Why Organisations Use Namespaces

Namespaces help organisations:

- Separate development and production
- Organise applications
- Support multiple teams
- Apply RBAC permissions
- Manage resources
- Improve security
- Simplify administration
- Enable multi-tenancy

Namespaces provide organisation without requiring multiple Kubernetes clusters.

---

# Built-in Kubernetes Namespaces

Every Kubernetes cluster includes several default Namespaces.

| Namespace | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| default | Default location for resources |
| kube-system | Core Kubernetes components |
| kube-public | Public cluster information |
| kube-node-lease | Node heartbeat information |

These Namespaces should be managed carefully.

---

# Enterprise Namespace Design

Large organisations commonly organise Namespaces by environment.

Example:

```text
Production

Development

Testing

Staging

Security

Monitoring

Logging

Platform

Networking
```

Each team manages resources within its own Namespace.

---

# Example Enterprise Architecture

```text
Kubernetes Cluster

├── prod-payments
├── prod-authentication
├── prod-customers
├── dev-payments
├── dev-authentication
├── monitoring
├── logging
└── security
```

This structure improves visibility and operational efficiency.

---

# Namespace Scope

Many Kubernetes resources exist within a Namespace.

Examples include:

- Pods
- Services
- Deployments
- ReplicaSets
- ConfigMaps
- Secrets
- Jobs
- Service Accounts

Some resources remain cluster-wide, such as:

- Nodes
- Persistent Volumes
- Namespaces
- ClusterRoles
- ClusterRoleBindings

Understanding this distinction is important when designing security controls.

---

# Namespace Isolation

Namespaces provide **logical isolation**, not complete security isolation.

Example:

```text
Namespace A

├── Application A

Namespace B

├── Application B
```

Applications are separated logically, but additional controls are required to prevent unauthorised communication.

For stronger isolation, organisations combine Namespaces with:

- RBAC
- Network Policies
- Resource Quotas
- Pod Security Standards
- Admission Controllers

---

# Multi-Tenancy

Multi-tenancy allows multiple teams or customers to share the same Kubernetes cluster securely.

Example:

```text
Cluster

├── Team Alpha
├── Team Beta
├── Team Gamma
└── Security Team
```

Each team operates within its own Namespace while sharing the underlying infrastructure.

---

# RBAC and Namespaces

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) commonly operates at the Namespace level.

Example:

```text
Namespace: Development

Developer
│
├── Create Pods
├── View Logs
└── Update Deployments
```

```text
Namespace: Production

Developer
│
└── Read-Only Access
```

This ensures users have only the permissions required for their responsibilities.

---

# Resource Quotas

Namespaces can enforce resource limits.

Examples include:

- Maximum CPU
- Maximum Memory
- Maximum Pods
- Maximum Persistent Volumes
- Maximum Services

Example:

```text
Development Namespace

CPU: 20 vCPUs

Memory: 64 GB

Pods: 50
```

This prevents one team from consuming excessive cluster resources.

---

# Limit Ranges

Limit Ranges define default resource requests and limits for Pods within a Namespace.

Example:

```text
Every Pod

CPU Request: 500m

Memory Request: 512Mi

CPU Limit: 1 vCPU

Memory Limit: 1Gi
```

This encourages consistent workload sizing.

---

# Namespace Labels

Namespaces can be labelled to support automation and governance.

Example:

```text
Environment=Production

Owner=SecurityTeam

Compliance=PCI-DSS

BusinessUnit=Finance
```

Labels simplify reporting, policy enforcement, and automation.

---

# Common Namespace Security Risks

Security teams frequently identify:

- Running everything in the default Namespace
- Shared production and development workloads
- Missing RBAC controls
- Excessive permissions
- Missing Resource Quotas
- Weak Namespace naming conventions
- No workload isolation
- Secrets shared across applications
- Unrestricted cross-Namespace communication

These issues increase operational and security risks.

---

# Enterprise Example

A financial organisation operates a single Amazon EKS cluster.

Namespaces are organised as follows:

```text
prod-payments

prod-banking

prod-authentication

dev-payments

dev-mobile

monitoring

security

logging

platform
```

RBAC restricts developers to development Namespaces.

Production access is limited to platform and security administrators.

This separation reduces the likelihood of accidental changes to critical workloads.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Never run production workloads in the default Namespace.
- Create separate Namespaces for each environment.
- Separate teams using dedicated Namespaces.
- Apply RBAC to every Namespace.
- Configure Resource Quotas and Limit Ranges.
- Use consistent naming conventions.
- Label Namespaces for governance.
- Apply Network Policies between Namespaces.
- Review Namespace permissions regularly.
- Remove unused Namespaces promptly.

Namespaces should form the foundation of your cluster organisation strategy.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Namespace creation
- Namespace deletion
- RBAC changes
- Resource Quota violations
- Cross-Namespace communication
- Secret access
- Unusual workload deployments
- Resource consumption
- Failed policy enforcement
- Administrative changes

Monitoring helps detect configuration drift and unauthorised activity.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What Kubernetes Namespaces are
- Why organisations use Namespaces
- How Namespaces support multi-tenancy
- The relationship between Namespaces and RBAC
- The importance of Resource Quotas
- Common Namespace security risks
- Enterprise best practices for organising Kubernetes environments

Namespaces provide the organisational foundation for building secure, scalable, and manageable Kubernetes clusters.

---

# Knowledge Check

### Question 1

- A. Encrypt application data
- B. Provide logical separation of resources within a cluster
- C. Replace Worker Nodes
- D. Store container images

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 2

Which Namespace is used by default when no Namespace is specified?

- A. kube-system
- B. kube-public
- C. default
- D. production

**Answer:** C

---

### Question 3

Which Kubernetes security feature is commonly applied at the Namespace level?

- A. kubelet
- B. RBAC
- C. Scheduler
- D. etcd

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 4

Which of the following is considered a Namespace best practice?

- A. Deploy all workloads into the default Namespace
- B. Use separate Namespaces for production and development
- C. Disable Resource Quotas
- D. Share Secrets across all Namespaces

**Answer:** B

---

### Question 5

Which combination provides stronger workload isolation than Namespaces alone?

- A. ClusterIP and kube-proxy
- B. RBAC, Network Policies, and Resource Quotas
- C. ReplicaSets and Deployments
- D. Services and Ingress

**Answer:** B

---

# Lesson 08 — ConfigMaps & Secrets

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand the purpose of ConfigMaps
- Understand the purpose of Kubernetes Secrets
- Differentiate between ConfigMaps and Secrets
- Learn how applications consume configuration data
- Identify common security risks involving Secrets
- Understand enterprise secrets management
- Apply security best practices for protecting sensitive information

---

# Why This Matters

Every application requires configuration.

Examples include:

- Database hostnames
- API endpoints
- Logging levels
- Feature flags
- Authentication tokens
- Database passwords
- API Keys
- TLS Certificates
- Cloud credentials

Hardcoding these values inside application code is a major security risk.

Instead, Kubernetes separates application configuration from application code using **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets**.

This approach improves:

- Security
- Flexibility
- Portability
- Configuration management
- DevSecOps automation

---

# Configuration vs Sensitive Data

Not all application data has the same sensitivity.

Example:

| Configuration | Sensitive Data |
|--------------|----------------|
| Application Name | Database Password |
| Logging Level | API Key |
| Feature Flags | AWS Access Key |
| Environment Name | OAuth Token |
| Application Port | TLS Private Key |

Configuration belongs in **ConfigMaps**.

Sensitive information belongs in **Secrets**.

---

# What is a ConfigMap?

A ConfigMap stores **non-sensitive application configuration**.

Examples include:

- Environment variables
- Configuration files
- Application settings
- URLs
- Feature toggles
- Port numbers
- Logging configuration

ConfigMaps allow applications to change behaviour without rebuilding container images.

---

# ConfigMap Architecture

```text
Application

↓

ConfigMap

↓

Configuration Values

• Environment
• URL
• Port
• Log Level
```

The application reads its configuration from the ConfigMap during startup.

---

# Example ConfigMap

```text
Application Name

GoHackersCloud Portal

Environment

Production

Log Level

INFO

Port

443
```

Notice that no sensitive information is stored.

---

# Benefits of ConfigMaps

ConfigMaps provide:

- Centralised configuration
- Easier application updates
- Environment-specific configuration
- Separation of configuration from code
- Simplified CI/CD deployments
- Improved maintainability

---

# What is a Kubernetes Secret?

A Secret stores **sensitive information** required by applications.

Examples include:

- Database passwords
- API tokens
- AWS credentials
- Azure credentials
- GCP credentials
- TLS certificates
- SSH keys
- OAuth tokens
- Service Account tokens

Secrets should never be stored directly inside container images or application source code.

---

# Secret Architecture

```text
Application

↓

Kubernetes Secret

↓

Sensitive Data

• Password

• API Key

• Certificate

• Token
```

Applications retrieve Secrets securely at runtime.

---

# Common Secret Types

Kubernetes supports several Secret types.

| Secret Type | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| Opaque | Generic secrets |
| kubernetes.io/tls | TLS certificates |
| kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson | Container registry credentials |
| kubernetes.io/service-account-token | Service Account tokens |
| Basic Authentication | Username and password |
| SSH Authentication | SSH private keys |

Each Secret type is designed for a specific use case.

---

# How Applications Use Secrets

Applications can consume Secrets as:

- Environment variables
- Mounted files
- Volume mounts
- Configuration files

Example:

```text
Application

↓

Reads Secret

↓

Database Password

↓

Connects Securely
```

This avoids embedding credentials directly in the application.

---

# ConfigMaps vs Secrets

| Feature | ConfigMap | Secret |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| Stores configuration | ✅ | ❌ |
| Stores passwords | ❌ | ✅ |
| Stores API Keys | ❌ | ✅ |
| Stores certificates | ❌ | ✅ |
| Stores feature flags | ✅ | ❌ |
| Stores application settings | ✅ | ❌ |

Choosing the correct resource type is an important security practice.

---

# Secret Storage

By default, Kubernetes stores Secrets in **etcd**.

```text
Application

↓

API Server

↓

etcd

↓

Encrypted Secret
```

If etcd is compromised and Secrets are not encrypted, attackers may gain access to sensitive credentials.

---

# Why Base64 is NOT Encryption

Many new Kubernetes users assume Secrets are encrypted because they appear unreadable.

In reality:

```text
Password

↓

Base64 Encoding

↓

UGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=
```

Base64 is simply an encoding mechanism.

Anyone can decode it easily.

Real protection requires **Encryption at Rest**.

---

# Encryption at Rest

Enterprise Kubernetes environments encrypt Secrets before storing them in etcd.

Example:

```text
Secret

↓

Encryption Provider

↓

Encrypted Data

↓

etcd
```

Cloud providers such as Amazon EKS support encryption using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).

---

# Enterprise Secrets Management

Many organisations integrate Kubernetes with dedicated secrets management platforms.

Common solutions include:

- AWS Secrets Manager
- AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
- HashiCorp Vault
- Azure Key Vault
- Google Secret Manager

These platforms provide:

- Secret rotation
- Access auditing
- Centralised management
- Fine-grained permissions
- Automatic key lifecycle management

---

# Secret Rotation

Passwords and API keys should not remain unchanged indefinitely.

Example:

```text
Old Password

↓

Rotate Secret

↓

Application Reloads

↓

New Password
```

Regular rotation reduces the impact of credential compromise.

---

# Secret Access

Not every application should access every Secret.

Example:

```text
Payment Service

↓

Payment Database Secret

✓ Allowed

------------------------

Monitoring Service

↓

Payment Database Secret

✗ Denied
```

Access should always follow the **Principle of Least Privilege**.

---

# Enterprise Example

An online banking platform contains:

- Authentication Service
- Payment Service
- Customer Portal

Each service uses:

**ConfigMaps**

- API URLs
- Logging configuration
- Environment settings

**Secrets**

- Database credentials
- Payment gateway API keys
- TLS certificates
- OAuth client secrets

Each application only receives access to the Secrets it requires.

---

# Common Security Risks

Security teams frequently discover:

- Passwords stored inside ConfigMaps
- Secrets committed to Git repositories
- Plain-text credentials inside YAML files
- Shared Secrets across applications
- Excessive Secret permissions
- Unencrypted etcd databases
- Long-lived API keys
- Hardcoded credentials inside container images
- Missing Secret rotation
- Public exposure of sensitive configuration

These mistakes can lead to credential theft and cluster compromise.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Store sensitive information only in Secrets.
- Store non-sensitive configuration in ConfigMaps.
- Enable Encryption at Rest.
- Use AWS KMS or another key management solution.
- Rotate Secrets regularly.
- Apply RBAC to Secret access.
- Avoid hardcoded credentials.
- Use external secret management platforms for production.
- Audit Secret access.
- Remove unused Secrets promptly.

Configuration should be managed securely throughout the application lifecycle.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Secret creation
- Secret deletion
- Secret modifications
- Failed Secret access
- RBAC changes
- Secret rotation events
- Unauthorised API requests
- Unusual Secret usage
- Configuration drift
- Encryption failures

Monitoring helps detect misuse of sensitive information before it results in a security incident.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A developer accidentally commits a Kubernetes Secret containing AWS access keys to a public Git repository.

An attacker discovers the repository within minutes and uses the exposed credentials to:

- Launch EC2 instances for cryptocurrency mining.
- Access sensitive Amazon S3 buckets.
- Enumerate IAM roles.
- Modify cloud resources.

If the organisation had:

- Used AWS Secrets Manager
- Rotated credentials regularly
- Implemented Git secret scanning
- Applied least privilege IAM permissions

the impact of the exposure would have been significantly reduced.

---

# Best Practices Summary

Always remember:

- ConfigMaps are for configuration.
- Secrets are for sensitive information.
- Base64 is **not** encryption.
- Encrypt Secrets stored in etcd.
- Limit Secret access using RBAC.
- Rotate credentials regularly.
- Integrate Kubernetes with enterprise secret management solutions.
- Continuously monitor Secret usage.
- Never expose credentials in source code or Git repositories.

Protecting Secrets is one of the most important responsibilities of a Kubernetes Security Engineer.

---

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- The purpose of ConfigMaps
- The purpose of Kubernetes Secrets
- The differences between ConfigMaps and Secrets
- How applications consume configuration
- Why Encryption at Rest is essential
- Enterprise secrets management approaches
- Security best practices for protecting credentials

These concepts prepare you for securing workloads that depend on sensitive configuration and lay the foundation for advanced identity and secrets management.

# Lesson 09 — Persistent Storage

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand why persistent storage is required
- Explain Kubernetes Volumes
- Understand Persistent Volumes (PV)
- Learn how Persistent Volume Claims (PVC) work
- Understand Storage Classes
- Identify enterprise storage options
- Recognise storage security risks
- Apply storage security best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Containers are designed to be **ephemeral**.

This means they are temporary by nature.

If a container crashes or a Pod is deleted, everything stored inside that container is lost unless persistent storage is used.

Imagine an online banking application.

Without persistent storage:

- Customer account information disappears
- Transaction history is lost
- Uploaded documents vanish
- Application logs cannot be recovered

Persistent storage ensures that important business data survives Pod restarts, upgrades and failures.

---

# Ephemeral Storage vs Persistent Storage

Without persistent storage:

```text
Pod

↓

Application

↓

Writes Data

↓

Pod Deleted

↓

Data Lost
```

With persistent storage:

```text
Pod

↓

Persistent Volume

↓

Pod Deleted

↓

Data Still Available

↓

New Pod

↓

Same Data Available
```

Persistent storage separates application data from the lifecycle of a Pod.

---

# What is a Kubernetes Volume?

A **Volume** is storage that can be mounted inside a Pod.

Volumes allow containers to:

- Read data
- Write data
- Share files
- Persist information

Unlike a container filesystem, a Volume can survive container restarts.

---

# Pod with Volume

```text
Pod

├── Application Container
│
└── Volume
      │
      ▼
Persistent Storage
```

Both the application and any sidecar containers inside the Pod can access the same Volume if configured.

---

# Types of Kubernetes Volumes

Kubernetes supports many different volume types.

Common examples include:

- emptyDir
- hostPath
- Persistent Volume (PV)
- ConfigMap
- Secret
- CSI Volumes
- NFS
- Amazon EBS
- Amazon EFS
- Azure Disk
- Azure Files
- Google Persistent Disk

Enterprise environments generally rely on CSI-based cloud storage rather than local node storage.

---

# What is a Persistent Volume (PV)?

A **Persistent Volume (PV)** is a storage resource available within the Kubernetes cluster.

It represents physical or cloud-backed storage that exists independently of any Pod.

Examples include:

- Amazon EBS Volume
- Amazon EFS File System
- Azure Managed Disk
- Azure Files
- Google Persistent Disk
- Network Attached Storage (NAS)

---

# Persistent Volume Architecture

```text
Application

↓

Pod

↓

Persistent Volume Claim

↓

Persistent Volume

↓

Cloud Storage
```

Pods never access storage directly.

They always request storage through a Persistent Volume Claim.

---

# What is a Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)?

A **Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)** is a request for storage.

Instead of specifying the exact storage device, an application simply requests:

- Storage size
- Access mode
- Storage class

Kubernetes automatically assigns an appropriate Persistent Volume.

---

# Example

Application requests:

```text
50 GB Storage

Read/Write Access

Standard SSD
```

Kubernetes provides:

```text
Amazon EBS Volume

50 GB

Mounted to Pod
```

The application does not need to know where the storage physically exists.

---

# Persistent Volume Lifecycle

```text
Application

↓

Persistent Volume Claim Created

↓

Persistent Volume Bound

↓

Pod Uses Storage

↓

Pod Deleted

↓

Persistent Volume Remains
```

Storage continues to exist independently of the application.

---

# Access Modes

Persistent Volumes support different access modes.

| Access Mode | Description |
|--------------|-------------|
| ReadWriteOnce (RWO) | Mounted by one node for read/write access |
| ReadOnlyMany (ROX) | Mounted by multiple nodes in read-only mode |
| ReadWriteMany (RWX) | Mounted by multiple nodes with read/write access |
| ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) | Mounted by a single Pod for read/write access |

Selecting the correct access mode depends on the application's architecture.

---

# Storage Classes

Storage Classes automate storage provisioning.

Instead of manually creating storage, Kubernetes creates it automatically.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

PVC

↓

Storage Class

↓

Amazon EBS Volume Created

↓

Application Starts
```

Storage Classes simplify deployment and improve operational efficiency.

---

# Common Storage Classes

Enterprise environments often use:

AWS

- gp3 SSD
- io2 High Performance
- Amazon EFS

Azure

- Premium SSD
- Standard SSD
- Azure Files

Google Cloud

- Persistent SSD
- Balanced Persistent Disk

Each Storage Class offers different performance and cost characteristics.

---

# Amazon EKS Storage

Amazon EKS commonly integrates with:

### Amazon EBS

Best for:

- Databases
- Stateful applications
- Single-node workloads

---

### Amazon EFS

Best for:

- Shared storage
- Multi-node applications
- Shared file systems
- Content management systems

---

### Amazon FSx

Best for:

- High-performance workloads
- Enterprise applications
- Windows-based workloads
- HPC environments

---

# Container Storage Interface (CSI)

Modern Kubernetes uses the **Container Storage Interface (CSI)**.

CSI allows Kubernetes to integrate with many storage providers using a standard interface.

Examples:

- Amazon EBS CSI Driver
- Amazon EFS CSI Driver
- Azure Disk CSI
- Azure Files CSI
- Google Persistent Disk CSI

CSI has become the standard approach for enterprise Kubernetes storage.

---

# Storage Security Risks

Improper storage configuration can expose sensitive information.

Common risks include:

- Unencrypted storage volumes
- Publicly accessible file systems
- Shared volumes between unrelated applications
- Missing backups
- Weak IAM permissions
- Excessive storage access
- Unused Persistent Volumes
- Sensitive data stored without encryption
- Insecure CSI drivers

Storage should be treated as a critical security asset.

---

# Encryption at Rest

Enterprise storage should always be encrypted.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

Persistent Volume

↓

AWS KMS Encryption

↓

Encrypted Amazon EBS
```

Encryption protects data even if physical storage is compromised.

---

# Encryption in Transit

Applications should also encrypt data while communicating with storage systems.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

TLS

↓

Encrypted Storage Connection

↓

Amazon EFS
```

Both **Encryption at Rest** and **Encryption in Transit** should be enabled.

---

# Backup and Disaster Recovery

Persistent storage should be backed up regularly.

Example:

```text
Persistent Volume

↓

Snapshot

↓

Encrypted Backup

↓

Recovery
```

AWS provides:

- Amazon EBS Snapshots
- AWS Backup
- Cross-Region backup
- Cross-Account backup

Backups are essential for business continuity and ransomware recovery.

---

# Enterprise Example

A healthcare organisation runs patient management software on Amazon EKS.

The environment includes:

- Web applications
- PostgreSQL database
- Medical document storage
- Image processing services

Storage architecture:

```text
Pods

↓

PVC

↓

Amazon EBS

↓

Encrypted using AWS KMS

↓

Daily Snapshots

↓

AWS Backup
```

Security controls include:

- Encryption
- IAM permissions
- Automated backups
- Monitoring
- Disaster recovery testing

This design ensures sensitive healthcare data remains available and protected.

---

# Storage Monitoring

Security and operations teams should monitor:

- Persistent Volume creation
- Persistent Volume deletion
- Storage utilisation
- Snapshot failures
- Backup status
- Encryption status
- Unusual storage access
- CSI driver events
- Disk performance
- Capacity growth

Continuous monitoring helps prevent data loss and identify potential security issues.

---

# Common Enterprise Mistakes

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Using hostPath volumes in production
- Running without backups
- Leaving unused Persistent Volumes attached
- Missing encryption
- Excessive IAM permissions
- Shared storage between production and development
- Missing snapshot policies
- Over-provisioned storage
- No disaster recovery testing

These mistakes increase operational and security risks.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use Persistent Volumes for stateful applications.
- Use Persistent Volume Claims instead of directly referencing storage.
- Enable Encryption at Rest.
- Enable Encryption in Transit.
- Use Storage Classes for dynamic provisioning.
- Follow the Principle of Least Privilege for storage access.
- Enable automated backups and snapshots.
- Monitor storage continuously.
- Remove unused Persistent Volumes.
- Test disaster recovery procedures regularly.

Secure storage is essential for protecting enterprise workloads and maintaining business continuity.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- Why persistent storage is required
- The purpose of Kubernetes Volumes
- How Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims work
- The role of Storage Classes
- Enterprise storage options in Amazon EKS
- Common storage security risks
- Best practices for securing Kubernetes storage

Persistent storage is a critical component of running reliable and secure stateful applications in Kubernetes.

---

- A. It improves CPU performance.

- C. It replaces Deployments.

### Question 2

---

What is a Kubernetes Volume?

Section titled “What is a Kubernetes Volume?”

A Volume is storage that can be mounted inside a Pod.

Volumes allow containers to:

  • Read data
  • Write data
  • Share files
  • Persist information

Unlike a container filesystem, a Volume can survive container restarts.

Pod with Volume

Section titled “Pod with Volume”

Both the application and any sidecar containers inside the Pod can access the same Volume if configured.

Types of Kubernetes Volumes

Section titled “Types of Kubernetes Volumes”

Kubernetes supports many different volume types.

Common examples include:

  • emptyDir
  • hostPath
  • Persistent Volume (PV)
  • ConfigMap
  • Secret
  • CSI Volumes
  • NFS
  • Amazon EBS
  • Amazon EFS
  • Azure Disk
  • Azure Files
  • Google Persistent Disk

Enterprise environments generally rely on CSI-based cloud storage rather than local node storage.

What is a Persistent Volume (PV)?

Section titled “What is a Persistent Volume (PV)?”

A Persistent Volume (PV) is a storage resource available within the Kubernetes cluster.

It represents physical or cloud-backed storage that exists independently of any Pod.

Examples include:

  • Amazon EBS Volume
  • Amazon EFS File System
  • Azure Managed Disk
  • Azure Files
  • Google Persistent Disk
  • Network Attached Storage (NAS)

Persistent Volume Architecture

Section titled “Persistent Volume Architecture”

Pods never access storage directly.

They always request storage through a Persistent Volume Claim.

What is a Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)?

Section titled “What is a Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)?”

A Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) is a request for storage.

Instead of specifying the exact storage device, an application simply requests:

  • Storage size
  • Access mode
  • Storage class

Kubernetes automatically assigns an appropriate Persistent Volume.

Example

Kubernetes provides:

The application does not need to know where the storage physically exists.

Persistent Volume Lifecycle

Section titled “Persistent Volume Lifecycle”

Storage continues to exist independently of the application.

Access Modes

Section titled “Access Modes”

Persistent Volumes support different access modes.

Access Mode Description
ReadWriteOnce (RWO) Mounted by one node for read/write access
ReadOnlyMany (ROX) Mounted by multiple nodes in read-only mode
ReadWriteMany (RWX) Mounted by multiple nodes with read/write access
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) Mounted by a single Pod for read/write access

Selecting the correct access mode depends on the application’s architecture.

Storage Classes

Section titled “Storage Classes”

Storage Classes automate storage provisioning.

Instead of manually creating storage, Kubernetes creates it automatically.

Storage Classes simplify deployment and improve operational efficiency.

Common Storage Classes

Section titled “Common Storage Classes”

Enterprise environments often use:

AWS

  • io2 High Performance

Azure

  • Azure Files

Google Cloud

  • Balanced Persistent Disk

Each Storage Class offers different performance and cost characteristics.

Amazon EKS Storage

Section titled “Amazon EKS Storage”

Amazon EKS commonly integrates with:

Amazon EBS

Section titled “Amazon EBS”

Best for:

  • Databases
  • Stateful applications
  • Single-node workloads

Amazon EFS

Section titled “Amazon EFS”

Best for:

  • Shared storage
  • Multi-node applications
  • Shared file systems
  • Content management systems

Amazon FSx

Section titled “Amazon FSx”

Best for:

  • High-performance workloads
  • Enterprise applications
  • Windows-based workloads
  • HPC environments

Container Storage Interface (CSI)

Section titled “Container Storage Interface (CSI)”

Modern Kubernetes uses the Container Storage Interface (CSI).

CSI allows Kubernetes to integrate with many storage providers using a standard interface.

Examples:

  • Amazon EBS CSI Driver
  • Amazon EFS CSI Driver
  • Azure Disk CSI
  • Azure Files CSI
  • Google Persistent Disk CSI

CSI has become the standard approach for enterprise Kubernetes storage.

Storage Security Risks

Section titled “Storage Security Risks”

Improper storage configuration can expose sensitive information.

Common risks include:

  • Unencrypted storage volumes
  • Publicly accessible file systems
  • Shared volumes between unrelated applications
  • Missing backups
  • Weak IAM permissions
  • Excessive storage access
  • Unused Persistent Volumes
  • Sensitive data stored without encryption
  • Insecure CSI drivers

Storage should be treated as a critical security asset.

Encryption at Rest

Section titled “Encryption at Rest”

Enterprise storage should always be encrypted.

Example:

Encryption protects data even if physical storage is compromised.

Encryption in Transit

Section titled “Encryption in Transit”

Applications should also encrypt data while communicating with storage systems.

Example:

Both Encryption at Rest and Encryption in Transit should be enabled.

Backup and Disaster Recovery

Section titled “Backup and Disaster Recovery”

Persistent storage should be backed up regularly.

Example:

AWS provides:

  • Amazon EBS Snapshots
  • AWS Backup
  • Cross-Region backup
  • Cross-Account backup

Backups are essential for business continuity and ransomware recovery.

Section titled “Enterprise Example”

A healthcare organisation runs patient management software on Amazon EKS.

The environment includes:

  • PostgreSQL database
  • Medical document storage
  • Image processing services

Storage architecture:

Security controls include:

  • IAM permissions
  • Automated backups
  • Monitoring
  • Disaster recovery testing

This design ensures sensitive healthcare data remains available and protected.

Storage Monitoring

Section titled “Storage Monitoring”

Security and operations teams should monitor:

  • Persistent Volume creation
  • Persistent Volume deletion
  • Storage utilisation
  • Snapshot failures
  • Backup status
  • Encryption status
  • Unusual storage access
  • CSI driver events
  • Disk performance
  • Capacity growth

Continuous monitoring helps prevent data loss and identify potential security issues.

Common Enterprise Mistakes

Section titled “Common Enterprise Mistakes”

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

  • Using hostPath volumes in production
  • Running without backups
  • Leaving unused Persistent Volumes attached
  • Missing encryption
  • Excessive IAM permissions
  • Shared storage between production and development
  • Missing snapshot policies
  • Over-provisioned storage
  • No disaster recovery testing

These mistakes increase operational and security risks.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

  • Use Persistent Volumes for stateful applications.
  • Use Persistent Volume Claims instead of directly referencing storage.
  • Enable Encryption at Rest.
  • Enable Encryption in Transit.
  • Use Storage Classes for dynamic provisioning.
  • Follow the Principle of Least Privilege for storage access.
  • Enable automated backups and snapshots.
  • Monitor storage continuously.
  • Remove unused Persistent Volumes.
  • Test disaster recovery procedures regularly.

Secure storage is essential for protecting enterprise workloads and maintaining business continuity.

# Why This Matters

Running Kubernetes in production is very different from deploying a small lab cluster.

Large organisations operate Kubernetes platforms that support:

- Thousands of applications
- Hundreds of development teams
- Millions of users
- Critical business services
- Financial transactions
- Healthcare platforms
- Government systems

A Cloud Security Engineer must understand how enterprise Kubernetes platforms are designed before they can secure them.

---

# Enterprise Kubernetes Platform

- Kubernetes Control Plane
- Worker Nodes
- Networking
- Identity
- Monitoring
- Logging
- Secrets Management
- Container Registry
- Security Services
- CI/CD Pipelines
- Backup & Disaster Recovery
- Compliance Controls

Every component contributes to the security and reliability of the platform.

# High Availability

Production workloads should never rely on a single Availability Zone.

Example:

```text
Region

├── Availability Zone A

├── Availability Zone B

└── Availability Zone C
```

Worker Nodes are distributed across multiple Availability Zones.

Benefits include:

- Fault tolerance
- Automatic recovery
- Improved resilience
- Maintenance without downtime

---

# Production Networking

Enterprise Kubernetes networking typically follows this model.

```text
Internet

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

Ingress Controller

↓

Kubernetes Services

↓

Pods
```

Internal services remain private while internet-facing applications are protected using multiple security layers.

---

# Enterprise VPC Design

Most organisations deploy Amazon EKS into a dedicated Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

Example:

```text
VPC

├── Public Subnets

│      └── Load Balancers

├── Private Subnets

│      └── Worker Nodes

├── Database Subnets

│      └── Amazon RDS

└── Management Subnets
```

Production Worker Nodes should always reside in private subnets.

---

# Identity Architecture

Identity controls are critical in enterprise Kubernetes environments.

Authentication commonly uses:

- AWS IAM
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- AWS IAM Identity Center
- OpenID Connect (OIDC)
- Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Applications should authenticate using temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys.

Enterprise workloads commonly use:

```text
Persistent Volume Claims

Storage Classes

↓

Amazon EBS

↓

AWS KMS Encryption
```

Shared workloads often use Amazon EFS instead of EBS.

```text
Container Logs

↓

CloudWatch Logs

↓

Amazon Security Lake

↓

SIEM

↓

SOC Team
```

This architecture provides visibility for security monitoring, incident response and compliance.

Monitoring collects operational metrics from across the platform.

```text
Pods

↓

Prometheus

↓

Grafana

↓

Operations Dashboard
```

CloudWatch provides infrastructure metrics while Prometheus collects Kubernetes metrics.

Enterprise Kubernetes environments implement multiple security layers.

```text
Internet

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Shield Advanced

Security Groups

↓

Network ACLs

↓

Kubernetes RBAC

↓

Pod Security Standards

↓

Network Policies

↓

Runtime Detection

↓

Amazon GuardDuty
```

This layered approach supports a defence-in-depth strategy.

# Secrets Management

Sensitive information should never be stored inside application code.

Enterprise environments commonly use:

```text
Application

↓

External Secrets Operator

↓

AWS Secrets Manager

↓

AWS KMS

↓

Encrypted Secrets
```

This improves credential security and simplifies secret rotation.

Before workloads reach production they should pass multiple security checks.

```text
Source Code

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Container Image Scan

↓

Policy Validation

↓

Container Registry

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Only validated images should be deployed into production.

Security testing should be integrated into every deployment pipeline.

Typical enterprise strategy includes:

```text
Recovery Testing
```

Recovery procedures should be tested regularly.

# Enterprise Security Monitoring

Security Operations Centres (SOC) continuously monitor:

- Kubernetes audit logs
- CloudTrail events
- GuardDuty findings
- Network activity
- Container runtime alerts
- IAM changes
- RBAC modifications
- Secret access
- Vulnerability findings
- Configuration drift

Continuous monitoring enables early threat detection and faster incident response.

Cloud Security Engineers help organisations enforce governance using:

- AWS Organizations
- Service Control Policies (SCPs)
- AWS Config Rules
- Admission Controllers
- OPA Gatekeeper
- Kyverno
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
- CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark

Governance ensures that every Kubernetes cluster follows organisational security policies.

A global financial services company operates multiple Amazon EKS clusters.

- Multi-AZ deployment

- AWS KMS encryption
- External Secrets Manager

- Daily backups
- Automated compliance reporting

This architecture provides high availability, strong security, and operational resilience for mission-critical workloads.

---

# Common Enterprise Design Mistakes

Cloud Security Engineers frequently encounter:

- Worker Nodes deployed in public subnets
- No network segmentation
- Flat cluster architecture
- Shared production and development workloads
- Missing RBAC controls
- Long-lived IAM credentials
- No logging strategy
- Unencrypted storage
- Public Kubernetes API endpoints
- No disaster recovery plan
- Weak monitoring
- Missing compliance controls

These issues increase the likelihood of compromise and operational failures.

---

# Enterprise Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Deploy Worker Nodes in private subnets.
- Distribute workloads across multiple Availability Zones.
- Use IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA).
- Encrypt all data using AWS KMS.
- Protect internet-facing applications with AWS WAF and Shield.
- Enable CloudTrail, CloudWatch, GuardDuty and Security Hub.
- Implement Network Policies and Pod Security Standards.
- Use external secrets management.
- Integrate security into CI/CD pipelines.
- Monitor continuously and test disaster recovery regularly.

Enterprise Kubernetes security requires a layered approach that protects every component of the platform.

## Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies is preparing to adopt Kubernetes for its internal development and security testing environments.

Before the platform team begins deploying enterprise applications, the Cloud Security team must build a small Kubernetes cluster and verify that its core components are operating correctly.

You have joined the CloudNova Technologies security engineering team as a Junior Kubernetes Security Engineer.

Your mission is to:

- Install the required Kubernetes tools
- Create a local Kubernetes cluster
- Inspect the Control Plane and Worker Node
- Review system workloads
- Deploy a test application
- Expose the application securely for local testing
- Perform an initial cluster security review
- Collect evidence of successful implementation
- Remove the lab resources after completion

This lab establishes the technical foundation for the remaining Kubernetes Security modules.

## Learning Objectives

By completing this lab, you will be able to:

- Create a local Kubernetes cluster using kind
- Connect to the cluster using `kubectl`
- Inspect Kubernetes nodes and system components
- Identify the Control Plane and Worker Node
- Create and inspect a Namespace
- Deploy a containerised application
- Create a Kubernetes Service
- Review Kubernetes workload configuration
- Perform basic cluster security validation
- Troubleshoot common cluster deployment issues

# Task 13 — Create the Test Deployment

Create a file named:

```text
nginx-deployment.yaml
```

Add the following configuration:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cloudnova-web
  namespace: cloudnova-lab
  labels:
    app: cloudnova-web
    environment: development
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cloudnova-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cloudnova-web
        environment: development
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 80
              protocol: TCP
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 128Mi
```

## Security Controls Included

This Deployment includes:

- A dedicated Namespace
- Workload labels
- Two replicas for availability
- CPU requests and limits
- Memory requests and limits
- A named container port
- No public Service exposure

Additional workload hardening will be introduced in later modules.

# Task 15 — Create an Internal Kubernetes Service

```text
nginx-service.yaml
```

Add:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: cloudnova-web-service
  namespace: cloudnova-lab
```

`ClusterIP` exposes the application only inside the Kubernetes cluster.

# Troubleshooting Guide

## Issue 01 — Docker Command Not Found

Error:

```text
docker is not recognized
```

Resolution:

- Confirm Docker Desktop is installed.
- Restart the terminal.
- Restart Docker Desktop.
- Confirm Docker is included in the system `PATH`.

## Issue 02 — Docker Engine Is Not Running

Error:

```text
Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
```

Resolution:

- Start Docker Desktop.
- Wait for the engine to report that it is running.
- Run `docker version` again.

## Issue 03 — kind Command Not Found

Error:

```text
kind is not recognized
```

Resolution:

- Close and reopen PowerShell.
- Confirm installation using `winget list`.
- Check whether the kind executable is in the system `PATH`.

## Issue 04 — Cluster Creation Fails

Possible causes:

- Docker Desktop is not running
- Insufficient memory
- Virtualisation is disabled
- Previous cluster resources exist
- Security software is blocking Docker networking

Check:

```bash
docker ps
kind get clusters
```

Delete a failed cluster:

```bash
kind delete cluster --name cloudnova-security-lab
```

Then retry:

```bash
kind create cluster --config kind-cluster.yaml
```

## Issue 05 — Nodes Show NotReady

Check:

```bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl describe node cloudnova-security-lab-worker
```

Wait for system Pods to finish starting.

Docker Desktop may require additional CPU or memory.

## Issue 06 — Pods Remain Pending

Check:

```bash
kubectl describe pod <POD-NAME> -n cloudnova-lab
```

Review the Events section for:

- Scheduling failures
- Resource shortages
- Image pull errors
- Node readiness issues

## Issue 07 — ImagePullBackOff

Check:

```bash
kubectl describe pod <POD-NAME> -n cloudnova-lab
```

Confirm:

- Internet access is available
- Docker can reach the image registry
- The image name is correct

## Issue 08 — Port 8080 Is Already in Use

Use another local port:

```bash
kubectl port-forward service/cloudnova-web-service 8081:80 -n cloudnova-lab
```

Open:

```text
http://localhost:8081
```

# Lab 02 — Deploy Your First Secure Application

## Mission Information

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| Lab ID | K8S-FND-LAB-02 |
| Difficulty | Beginner to Intermediate |
| Estimated Time | 90–120 minutes |
| Environment | Local Kubernetes cluster |
| Platform | Docker Desktop and kind |
| Cost | Free |
| Primary Role | Kubernetes Security Engineer |
| Module | Module 01 — Kubernetes Fundamentals for Security Engineers |
| Previous Lab | Lab 01 — Build Your First Kubernetes Cluster |

## Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has successfully created its first Kubernetes development cluster.

The application team now wants to deploy an internal web application for testing. During an initial security review, the Cloud Security team identified several weaknesses in the proposed deployment:

- The container would run without a defined security context.
- The default Service Account would be used.
- Service Account tokens could be mounted unnecessarily.
- The container filesystem would remain writable.
- Linux capabilities would not be restricted.
- Resource limits would not be configured.
- Network communication would be unrestricted.
- Application health checks would be missing.
- The workload would use a floating container image tag.
- Security-related Namespace controls would not be enabled.

You have been assigned to create a more secure deployment standard.

Your mission is to deploy the application using Kubernetes security controls that reduce privilege, restrict network access, improve availability, and provide evidence that the controls are operating correctly.

## Learning Objectives

By completing this lab, you will be able to:

- Deploy a container using a dedicated Namespace
- Apply Kubernetes Pod Security Admission labels
- Create and use a dedicated Service Account
- Disable unnecessary Service Account token mounting
- Configure Pod-level and container-level security contexts
- Run a container as a non-root user
- Prevent privilege escalation
- remove unnecessary Linux capabilities
- Use a read-only root filesystem
- Configure resource requests and limits
- Add readiness and liveness probes
- Create an internal ClusterIP Service
- Apply default-deny Network Policies
- Allow only approved application communication
- Perform positive and negative network tests
- Validate workload security controls
- Document security findings and evidence
