# Lesson 06 — Identity Federation

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand Identity Federation
- Learn why enterprises use federated identities
- Understand Identity Providers (IdPs)
- Learn how OpenID Connect (OIDC) works
- Understand Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
- Explore AWS IAM Identity Center integration
- Understand enterprise authentication architecture
- Apply federation security best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Modern organisations rarely create separate usernames and passwords for every application.

Imagine an enterprise with:

- AWS Management Console
- Amazon EKS
- Microsoft 365
- GitHub Enterprise
- Jira
- ServiceNow
- Salesforce
- VPN
- Internal Applications

Without federation:

Each employee would need a separate account for every application.

This creates:

- Password fatigue
- Increased support costs
- Weak password reuse
- Difficult user management
- Higher security risks

Identity Federation solves these challenges by allowing users to authenticate once using a trusted identity provider and securely access multiple systems.

---

# What is Identity Federation?

Identity Federation is the process of trusting an external Identity Provider (IdP) to authenticate users instead of maintaining separate user accounts within every application.

Instead of Kubernetes storing usernames and passwords, authentication is delegated to an enterprise identity platform.

```text
User

↓

Identity Provider

↓

Verified Identity

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Kubernetes Access
```

The Kubernetes cluster trusts the identity verified by the external provider.

---

# Benefits of Identity Federation

Identity Federation provides:

- Single Sign-On (SSO)
- Centralised identity management
- Improved user experience
- Stronger security
- Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
- Simplified onboarding
- Simplified offboarding
- Reduced password reuse
- Better compliance
- Centralised auditing

Most enterprise cloud environments use federated identity.

---

# Federation vs Local Accounts

| Local Accounts | Federated Identity |
|----------------|--------------------|
| Separate credentials | Corporate credentials |
| Multiple passwords | Single Sign-On (SSO) |
| Difficult to manage | Centralised management |
| Individual account lifecycle | Automated provisioning |
| Manual access removal | Centralised offboarding |

Federation significantly reduces administrative overhead.

---

# Identity Federation Architecture

```text
User

↓

Corporate Identity Provider

↓

Authentication

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC Authorization

↓

Cluster Resources
```

Authentication happens outside Kubernetes.

Authorization still occurs inside Kubernetes using RBAC.

---

# Enterprise Identity Providers (IdPs)

Common Identity Providers include:

- Microsoft Entra ID
- Okta
- Ping Identity
- Google Workspace
- OneLogin
- Keycloak
- Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)

These platforms manage user identities centrally across the organisation.

---

# Single Sign-On (SSO)

Single Sign-On allows users to authenticate once and access multiple services.

```text
Employee Login

↓

Identity Provider

↓

Authenticated

↓

AWS Console

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

GitHub

↓

Jira
```

Users no longer need separate passwords for every platform.

---

# Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Federated authentication commonly requires MFA.

Example:

```text
Username

↓

Password

↓

Authenticator App

↓

Authenticated
```

MFA dramatically reduces the likelihood of credential compromise.

---

# OpenID Connect (OIDC)

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is the most common federation protocol used by Amazon EKS.

OIDC provides:

- Identity verification
- Authentication tokens
- Secure federation
- Token-based authentication

Authentication flow:

```text
User

↓

Identity Provider

↓

OIDC Token

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Authenticated
```

OIDC is lightweight, modern, and cloud-native.

---

# JSON Web Tokens (JWT)

OIDC authentication uses JSON Web Tokens (JWTs).

A JWT contains claims about the authenticated user, such as:

- User ID
- Email address
- Group membership
- Token expiration
- Issuing authority

```text
User Login

↓

JWT Issued

↓

Amazon EKS Validates Token

↓

Access Granted
```

JWTs are digitally signed to prevent tampering.

---

# Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)

Many enterprise Identity Providers also support SAML.

SAML is an XML-based federation protocol widely used in enterprise environments.

```text
Employee

↓

Corporate Identity Provider

↓

SAML Assertion

↓

AWS IAM Identity Center

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Although OIDC is more common for cloud-native applications, SAML remains important for enterprise integrations.

---

# AWS IAM Identity Center

AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralised workforce authentication for AWS environments.

It integrates with:

- Microsoft Entra ID
- Okta
- Active Directory
- Google Workspace
- Ping Identity

Architecture:

```text
Employee

↓

Corporate Login

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM Role

↓

Amazon EKS
```

This simplifies user management across AWS accounts and Kubernetes clusters.

---

# Federation in Amazon EKS

Authentication process:

```text
User

↓

Identity Provider

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM Role

↓

AWS STS

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC
```

Identity is verified before Kubernetes evaluates permissions.

---

# AWS Security Token Service (STS)

AWS STS issues temporary credentials after successful authentication.

```text
Identity Provider

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Benefits include:

- Temporary access
- Automatic expiration
- Reduced credential theft
- Better auditing

Long-lived credentials should be avoided wherever possible.

---

# Federation for Applications

Identity Federation is not limited to human users.

Applications also authenticate using federation.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

Service Account

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials
```

This architecture underpins IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA), which you will explore in the next lesson.

---

# Enterprise Federation Architecture

```text
Employee

↓

Microsoft Entra ID

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM Role

↓

AWS STS

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

↓

Production Cluster
```

Every authentication request is centrally managed and audited.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational healthcare provider operates Amazon EKS across several AWS accounts.

Authentication architecture:

```text
Doctor

↓

Microsoft Entra ID

↓

MFA

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM Role

↓

AWS STS

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

↓

Patient Management System
```

Benefits include:

- Single Sign-On
- Centralised account management
- Immediate account revocation
- MFA enforcement
- Temporary credentials
- Comprehensive audit logging

This approach simplifies operations while improving security.

---

# Identity Federation Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Missing MFA
- Weak Identity Provider configuration
- Long-lived credentials
- Excessive IAM permissions
- Misconfigured trust relationships
- Expired certificates
- Stolen authentication tokens
- Shared administrator accounts
- Inactive user accounts
- Unmonitored federation events

Weak federation controls can allow attackers to gain unauthorised access to enterprise environments.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- User login events
- Failed authentication attempts
- MFA failures
- Identity Provider configuration changes
- AWS STS AssumeRole events
- OIDC authentication events
- SAML authentication events
- IAM Role assumptions
- New federated identities
- Suspicious authentication patterns

CloudTrail and GuardDuty provide visibility into identity-related activity.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use enterprise Identity Providers for authentication.
- Enable Single Sign-On (SSO).
- Require Multi-Factor Authentication.
- Use OIDC for cloud-native authentication.
- Prefer temporary credentials over long-lived access keys.
- Integrate Amazon EKS with AWS IAM Identity Center.
- Regularly review federation trust relationships.
- Monitor authentication events continuously.
- Remove inactive identities promptly.
- Apply the Principle of Least Privilege.

Identity Federation should be the standard authentication model for enterprise Kubernetes environments.

---

A company uses local Kubernetes administrator accounts with shared passwords instead of federated identities.

An employee leaves the organisation, but their account remains active.

Months later, the credentials are used by an attacker to:

- Read Kubernetes Secrets.
- Deploy malicious workloads.

Learn how IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) enables Kubernetes workloads running on Amazon EKS to securely access AWS services without storing long-lived AWS credentials.

# Lesson 07 — IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) is
- Explain why IRSA is required in Amazon EKS
- Understand how IRSA works
- Learn the relationship between Kubernetes Service Accounts and AWS IAM Roles
- Understand the role of OIDC and AWS STS
- Identify common IRSA security risks
- Apply enterprise best practices for workload identity

---

# Why This Matters

Applications running inside Kubernetes often need to access AWS services.

Examples include:

- Amazon S3
- Amazon DynamoDB
- Amazon SQS
- Amazon SNS
- AWS Secrets Manager
- Amazon ECR
- AWS KMS
- Amazon CloudWatch

The question is:

> **How can a Pod securely access AWS services without storing AWS Access Keys inside the container?**

Historically, developers embedded AWS credentials inside:

- Source code
- Docker images
- Environment variables
- Configuration files

This created serious security risks.

Amazon EKS solves this problem using **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)**.

---

# What is IRSA?

IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) is an Amazon EKS feature that allows Kubernetes workloads to securely assume AWS IAM Roles.

Instead of storing AWS credentials inside Pods, workloads receive temporary AWS credentials automatically.

```text
Application

↓

Service Account

↓

IAM Role

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

AWS Service
```

This provides secure, cloud-native authentication.

---

# Traditional Authentication (Not Recommended)

Older Kubernetes deployments often stored AWS credentials directly inside applications.

```text
Application

↓

AWS Access Key

↓

AWS Secret Key

↓

Amazon S3
```

Problems include:

- Hardcoded credentials
- Credential theft
- Difficult rotation
- Shared secrets
- Compliance issues

This approach should never be used in production.

---

# Modern Authentication with IRSA

IRSA removes the need for static AWS credentials.

```text
Application

↓

Service Account

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

Amazon S3
```

No AWS Access Keys are stored inside the container.

---

# Why IRSA is Important

IRSA provides several security benefits.

Without IRSA:

- Static credentials
- Difficult credential rotation
- Shared AWS accounts
- Weak auditing
- High attack surface

With IRSA:

- Temporary credentials
- Automatic credential rotation
- Fine-grained permissions
- Better auditing
- Least privilege access

---

# Components of IRSA

IRSA relies on several AWS and Kubernetes components.

```text
Amazon EKS

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

IAM Role

↓

Service Account

↓

AWS STS

↓

AWS Service
```

Each component contributes to secure workload authentication.

---

# How IRSA Works

Authentication process:

```text
Pod Starts

↓

Uses Service Account

↓

OIDC Token Generated

↓

AWS STS Validates Token

↓

IAM Role Assumed

↓

Temporary Credentials Issued

↓

Application Calls AWS APIs
```

This entire process is automatic and transparent to the application.

---

# Step-by-Step IRSA Workflow

### Step 1

Developer deploys an application.

↓

### Step 2

Application uses a Kubernetes Service Account.

↓

### Step 3

The Service Account is associated with an AWS IAM Role.

↓

### Step 4

Amazon EKS issues an OIDC token.

↓

### Step 5

AWS STS validates the token.

↓

### Step 6

STS issues temporary AWS credentials.

↓

### Step 7

Application accesses AWS securely.

---

# OpenID Connect (OIDC)

IRSA depends on OpenID Connect (OIDC).

Amazon EKS creates an OIDC identity provider for every cluster.

```text
Amazon EKS

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

AWS IAM Trust
```

The IAM Role trusts identities issued by this OIDC provider.

Without OIDC, IRSA cannot function.

---

# AWS Security Token Service (STS)

AWS STS issues temporary AWS credentials after validating the workload identity.

```text
OIDC Token

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

AWS Service
```

Temporary credentials:

- Automatically expire
- Cannot be reused indefinitely
- Improve security
- Reduce credential theft

---

# IAM Trust Relationship

Every IAM Role used by IRSA includes a trust policy.

```text
IAM Role

↓

Trust Policy

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

Specific Service Account
```

Only authorised Service Accounts can assume the IAM Role.

---

# IRSA Architecture

```text
                    Amazon EKS Cluster

              ┌────────────────────────────┐
              │        Application Pod      │
              │                             │
              │  Service Account            │
              └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                     OIDC Authentication
                             │
                             ▼
                        AWS STS
                             │
                             ▼
                       IAM Role
                             │
                             ▼
               Amazon S3 / DynamoDB / SQS
```

Applications authenticate without requiring embedded AWS credentials.

---

# Enterprise Example

An image processing application uploads photographs to Amazon S3.

Architecture:

```text
Image Processing Pod

↓

Service Account

↓

IAM Role

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

Amazon S3
```

IAM permissions:

- Upload images
- Read images
- List bucket contents

Denied permissions:

- Delete bucket
- Manage IAM
- Launch EC2
- Modify networking

The application receives only the permissions it needs.

---

# IRSA with AWS Secrets Manager

Many applications retrieve secrets from AWS Secrets Manager.

```text
Application

↓

IRSA

↓

IAM Role

↓

AWS Secrets Manager

↓

Database Password
```

The password never exists inside the application image.

---

# IRSA with Amazon DynamoDB

```text
Order Service

↓

IRSA

↓

IAM Role

↓

Amazon DynamoDB
```

The application receives temporary permissions to read and update only its required DynamoDB tables.

---

# IRSA with Amazon SQS

```text
Payment Service

↓

IRSA

↓

IAM Role

↓

Amazon SQS
```

Only queue operations required by the application are permitted.

---

# Enterprise Identity Architecture

```text
Application

↓

Service Account

↓

RBAC

↓

OIDC Provider

↓

AWS STS

↓

IAM Role

↓

AWS Service
```

Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources.

IAM controls access to AWS resources.

Together they provide complete workload identity.

---

# Common IRSA Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers commonly identify:

- Shared Service Accounts
- Overprivileged IAM Roles
- Wildcard IAM policies
- Default Service Accounts
- Missing OIDC validation
- Excessive AWS permissions
- Unused IAM Roles
- Weak trust policies
- Overprivileged RBAC
- Long-lived credentials still present

Misconfigured IRSA can allow workloads to access resources beyond their intended scope.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- IAM Role assumptions
- AWS STS activity
- OIDC authentication events
- Service Account changes
- IAM policy updates
- Trust policy modifications
- Failed AssumeRole requests
- Unusual AWS API calls
- RBAC changes
- Privilege escalation attempts

CloudTrail and GuardDuty provide valuable visibility into IRSA activity.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global healthcare provider runs patient management applications on Amazon EKS.

Each workload has its own identity.

```text
Patient API

↓

Service Account

↓

Patient IAM Role

↓

AWS Secrets Manager

↓

Database Credentials

----------------------------

Image Service

↓

Service Account

↓

Image IAM Role

↓

Amazon S3

↓

Medical Images
```

Every workload receives only the permissions required for its business function.

This architecture improves:

- Security
- Compliance
- Auditing
- Operational efficiency

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Create dedicated Service Accounts for every workload.
- Implement IRSA for all production applications.
- Follow the Principle of Least Privilege.
- Use narrowly scoped IAM policies.
- Never store AWS Access Keys inside Pods.
- Enable CloudTrail logging.
- Monitor AWS STS activity.
- Review IAM trust policies regularly.
- Rotate application permissions as requirements change.
- Remove unused IAM Roles and Service Accounts.

IRSA should be the standard method for granting AWS permissions to Kubernetes workloads.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A media company stores AWS Access Keys inside a Docker image used by several applications.

The image is accidentally published to a public container registry.

An attacker extracts the credentials and:

- Downloads confidential data from Amazon S3.
- Launches EC2 instances.
- Reads DynamoDB tables.
- Deletes backups.

After migrating to IRSA:

- No AWS credentials exist inside container images.
- Temporary credentials expire automatically.
- IAM Roles restrict access to specific AWS resources.
- CloudTrail records every AssumeRole event.

The organisation significantly reduces its attack surface and improves compliance.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) is
- Why IRSA is important in Amazon EKS
- How OIDC and AWS STS enable workload authentication
- How Service Accounts integrate with IAM Roles
- The benefits of temporary credentials
- Common IRSA security risks
- Enterprise best practices for workload identity

IRSA is one of the most important Amazon EKS security features because it eliminates long-lived AWS credentials while providing secure, auditable, and least-privilege access to AWS services.

---

---

Section titled “OpenID Connect (OIDC)”

IRSA depends on OpenID Connect (OIDC).

Amazon EKS creates an OIDC identity provider for every cluster.

The IAM Role trusts identities issued by this OIDC provider.

Without OIDC, IRSA cannot function.

AWS Security Token Service (STS)

Section titled “AWS Security Token Service (STS)”

AWS STS issues temporary AWS credentials after validating the workload identity.

Temporary credentials:

  • Automatically expire
  • Cannot be reused indefinitely
  • Improve security
  • Reduce credential theft

IAM Trust Relationship

Section titled “IAM Trust Relationship”

Every IAM Role used by IRSA includes a trust policy.

Only authorised Service Accounts can assume the IAM Role.

IRSA Architecture

Section titled “IRSA Architecture”

Applications authenticate without requiring embedded AWS credentials.

Enterprise Example

Section titled “Enterprise Example”

An image processing application uploads photographs to Amazon S3.

Architecture:

IAM permissions:

  • Upload images
  • Read images
  • List bucket contents

Denied permissions:

  • Delete bucket
  • Manage IAM
  • Launch EC2
  • Modify networking

The application receives only the permissions it needs.

IRSA with AWS Secrets Manager

Section titled “IRSA with AWS Secrets Manager”

Many applications retrieve secrets from AWS Secrets Manager.

The password never exists inside the application image.

IRSA with Amazon DynamoDB

Section titled “IRSA with Amazon DynamoDB”

The application receives temporary permissions to read and update only its required DynamoDB tables.

IRSA with Amazon SQS

Section titled “IRSA with Amazon SQS”

Only queue operations required by the application are permitted.

Enterprise Identity Architecture

Section titled “Enterprise Identity Architecture”

Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources.

IAM controls access to AWS resources.

Together they provide complete workload identity.

Common IRSA Security Risks

Section titled “Common IRSA Security Risks”

Cloud Security Engineers commonly identify:

  • Shared Service Accounts
  • Overprivileged IAM Roles
  • Wildcard IAM policies
  • Default Service Accounts
  • Missing OIDC validation
  • Excessive AWS permissions
  • Unused IAM Roles
  • Weak trust policies
  • Overprivileged RBAC
  • Long-lived credentials still present

Misconfigured IRSA can allow workloads to access resources beyond their intended scope.

Enterprise Monitoring

Section titled “Enterprise Monitoring”

Security teams should monitor:

  • IAM Role assumptions
  • AWS STS activity
  • OIDC authentication events
  • Service Account changes
  • IAM policy updates
  • Trust policy modifications
  • Failed AssumeRole requests
  • Unusual AWS API calls
  • RBAC changes
  • Privilege escalation attempts

CloudTrail and GuardDuty provide valuable visibility into IRSA activity.

Enterprise Example

Section titled “Enterprise Example”

A global healthcare provider runs patient management applications on Amazon EKS.

Each workload has its own identity.

Every workload receives only the permissions required for its business function.

This architecture improves:

  • Security
  • Compliance
  • Auditing
  • Operational efficiency

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

  • Create dedicated Service Accounts for every workload.
  • Implement IRSA for all production applications.
  • Follow the Principle of Least Privilege.
  • Use narrowly scoped IAM policies.
  • Never store AWS Access Keys inside Pods.
  • Enable CloudTrail logging.
  • Monitor AWS STS activity.
  • Review IAM trust policies regularly.
  • Rotate application permissions as requirements change.
  • Remove unused IAM Roles and Service Accounts.

IRSA should be the standard method for granting AWS permissions to Kubernetes workloads.

Real-World Scenario

Section titled “Real-World Scenario”

A media company stores AWS Access Keys inside a Docker image used by several applications.

The image is accidentally published to a public container registry.

An attacker extracts the credentials and:

  • Downloads confidential data from Amazon S3.
  • Launches EC2 instances.
  • Reads DynamoDB tables.
  • Deletes backups.

After migrating to IRSA:

  • No AWS credentials exist inside container images.
  • Temporary credentials expire automatically.
  • IAM Roles restrict access to specific AWS resources.
  • CloudTrail records every AssumeRole event.

The organisation significantly reduces its attack surface and improves compliance.

  • Why IRSA is important in Amazon EKS
  • How OIDC and AWS STS enable workload authentication
  • How Service Accounts integrate with IAM Roles
  • The benefits of temporary credentials
  • Common IRSA security risks
  • Enterprise best practices for workload identity

IRSA is one of the most important Amazon EKS security features because it eliminates long-lived AWS credentials while providing secure, auditable, and least-privilege access to AWS services.

# Lesson 08 — Least Privilege Design

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)
- Learn why least privilege is critical in Kubernetes
- Design least privilege architectures for Amazon EKS
- Apply least privilege to Kubernetes RBAC
- Secure AWS IAM permissions
- Secure Service Accounts using IRSA
- Prevent privilege escalation
- Apply enterprise best practices

---

# Why This Matters

One of the biggest causes of cloud security incidents is **overprivileged identities**.

When users or applications have more permissions than necessary, attackers can exploit those permissions to:

- Access sensitive data
- Delete production workloads
- Modify Kubernetes resources
- Steal Secrets
- Escalate privileges
- Move laterally across environments

Most organisations don't fail because authentication is weak.

They fail because **authenticated identities have excessive permissions.**

Least Privilege reduces the attack surface by ensuring identities receive **only the permissions required to perform their jobs.**

---

# What is Least Privilege?

The **Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)** means:

> Every user, application, Service Account and system component should receive only the minimum permissions required to perform its intended function—and nothing more.

Permissions should be:

- Limited
- Temporary where possible
- Continuously reviewed
- Removed when no longer required

---

# Least Privilege Architecture

```text
Identity

↓

Authentication

↓

RBAC

↓

IAM Policy

↓

Allowed Resources

↓

Allowed Actions Only
```

Every layer reduces unnecessary access.

---

# Why Least Privilege Matters

Without least privilege:

```text
Developer

↓

Cluster Admin

↓

Entire Cluster
```

With least privilege:

```text
Developer

↓

Developer Role

↓

Development Namespace

↓

Read / Create / Update Only
```

If the developer account is compromised, the attacker is restricted to a much smaller scope.

---

# Least Privilege Across Amazon EKS

Least privilege should be implemented at multiple layers.

```text
Users

↓

AWS IAM

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

↓

Namespaces

↓

Service Accounts

↓

IAM Roles

↓

AWS Resources
```

Every layer contributes to reducing the overall attack surface.

---

# Least Privilege for Users

Human users should receive permissions based on their responsibilities.

Example:

| Role | Typical Access |
|------|----------------|
| Developer | Development Namespace |
| DevOps Engineer | CI/CD and deployments |
| Security Engineer | Read logs, audit resources |
| Platform Administrator | Cluster administration |
| SOC Analyst | Read-only monitoring |

No user should automatically receive administrative permissions.

---

# Least Privilege with RBAC

RBAC provides fine-grained authorization.

Example:

```text
Developer

↓

Role

↓

Pods

Deployments

Services

↓

Development Namespace
```

The same developer cannot:

- Modify production
- Delete Namespaces
- View Secrets in other environments

---

# Least Privilege with Namespaces

Namespaces create logical security boundaries.

```text
Cluster

├── Development
├── Testing
├── Staging
└── Production
```

Access should be restricted to only the required Namespace.

For example:

- Developers → Development
- QA Engineers → Testing
- Platform Team → Production

---

# Least Privilege for Service Accounts

Applications should never inherit broad permissions.

Instead:

```text
Payment API

↓

Payment Service Account

↓

Payment Role

↓

Read Payment Secret

↓

Write Payment Logs
```

The application cannot access unrelated resources.

---

# Least Privilege with IRSA

IRSA applies least privilege to AWS resources.

Example:

```text
Payment Service

↓

IAM Role

↓

Amazon S3

↓

Upload Receipts Only
```

Denied:

- EC2
- IAM
- Route 53
- CloudFormation

Applications receive only the AWS permissions they require.

---

# IAM Policy Design

Instead of:

```text
Amazon S3

↓

Full Access
```

Grant:

```text
Amazon S3

↓

GetObject

PutObject

Specific Bucket Only
```

Restrict:

- Actions
- Resources
- Conditions

Avoid wildcard (`*`) permissions whenever possible.

---

# Temporary Privileged Access

Some tasks require elevated permissions.

Examples include:

- Cluster upgrades
- Emergency troubleshooting
- Incident response

Rather than granting permanent administrator access:

```text
User

↓

Approval

↓

Temporary Admin Role

↓

Expires Automatically
```

This is commonly known as **Just-in-Time (JIT) Access**.

---

# Separation of Duties

Enterprise environments separate responsibilities to reduce risk.

Example:

```text
Developers

↓

Build Applications

--------------------

Platform Team

↓

Manage Infrastructure

--------------------

Security Team

↓

Audit & Monitor

--------------------

SOC Team

↓

Incident Response
```

No single team should control every aspect of the environment.

---

# Privilege Escalation

Improper permissions can allow attackers to gain additional privileges.

Example:

```text
Developer

↓

Can Create ClusterRoleBinding

↓

Assign Cluster Admin

↓

Full Cluster Access
```

RBAC should prevent identities from granting themselves additional permissions.

---

# Enterprise Least Privilege Architecture

```text
Employee

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM Role

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

↓

Namespace

↓

Service Account

↓

IRSA

↓

AWS Services
```

Every permission is intentionally limited.

---

# Enterprise Example

A financial organisation operates Amazon EKS for online banking.

### Developer

- Development Namespace
- Deploy applications
- View logs

### Security Engineer

- Read audit logs
- Review RBAC
- View GuardDuty findings

### Platform Administrator

- Upgrade EKS
- Manage Nodes
- Configure networking

### Payment Service

- Read payment Secrets
- Upload receipts to Amazon S3
- Access payment database

No identity receives permissions outside its responsibilities.

---

# Common Least Privilege Mistakes

Security teams frequently discover:

- Everyone assigned `cluster-admin`
- Wildcard IAM policies (`*`)
- Shared administrator accounts
- Default Service Accounts
- Overprivileged CI/CD pipelines
- Broad Secret access
- Production write access for developers
- Unused IAM Roles
- Forgotten administrator accounts
- Excessive Namespace permissions

These issues significantly increase the impact of compromised identities.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Privileged Role assignments
- IAM policy changes
- RBAC modifications
- ClusterRoleBinding creation
- New administrator accounts
- Privilege escalation attempts
- IRSA role assumptions
- Namespace permission changes
- Service Account updates
- Unusual API activity

Identity-related monitoring is a critical part of enterprise security operations.

---

# Least Privilege Review Process

Least privilege is not a one-time activity.

Organisations should perform regular access reviews.

```text
Review Users

↓

Review Roles

↓

Review IAM Policies

↓

Remove Unused Access

↓

Audit Changes
```

Periodic reviews reduce permission creep over time.

---

# Enterprise Security Controls

Least privilege should be supported by additional security controls:

- Kubernetes RBAC
- AWS IAM
- IAM Identity Center
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs)
- Network Policies
- Pod Security Standards
- AWS Config
- Amazon GuardDuty
- AWS CloudTrail

Together these controls create a layered defence.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A developer is mistakenly granted the **cluster-admin** ClusterRole.

Their workstation is compromised through a phishing attack.

The attacker:

- Deletes production Deployments
- Reads Kubernetes Secrets
- Creates privileged Pods
- Modifies RBAC
- Disables security monitoring

If least privilege had been implemented:

- The developer would only have access to the Development Namespace.
- Production resources would remain protected.
- The attacker would be unable to escalate privileges.
- Security teams would have more time to detect and contain the incident.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Apply the Principle of Least Privilege to every identity.
- Grant only the permissions required for each role.
- Use Namespace-scoped Roles whenever possible.
- Restrict ClusterRoles to platform administrators.
- Avoid wildcard IAM permissions.
- Implement IRSA for application workloads.
- Use temporary privileged access for administrative tasks.
- Perform regular access reviews.
- Monitor privilege escalation attempts.
- Remove unused identities, Roles and IAM permissions promptly.

Least privilege should be embedded into every stage of the Kubernetes lifecycle.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- The Principle of Least Privilege
- Why least privilege is essential for Kubernetes security
- How RBAC supports least privilege
- How IAM and IRSA reduce AWS permissions
- The importance of Namespace isolation
- How to prevent privilege escalation
- Enterprise least privilege design patterns
- Best practices for securing identities and workloads

Least privilege is one of the most effective security controls for reducing risk in Amazon EKS and Kubernetes environments. It limits the blast radius of compromised accounts, supports compliance requirements, and forms the foundation of Zero Trust security.

---

---

---

Which of the following increases the risk of privilege escalation?

---

Which practice helps prevent permission creep over time?

- A. Permanently granting administrator access
- B. Regular access reviews and removal of unused permissions

# Lesson 09 — Kubernetes Multi-Tenant Security

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand multi-tenancy in Kubernetes
- Differentiate between soft and hard multi-tenancy
- Design secure multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters
- Understand Namespace isolation
- Implement RBAC for tenant separation
- Secure tenant communication using Network Policies
- Apply Resource Quotas and Limit Ranges
- Identify common multi-tenancy security risks
- Apply enterprise best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Modern enterprises rarely dedicate one Kubernetes cluster to a single application.

Instead, organisations commonly host:

- Multiple development teams
- Business units
- Customers
- Projects
- Applications
- Environments

...within the same Kubernetes cluster.

For example:

A financial organisation may run:

- Online Banking
- Credit Card Services
- Loan Processing
- Fraud Detection
- Customer Portal

inside a shared Amazon EKS cluster.

Without proper isolation, one workload could accidentally—or intentionally—access another team's applications or sensitive data.

Multi-tenant security ensures that each tenant remains isolated while sharing the same infrastructure.

---

# What is Multi-Tenancy?

Multi-tenancy is the practice of allowing multiple independent tenants to share the same Kubernetes infrastructure securely.

A tenant may represent:

- A team
- A department
- A customer
- A project
- A business unit
- An application

Each tenant operates independently while sharing the cluster.

---

# Multi-Tenant Architecture

```text
Amazon EKS Cluster

├── Finance Team
│
├── Security Team
│
├── HR Team
│
├── Marketing Team
│
└── Operations Team
```

Although everyone shares the same cluster, security controls prevent unauthorised access between tenants.

---

# Benefits of Multi-Tenancy

Multi-tenancy provides:

- Better resource utilisation
- Reduced infrastructure costs
- Simplified management
- Centralised monitoring
- Easier governance
- Faster deployments
- Consistent security controls
- Improved scalability

Large organisations commonly operate shared Kubernetes platforms to maximise efficiency.

---

# Types of Multi-Tenancy

Kubernetes supports two primary models.

| Model | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Soft Multi-Tenancy | Logical isolation within a shared cluster |
| Hard Multi-Tenancy | Strong isolation using dedicated clusters or virtual clusters |

Choosing the right model depends on security, compliance, and operational requirements.

---

# Soft Multi-Tenancy

Soft multi-tenancy uses Kubernetes security features to separate tenants.

Example:

```text
Cluster

├── Namespace A

├── Namespace B

├── Namespace C

└── Namespace D
```

Isolation is achieved using:

- Namespaces
- RBAC
- Network Policies
- Resource Quotas
- Pod Security Standards

This is the most common enterprise deployment model.

---

# Hard Multi-Tenancy

Hard multi-tenancy provides stronger isolation.

```text
Production Cluster

↓

Finance Cluster

↓

HR Cluster

↓

Government Cluster
```

Each tenant operates in a dedicated cluster or isolated Kubernetes environment.

Hard multi-tenancy is often required for:

- Government
- Defence
- Healthcare
- Financial services
- Highly regulated industries

---

# Namespace Isolation

Namespaces provide the first layer of tenant isolation.

Example:

```text
Amazon EKS

├── finance

├── hr

├── security

├── operations

└── monitoring
```

Each Namespace contains its own:

- Pods
- Services
- Secrets
- ConfigMaps
- Deployments

Namespaces prevent accidental interaction between teams.

---

# RBAC Isolation

RBAC restricts tenant permissions.

Example:

```text
Finance Developers

↓

Finance Role

↓

Finance Namespace
```

The Finance team cannot:

- Read HR Secrets
- Modify Security workloads
- Delete Operations Pods

Each tenant receives only the permissions required for its Namespace.

---

# Network Policies

Namespaces alone do not prevent network communication.

Network Policies define which Pods can communicate.

```text
Finance Namespace

↓

Network Policy

↓

Only Finance Pods
```

Blocked:

```text
HR Pod

↓

Finance Database

✗ Denied
```

Network Policies enforce Zero Trust networking within the cluster.

---

# Resource Quotas

Resource Quotas prevent one tenant from consuming all cluster resources.

Example:

```text
Finance Namespace

CPU

20 vCPU

Memory

64 GB

Pods

100
```

Without quotas, a single tenant could exhaust cluster capacity and impact other workloads.

---

# Limit Ranges

Limit Ranges define default resource requests and limits.

Example:

```text
Every Pod

CPU Request

500m

Memory Request

512Mi

CPU Limit

2 vCPU

Memory Limit

2Gi
```

This prevents poorly configured workloads from monopolising compute resources.

---

# Pod Security Standards

Pod Security Standards restrict what workloads are allowed to do.

Examples include:

- Prevent privileged containers
- Restrict hostPath volumes
- Prevent host networking
- Block privilege escalation
- Restrict Linux capabilities

These controls reduce the impact of compromised workloads.

---

# Tenant Identity

Each tenant should have its own:

- Namespace
- RBAC Roles
- Service Accounts
- IAM Roles (IRSA)
- Secrets
- Network Policies

Example:

```text
Finance

↓

Finance Service Account

↓

Finance IAM Role

↓

Finance Secrets
```

Tenant identities should never be shared.

---

# Shared Services

Some services are intentionally shared across tenants.

Examples include:

- Prometheus
- Grafana
- Fluent Bit
- Amazon CloudWatch
- AWS Security Hub
- Amazon GuardDuty
- AWS Config

Architecture:

```text
Shared Monitoring Namespace

↓

Prometheus

↓

Grafana

↓

CloudWatch
```

Shared services should be carefully secured because they often have visibility across multiple tenants.

---

# Enterprise Multi-Tenant Architecture

```text
Amazon EKS Cluster

├── finance
│      ├── RBAC
│      ├── Network Policy
│      ├── IRSA
│      └── Resource Quota
│
├── hr
│      ├── RBAC
│      ├── Network Policy
│      ├── IRSA
│      └── Resource Quota
│
├── security
│      ├── RBAC
│      ├── Network Policy
│      ├── IRSA
│      └── Resource Quota
│
└── shared-services
       ├── Monitoring
       ├── Logging
       ├── Security
       └── Backup
```

Every tenant operates independently while platform services remain centrally managed.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational bank hosts more than 300 applications in Amazon EKS.

Tenant structure:

```text
Retail Banking

Corporate Banking

Payments

Fraud Detection

Customer Portal

Risk Management

Security Operations
```

Security controls include:

- Namespace isolation
- RBAC
- Network Policies
- IRSA
- Resource Quotas
- Pod Security Standards
- AWS WAF
- GuardDuty
- CloudTrail
- AWS Config

This enables secure multi-team collaboration while maintaining regulatory compliance.

---

# Common Multi-Tenant Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Shared Namespaces
- Excessive RBAC permissions
- Missing Network Policies
- Shared Service Accounts
- Shared Secrets
- No Resource Quotas
- Privileged containers
- Default Service Accounts
- Cross-namespace communication
- Shared IAM Roles

These issues can lead to lateral movement and data exposure.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should continuously monitor:

- Namespace creation
- Namespace deletion
- RBAC changes
- Network Policy updates
- Cross-namespace communication
- Service Account changes
- Resource Quota violations
- Privileged Pod creation
- IRSA activity
- Tenant resource usage

Monitoring helps identify isolation failures and unauthorised activity.

---

# Zero Trust in Multi-Tenant Kubernetes

Enterprise Kubernetes platforms increasingly adopt a **Zero Trust** approach.

Core principles include:

- Never trust by default
- Verify every identity
- Enforce least privilege
- Restrict east-west traffic
- Continuously monitor workloads
- Assume breach

Example:

```text
Tenant A

↓

Authentication

↓

RBAC

↓

Network Policy

↓

Pod Security

↓

AWS IAM

↓

Access Granted
```

Each request is evaluated independently before access is allowed.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A SaaS company hosts multiple customers in a shared Amazon EKS cluster.

Due to missing Network Policies, a compromised application in **Customer A's Namespace** scans the cluster and successfully connects to **Customer B's database service**.

The attacker:

- Enumerates internal services
- Attempts credential theft
- Accesses sensitive customer information

Following the incident, the company implements:

- Namespace isolation
- Default deny Network Policies
- Dedicated Service Accounts
- IRSA
- Resource Quotas
- Pod Security Standards

These controls prevent lateral movement between tenants and significantly improve the platform's security posture.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Isolate every tenant using dedicated Namespaces.
- Implement RBAC with the Principle of Least Privilege.
- Apply default deny Network Policies.
- Use dedicated Service Accounts for every application.
- Implement IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA).
- Configure Resource Quotas and Limit Ranges.
- Enforce Pod Security Standards.
- Separate shared platform services from tenant workloads.
- Monitor tenant activity continuously.
- Perform regular access and configuration reviews.

A secure multi-tenant architecture protects individual workloads while enabling efficient use of shared Kubernetes infrastructure.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What Kubernetes multi-tenancy is
- The difference between soft and hard multi-tenancy
- How Namespaces isolate tenants
- How RBAC enforces tenant permissions
- Why Network Policies are essential
- The importance of Resource Quotas and Limit Ranges
- How Pod Security Standards strengthen isolation
- Common multi-tenant security risks
- Enterprise best practices for building secure shared Kubernetes platforms

Multi-tenant security is a core capability of Amazon EKS and Kubernetes. When properly implemented, it allows organisations to securely operate shared clusters while maintaining strong isolation, compliance, and operational efficiency.

# Lesson 10 — Enterprise Access Governance

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand Enterprise Access Governance
- Learn the principles of Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)
- Understand Privileged Access Management (PAM)
- Learn identity lifecycle management
- Perform enterprise access reviews
- Understand audit logging and compliance
- Identify governance risks
- Apply enterprise access governance best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Enterprise Kubernetes environments may have:

- Thousands of employees
- Hundreds of developers
- Multiple DevOps teams
- Third-party contractors
- CI/CD pipelines
- Automated workloads
- Multiple Amazon EKS clusters
- Multiple AWS accounts

Without proper governance:

- Former employees may retain access.
- Developers may accumulate excessive permissions.
- Contractors may never be removed.
- Privileged accounts may be shared.
- Compliance requirements may not be met.

Access Governance ensures that the **right people have the right access at the right time—for the right reason.**

---

# What is Enterprise Access Governance?

Enterprise Access Governance is the collection of policies, processes and technologies used to control, review, monitor and audit access to systems and data.

It ensures that:

- Only authorised identities receive access.
- Access is approved.
- Access is periodically reviewed.
- Access is removed when no longer required.
- Privileged activities are audited.

Governance is a continuous process rather than a one-time configuration.

---

# Enterprise Access Governance Architecture

```text
User

↓

Identity Provider

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

AWS IAM

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

↓

Kubernetes Resources
```

Every access request passes through multiple governance controls before reaching Kubernetes.

---

# Identity Governance and Administration (IGA)

Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) manages the complete lifecycle of user identities.

IGA includes:

- User provisioning
- Role assignment
- Access approvals
- Periodic access reviews
- Identity certification
- Deprovisioning

IGA ensures access remains aligned with business responsibilities.

---

# Identity Lifecycle Management

Every enterprise identity follows a lifecycle.

```text
Join

↓

Provision

↓

Role Assignment

↓

Permission Updates

↓

Periodic Review

↓

Role Change

↓

Offboarding

↓

Access Removed
```

Access should evolve as employees change roles and should be removed immediately when no longer required.

---

# Joiner, Mover and Leaver (JML)

Most organisations manage access using the **JML** model.

| Lifecycle Stage | Governance Activity |
|-----------------|---------------------|
| Joiner | Create identity and assign appropriate access |
| Mover | Update permissions when responsibilities change |
| Leaver | Remove all access immediately |

This process helps reduce stale accounts and excessive permissions.

---

# Role-Based Access Governance

Enterprise access is usually based on predefined job roles.

Example:

```text
Cloud Security Engineer

↓

Security Role

↓

Read Security Hub

Read GuardDuty

View Audit Logs

Review RBAC
```

Users receive permissions based on their responsibilities rather than individual requests.

---

# Privileged Access Management (PAM)

Privileged accounts require stronger controls than standard user accounts.

Examples include:

- Kubernetes Cluster Administrators
- AWS Administrators
- Security Administrators
- Database Administrators
- Platform Engineers

These identities have the ability to modify critical infrastructure.

---

# Just-in-Time (JIT) Privileged Access

Permanent administrator access should be avoided.

Instead:

```text
Engineer

↓

Approval

↓

Temporary Admin Role

↓

Time-Limited Access

↓

Automatic Removal
```

Just-in-Time (JIT) access reduces the attack surface and limits the duration of privileged permissions.

---

# Separation of Duties (SoD)

Critical responsibilities should be divided among multiple individuals or teams.

Example:

```text
Developer

↓

Build Application

------------------------

DevOps Engineer

↓

Deploy Application

------------------------

Security Engineer

↓

Approve Security Controls

------------------------

Platform Team

↓

Manage Cluster
```

No single person should control the entire deployment lifecycle.

---

# Access Approval Workflow

Enterprise organisations often require approvals before granting privileged access.

```text
User Requests Access

↓

Manager Approval

↓

Security Approval

↓

IAM Role Assigned

↓

Amazon EKS Access
```

Approval workflows improve accountability and reduce unauthorised privilege assignments.

---

# Periodic Access Reviews

Access should be reviewed regularly.

Review process:

```text
Review Users

↓

Review IAM Roles

↓

Review RBAC

↓

Remove Unused Permissions

↓

Document Changes
```

Quarterly and annual reviews are common for production environments.

---

# Identity Certification

Managers and system owners periodically certify that users still require their assigned access.

Example:

```text
Finance Manager

↓

Review Finance Team Access

↓

Approve

or

Revoke
```

Identity certification is a common compliance requirement.

---

# Audit Logging

Every privileged action should be recorded.

Examples include:

- User logins
- RBAC changes
- IAM policy changes
- ClusterRoleBinding creation
- Secret access
- Namespace deletion
- Service Account creation
- IRSA role assumptions

Comprehensive audit logs support investigations and compliance reporting.

---

# Governance Monitoring Architecture

```text
User Activity

↓

AWS CloudTrail

↓

Kubernetes Audit Logs

↓

Amazon CloudWatch

↓

AWS Security Hub

↓

SOC Team
```

Security teams monitor governance events continuously.

---

# Compliance Frameworks

Access Governance supports compliance with many industry standards.

Common frameworks include:

- ISO/IEC 27001
- SOC 2
- PCI DSS
- HIPAA
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
- NIST SP 800-53
- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
- CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark

These frameworks require organisations to demonstrate effective access controls and auditing.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global financial institution operates multiple Amazon EKS clusters.

Access model:

```text
Developer

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

Developer IAM Role

↓

Development Namespace

------------------------

Security Engineer

↓

Security IAM Role

↓

Read Audit Logs

↓

Review RBAC

------------------------

Platform Administrator

↓

Temporary PAM Role

↓

Cluster Administration
```

Every privileged action is logged using:

- AWS CloudTrail
- Kubernetes Audit Logs
- Amazon GuardDuty
- AWS Security Hub

Quarterly access reviews ensure permissions remain appropriate.

---

# Common Governance Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently discover:

- Shared administrator accounts
- Stale employee accounts
- Contractors retaining access
- Excessive IAM permissions
- Overprivileged RBAC roles
- Missing approval workflows
- No access reviews
- Permanent administrator privileges
- Unmonitored privileged activity
- Incomplete audit logging

These issues increase the likelihood of unauthorised access and compliance failures.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- New administrator accounts
- Failed authentication attempts
- IAM Role creation
- IAM policy changes
- RBAC modifications
- Privilege escalation attempts
- Access review completion
- JIT access requests
- Service Account changes
- High-risk administrative actions

Monitoring provides visibility into changes that could impact the security of the Kubernetes environment.

---

# Governance Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Integrate Amazon EKS with IAM Identity Center.
- Implement Identity Governance and Administration (IGA).
- Follow the Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) process.
- Use Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
- Apply the Principle of Least Privilege.
- Implement Privileged Access Management (PAM).
- Use Just-in-Time (JIT) administrative access.
- Conduct periodic access reviews.
- Enable comprehensive audit logging.
- Remove unused identities and permissions promptly.

Governance should be embedded into daily operations rather than treated as an annual compliance exercise.

# Real-World Scenario

An employee leaves an organisation after working as a Platform Engineer.

Because the offboarding process fails:

- Their IAM account remains active.
- Their Kubernetes RBAC permissions remain unchanged.
- Their VPN account is still enabled.

Months later, the employee's credentials are compromised.

An attacker:

- Authenticates to AWS.
- Accesses Amazon EKS.
- Creates privileged Pods.
- Reads Kubernetes Secrets.
- Disables monitoring.

Following the incident, the organisation implements:

- Joiner-Mover-Leaver lifecycle management
- IAM Identity Center integration
- Quarterly access reviews
- Just-in-Time privileged access
- Automated account deprovisioning
- Continuous audit monitoring

These governance improvements significantly reduce the risk of stale identities and unauthorised access.

# Lesson 11 — IAM Security Best Practices

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand AWS IAM security best practices
- Secure human and workload identities
- Implement enterprise IAM architectures
- Apply least privilege principles
- Secure IAM Roles and Service Accounts
- Protect privileged identities
- Monitor IAM activities
- Implement continuous IAM governance

---

# Why This Matters

Identity is the new security perimeter.

In cloud environments, attackers rarely target infrastructure first.

Instead, they target:

- IAM Users
- IAM Roles
- Service Accounts
- AWS Access Keys
- Temporary Credentials
- Identity Providers
- Administrator Accounts

According to numerous cloud security incident investigations, compromised identities are one of the most common attack vectors.

Strong IAM practices significantly reduce the likelihood and impact of these attacks.

---

# What is IAM Security?

IAM Security is the practice of protecting identities, authentication mechanisms, authorisation controls and access permissions within AWS.

A secure IAM implementation ensures that:

- Only authorised identities can authenticate.
- Permissions are limited to business requirements.
- Privileged access is tightly controlled.
- Identity activity is continuously monitored.
- Credentials are protected and regularly reviewed.

IAM security is the foundation of cloud security.

---

# Enterprise IAM Security Architecture

```text
                     Users & Applications
                              │
                              ▼
                 Identity Provider (Entra ID / Okta)
                              │
                              ▼
                  AWS IAM Identity Center
                              │
               ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
               ▼                             ▼
         Human IAM Roles              Workload Identities
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                          IRSA
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                     AWS Services
```

Human users and workloads should use different identity mechanisms while following the same security principles.

---

# IAM Security Principles

Enterprise IAM security is built on several core principles:

- Least Privilege
- Zero Trust
- Separation of Duties
- Temporary Credentials
- Strong Authentication
- Continuous Monitoring
- Identity Lifecycle Management
- Regular Access Reviews

These principles should be applied consistently across every AWS account and Amazon EKS cluster.

---

# Avoid Long-Term IAM Users

Enterprise environments should minimise the use of permanent IAM Users.

Instead of:

```text
Developer

↓

IAM User

↓

Access Keys
```

Use:

```text
Developer

↓

Identity Provider

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

Temporary IAM Role
```

Temporary credentials reduce the risk of credential theft and simplify identity management.

---

# Protect the AWS Root User

The AWS Root User has unrestricted access to the AWS account.

Best practices include:

- Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
- Use a strong, unique password
- Do not create access keys
- Store credentials securely
- Use the Root User only for tasks that explicitly require it

The Root User should never be used for day-to-day administration.

---

# Use IAM Identity Center

AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralised workforce identity management.

Benefits include:

- Single Sign-On (SSO)
- Centralised access management
- Integration with enterprise Identity Providers
- Temporary credentials
- Simplified onboarding and offboarding
- Improved auditability

Most enterprise organisations use IAM Identity Center rather than individual IAM Users.

---

# Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

MFA adds an additional verification step before access is granted.

```text
Username

↓

Password

↓

Authenticator App

↓

Access Granted
```

MFA significantly reduces the risk of compromised credentials leading to unauthorised access.

---

# Apply the Principle of Least Privilege

Every identity should receive only the permissions required to perform its tasks.

Instead of:

```text
Amazon S3

↓

FullAccess
```

Grant:

```text
Amazon S3

↓

GetObject

PutObject

Specific Bucket
```

Permissions should be:

- Resource-specific
- Action-specific
- Time-limited where possible

---

# Prefer IAM Roles Over IAM Users

IAM Roles provide temporary credentials that are automatically rotated.

```text
User

↓

IAM Role

↓

AWS STS

↓

Temporary Credentials
```

Benefits include:

- No long-term credentials
- Reduced attack surface
- Automatic credential expiration
- Improved auditing

---

# Secure Kubernetes Workloads with IRSA

Applications running in Amazon EKS should use **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)**.

```text
Application

↓

Service Account

↓

OIDC

↓

AWS STS

↓

IAM Role

↓

Amazon S3
```

Benefits include:

- No embedded AWS Access Keys
- Temporary credentials
- Fine-grained AWS permissions
- Improved workload isolation

---

# Secure IAM Policies

IAM policies should be as restrictive as possible.

Avoid:

```json
"Action": "*",
"Resource": "*"
```

Prefer:

```text
Amazon S3

↓

Specific Bucket

↓

Read Objects

↓

Upload Objects
```

Restrict:

- Actions
- Resources
- Conditions
- Principals

---

# Secure Trust Relationships

IAM Roles rely on trust policies to determine who can assume them.

Example:

```text
IAM Role

↓

Trust Policy

↓

Specific OIDC Provider

↓

Specific Service Account
```

Avoid wildcard trust relationships that allow unintended identities to assume privileged roles.

---

# Rotate and Eliminate Credentials

Where possible:

- Avoid long-lived access keys.
- Rotate any required credentials regularly.
- Use AWS Secrets Manager for application secrets.
- Prefer temporary credentials issued by AWS STS.

Short-lived credentials minimise the impact of credential compromise.

---

# Separate Human and Workload Identities

Human users and applications should never share identities.

```text
Human User

↓

IAM Role

-------------------------

Application

↓

Service Account

↓

IRSA

↓

Dedicated IAM Role
```

This separation improves auditing and reduces the risk of privilege misuse.

---

# Implement Permission Boundaries

Permission Boundaries define the maximum permissions an IAM identity can receive.

```text
Developer IAM Role

↓

Permission Boundary

↓

Maximum Allowed Permissions
```

This prevents administrators from accidentally assigning excessive privileges.

---

# Use Service Control Policies (SCPs)

In AWS Organizations, **Service Control Policies (SCPs)** provide guardrails across multiple AWS accounts.

Example restrictions:

- Prevent deletion of CloudTrail
- Prevent disabling GuardDuty
- Restrict Regions
- Block creation of unrestricted IAM Users
- Require encryption

SCPs complement IAM policies by enforcing organisation-wide security controls.

---

# Monitor IAM Activity

Security teams should continuously monitor:

- User logins
- Failed authentication attempts
- IAM Role assumptions
- Access key creation
- IAM policy changes
- Trust policy modifications
- Root account activity
- IRSA role assumptions
- Privilege escalation attempts
- Unusual API activity

Monitoring enables early detection of suspicious identity behaviour.

---

# Enterprise IAM Monitoring Architecture

```text
IAM Events

↓

AWS CloudTrail

↓

Amazon CloudWatch

↓

Amazon GuardDuty

↓

AWS Security Hub

↓

SOC Team
```

These services provide visibility into identity-related activity and security findings.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational healthcare provider operates Amazon EKS across multiple AWS accounts.

Identity architecture:

```text
Employees

↓

Microsoft Entra ID

↓

IAM Identity Center

↓

Temporary IAM Roles

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

RBAC

------------------------

Applications

↓

Service Accounts

↓

IRSA

↓

AWS STS

↓

Amazon S3

↓

AWS Secrets Manager
```

Security controls include:

- MFA enforcement
- IRSA for workloads
- Least Privilege IAM policies
- SCP guardrails
- CloudTrail logging
- GuardDuty monitoring
- Quarterly access reviews

This approach provides strong security while maintaining operational efficiency.

---

# Common IAM Security Mistakes

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Use of Root User for daily administration
- Missing MFA
- Long-lived IAM Users
- Shared administrator accounts
- Wildcard IAM policies
- Overprivileged IAM Roles
- Hardcoded AWS credentials
- Shared Service Accounts
- Unused access keys
- Missing CloudTrail logging

These issues increase the likelihood of identity compromise and privilege escalation.

---

# Enterprise Governance

IAM security should include:

- Identity lifecycle management
- Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) processes
- Regular access reviews
- Just-in-Time (JIT) privileged access
- Separation of Duties (SoD)
- Continuous compliance monitoring
- Automated remediation where appropriate

Governance ensures IAM remains secure as the organisation evolves.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Protect the AWS Root User with MFA and avoid using it for daily tasks.
- Integrate AWS with IAM Identity Center and enterprise Identity Providers.
- Prefer IAM Roles over IAM Users.
- Implement IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for all Kubernetes workloads.
- Apply the Principle of Least Privilege to every IAM policy.
- Avoid wildcard permissions and overly broad trust policies.
- Use temporary credentials issued by AWS STS.
- Enable CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub for continuous monitoring.
- Perform regular IAM reviews and remove unused identities, roles and permissions.
- Enforce organisation-wide guardrails using Service Control Policies (SCPs).

Strong IAM practices form the foundation of a secure Amazon EKS environment.

---

# Real-World Scenario

An organisation allows developers to use permanent IAM Users with long-lived access keys stored on local workstations.

A phishing attack compromises one developer's credentials.

The attacker:

- Logs into AWS.
- Creates new IAM Users.
- Assumes privileged roles.
- Disables CloudTrail.
- Exfiltrates sensitive customer data from Amazon S3.

Following the incident, the organisation implements:

- IAM Identity Center
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Temporary IAM Roles
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- Service Control Policies
- CloudTrail monitoring
- Quarterly IAM reviews

These controls dramatically reduce the attack surface and improve compliance.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- AWS IAM security principles
- Root User protection
- IAM Identity Center best practices
- Multi-Factor Authentication
- Least Privilege IAM design
- IAM Roles and temporary credentials
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- Secure IAM policies and trust relationships
- Service Control Policies (SCPs)
- Continuous IAM monitoring and governance

Strong IAM security is the cornerstone of enterprise cloud security. By combining Identity Federation, IAM Roles, IRSA, Least Privilege, Service Control Policies and continuous monitoring, organisations can build resilient and secure Amazon EKS environments.

Protect the AWS Root User

Section titled “Protect the AWS Root User”

The AWS Root User has unrestricted access to the AWS account.

Best practices include:

  • Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
  • Use a strong, unique password
  • Do not create access keys
  • Store credentials securely
  • Use the Root User only for tasks that explicitly require it

The Root User should never be used for day-to-day administration.

Use IAM Identity Center

Section titled “Use IAM Identity Center”

AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralised workforce identity management.

Benefits include:

  • Single Sign-On (SSO)
  • Centralised access management
  • Integration with enterprise Identity Providers
  • Temporary credentials
  • Simplified onboarding and offboarding
  • Improved auditability

Most enterprise organisations use IAM Identity Center rather than individual IAM Users.

Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Section titled “Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)”

MFA adds an additional verification step before access is granted.

MFA significantly reduces the risk of compromised credentials leading to unauthorised access.

Apply the Principle of Least Privilege

Section titled “Apply the Principle of Least Privilege”

Every identity should receive only the permissions required to perform its tasks.

Instead of:

Grant:

Permissions should be:

  • Resource-specific
  • Action-specific
  • Time-limited where possible

Prefer IAM Roles Over IAM Users

Section titled “Prefer IAM Roles Over IAM Users”

IAM Roles provide temporary credentials that are automatically rotated.

Benefits include:

  • No long-term credentials
  • Reduced attack surface
  • Automatic credential expiration
  • Improved auditing

Secure Kubernetes Workloads with IRSA

Section titled “Secure Kubernetes Workloads with IRSA”

Applications running in Amazon EKS should use IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA).

Benefits include:

  • No embedded AWS Access Keys
  • Temporary credentials
  • Fine-grained AWS permissions
  • Improved workload isolation

Secure IAM Policies

Section titled “Secure IAM Policies”

IAM policies should be as restrictive as possible.

Avoid:

Prefer:

Restrict:

  • Actions
  • Resources
  • Conditions
  • Principals

Secure Trust Relationships

Section titled “Secure Trust Relationships”

IAM Roles rely on trust policies to determine who can assume them.

Example:

Avoid wildcard trust relationships that allow unintended identities to assume privileged roles.

Rotate and Eliminate Credentials

Section titled “Rotate and Eliminate Credentials”

Where possible:

  • Avoid long-lived access keys.
  • Rotate any required credentials regularly.
  • Use AWS Secrets Manager for application secrets.
  • Prefer temporary credentials issued by AWS STS.

Short-lived credentials minimise the impact of credential compromise.

Separate Human and Workload Identities

Section titled “Separate Human and Workload Identities”

Human users and applications should never share identities.

This separation improves auditing and reduces the risk of privilege misuse.

Implement Permission Boundaries

Section titled “Implement Permission Boundaries”

Permission Boundaries define the maximum permissions an IAM identity can receive.

This prevents administrators from accidentally assigning excessive privileges.

Use Service Control Policies (SCPs)

Section titled “Use Service Control Policies (SCPs)”

In AWS Organizations, Service Control Policies (SCPs) provide guardrails across multiple AWS accounts.

Example restrictions:

  • Prevent deletion of CloudTrail
  • Prevent disabling GuardDuty
  • Restrict Regions
  • Block creation of unrestricted IAM Users
  • Require encryption

SCPs complement IAM policies by enforcing organisation-wide security controls.

Monitor IAM Activity

Section titled “Monitor IAM Activity”

Security teams should continuously monitor:

  • User logins
  • Failed authentication attempts
  • IAM Role assumptions
  • Access key creation
  • IAM policy changes
  • Trust policy modifications
  • Root account activity
  • IRSA role assumptions
  • Privilege escalation attempts
  • Unusual API activity

Monitoring enables early detection of suspicious identity behaviour.

Enterprise IAM Monitoring Architecture

Section titled “Enterprise IAM Monitoring Architecture”

These services provide visibility into identity-related activity and security findings.

Enterprise Example

Section titled “Enterprise Example”

A multinational healthcare provider operates Amazon EKS across multiple AWS accounts.

Identity architecture:

Security controls include:

  • MFA enforcement
  • IRSA for workloads
  • Least Privilege IAM policies
  • SCP guardrails
  • CloudTrail logging
  • GuardDuty monitoring
  • Quarterly access reviews

This approach provides strong security while maintaining operational efficiency.

Common IAM Security Mistakes

Section titled “Common IAM Security Mistakes”

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

  • Use of Root User for daily administration
  • Missing MFA
  • Long-lived IAM Users
  • Shared administrator accounts
  • Wildcard IAM policies
  • Overprivileged IAM Roles
  • Hardcoded AWS credentials
  • Shared Service Accounts
  • Unused access keys
  • Missing CloudTrail logging

These issues increase the likelihood of identity compromise and privilege escalation.

Enterprise Governance

Section titled “Enterprise Governance”

IAM security should include:

  • Identity lifecycle management
  • Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) processes
  • Regular access reviews
  • Just-in-Time (JIT) privileged access
  • Separation of Duties (SoD)
  • Continuous compliance monitoring
  • Automated remediation where appropriate

Governance ensures IAM remains secure as the organisation evolves.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

  • Protect the AWS Root User with MFA and avoid using it for daily tasks.
  • Integrate AWS with IAM Identity Center and enterprise Identity Providers.
  • Prefer IAM Roles over IAM Users.
  • Implement IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for all Kubernetes workloads.
  • Apply the Principle of Least Privilege to every IAM policy.
  • Avoid wildcard permissions and overly broad trust policies.
  • Use temporary credentials issued by AWS STS.
  • Enable CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Security Hub for continuous monitoring.
  • Perform regular IAM reviews and remove unused identities, roles and permissions.
  • Enforce organisation-wide guardrails using Service Control Policies (SCPs).

Strong IAM practices form the foundation of a secure Amazon EKS environment.

Real-World Scenario

Section titled “Real-World Scenario”

An organisation allows developers to use permanent IAM Users with long-lived access keys stored on local workstations.

A phishing attack compromises one developer’s credentials.

The attacker:

  • Logs into AWS.
  • Creates new IAM Users.
  • Assumes privileged roles.
  • Disables CloudTrail.
  • Exfiltrates sensitive customer data from Amazon S3.

Following the incident, the organisation implements:

  • IAM Identity Center
  • Multi-Factor Authentication
  • Temporary IAM Roles
  • IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
  • Service Control Policies
  • CloudTrail monitoring
  • Quarterly IAM reviews

These controls dramatically reduce the attack surface and improve compliance.

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

  • AWS IAM security principles
  • Root User protection
  • IAM Identity Center best practices
  • Multi-Factor Authentication
  • Least Privilege IAM design
  • IAM Roles and temporary credentials
  • IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
  • Secure IAM policies and trust relationships
  • Service Control Policies (SCPs)
  • Continuous IAM monitoring and governance

Strong IAM security is the cornerstone of enterprise cloud security. By combining Identity Federation, IAM Roles, IRSA, Least Privilege, Service Control Policies and continuous monitoring, organisations can build resilient and secure Amazon EKS environments.

# Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has successfully deployed its Kubernetes platform.

The next phase of the migration involves onboarding multiple internal teams.

Currently, every engineer is using administrative credentials to access the Kubernetes cluster. During a recent security assessment, several issues were identified:

- Developers have unnecessary administrative privileges.
- Security analysts can modify workloads instead of only reviewing them.
- Operations engineers can access confidential application Secrets.
- Audit teams have excessive permissions.
- There is no separation of duties.

The Cloud Security Team has decided to implement Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to enforce least-privilege access.

You have been assigned to design and implement the RBAC model.

---

# Learning Objectives

By completing this lab, you will learn how to:

- Understand Kubernetes RBAC
- Create Service Accounts
- Create Roles
- Create ClusterRoles
- Create RoleBindings
- Create ClusterRoleBindings
- Apply least privilege
- Validate user permissions
- Test RBAC access
- Troubleshoot permission issues
- Document enterprise access models

---

# Enterprise Architecture

```text
                 CloudNova Kubernetes Cluster

                     Kubernetes API Server
                              │
                    Authentication
                              │
                     Authorization (RBAC)
                              │
         ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
         │              │              │              │
    Developers      Operations      Security      Auditors
         │              │              │              │
   RoleBinding     RoleBinding   RoleBinding   ClusterRoleBinding
         │              │              │              │
       Roles          Roles        Roles      ClusterRoles
```

---

# Lab Outcomes

By the end of this lab, you will have created:

- Dedicated RBAC Namespace
- Multiple Service Accounts
- Developer Role
- Operations Role
- Security Analyst Role
- Auditor ClusterRole
- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoleBindings
- Permission validation report
- RBAC assessment report

# Task 01 — Verify Cluster Health

Verify cluster connectivity.

```bash
kubectl cluster-info
```

Verify nodes.

```bash
kubectl get nodes
```

Ensure all nodes are in the **Ready** state.

---

# Task 02 — Create the RBAC Namespace

Create:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: cloudnova-rbac-lab
  labels:
    environment: development
    owner: cloud-security-team
```

Apply:

```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
```

Verify:

```bash
kubectl get namespace cloudnova-rbac-lab
```

---

# Task 03 — Create Service Accounts

Create dedicated Service Accounts for:

- developer-sa
- operations-sa
- security-sa
- auditor-sa

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: developer-sa
  namespace: cloudnova-rbac-lab
```

Apply all Service Accounts.

Verify:

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -n cloudnova-rbac-lab
```

---

# Task 04 — Create a Developer Role

Create a Role allowing developers to:

- View Pods
- Create Pods
- Update Pods
- Delete Pods

Example:

```yaml
kind: Role
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: developer-role
  namespace: cloudnova-rbac-lab

rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs:
    - get
    - list
    - watch
    - create
    - update
    - delete
```

Apply:

```bash
kubectl apply -f developer-role.yaml
```

---

# Task 05 — Create an Operations Role

Allow Operations to manage:

- Deployments
- Services
- ConfigMaps

but **not Secrets**.

Validate permissions after creation.

---

# Task 06 — Create a Security Analyst Role

Allow Security Analysts to:

- View Pods
- View Deployments
- View Secrets
- View Events

without modification rights.

---

# Task 07 — Create an Auditor ClusterRole

Auditors require read-only access across the cluster.

Create a ClusterRole with:

- get
- list
- watch

on common resources.

---

# Task 08 — Create RoleBindings

Bind:

| Service Account | Role |
|---|---|
| developer-sa | developer-role |
| operations-sa | operations-role |
| security-sa | security-role |

Verify:

```bash
kubectl get rolebindings -n cloudnova-rbac-lab
```

---

# Task 09 — Create ClusterRoleBinding

Bind:

```
auditor-sa
```

to

```
auditor-cluster-role
```

Verify:

```bash
kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

---

# Task 10 — Validate Permissions

Use:

```bash
kubectl auth can-i
```

Examples:

```bash
kubectl auth can-i get pods

kubectl auth can-i create deployments

kubectl auth can-i get secrets

kubectl auth can-i delete namespaces
```

Compare results for each role.

---

# Task 11 — Test Least Privilege

Validate that:

- Developers cannot access Secrets.
- Operations cannot delete Namespaces.
- Security Analysts cannot modify Deployments.
- Auditors cannot create resources.

Document all denied actions.

---

# Task 12 — Review RBAC Resources

Review:

```bash
kubectl get roles -A

kubectl get clusterroles

kubectl get rolebindings -A

kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

Understand how Roles and Bindings work together.

---

# Task 13 — Simulate an Access Request

Scenario:

A developer requests access to read ConfigMaps.

Update the existing Role to grant only the required permission.

Avoid granting unnecessary administrative access.

---

# Task 14 — Review Security Risks

Discuss the impact of:

- Excessive ClusterRoleBindings
- cluster-admin misuse
- Shared Service Accounts
- Default Service Accounts
- Overly permissive Roles
- Wildcard permissions (`*`)

Identify mitigation strategies.

---

# Task 15 — Enterprise RBAC Assessment

Review:

- Least privilege implementation
- Separation of duties
- Namespace isolation
- Administrative accounts
- Service Account usage
- RBAC documentation

Produce a short assessment summarising strengths and improvement areas.

---

# Task 16 — Evidence Collection

Capture evidence for:

- Namespace
- Service Accounts
- Roles
- ClusterRoles
- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoleBindings
- Permission tests
- RBAC assessment report

---

# Task 17 — Clean Up

Delete:

- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoleBindings
- Roles
- ClusterRoles
- Service Accounts
- Namespace

Verify the environment has been cleaned successfully.

You validated permissions using `kubectl auth can-i`, tested access restrictions, and reviewed common RBAC security risks such as excessive privileges and misuse of the `cluster-admin` role.

These RBAC patterns are widely used in production Kubernetes environments on Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Google Kubernetes Engine to implement secure, auditable, and scalable identity governance.
