# Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has successfully implemented Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) across its Kubernetes platform.

During a recent security assessment, the Cloud Security team discovered that many application workloads continue to use the **default Service Account**, automatically receive authentication tokens, and possess unnecessary permissions.

Several security concerns were identified:

- Applications share the default Service Account.
- Pods automatically mount authentication tokens even when they do not communicate with the Kubernetes API.
- Workloads lack workload identity separation.
- There is no documented Service Account governance process.
- Administrative Service Accounts are being reused across multiple applications.

To improve the platform's security posture, the Cloud Security Team has initiated a Service Account hardening project.

Your task is to secure workload authentication by implementing dedicated Service Accounts, validating authentication behaviour, restricting unnecessary token exposure, and preparing the cluster for enterprise workload identity integration.

---

# Learning Objectives

By completing this lab, you will learn how to:

- Understand Kubernetes authentication
- Understand Service Accounts
- Create dedicated Service Accounts
- Configure workload identity
- Disable automatic Service Account token mounting
- Inspect projected Service Account tokens
- Validate Pod authentication
- Review authentication logs
- Apply least privilege
- Prepare for IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- Implement enterprise Service Account governance

---

# Enterprise Architecture

```text
                CloudNova Kubernetes Cluster

                       Kubernetes API Server
                                │
                        Authentication
                                │
                     Service Account Token
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             │                  │                  │
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
      Inventory App      Payment API      Monitoring App
             │                  │                  │
     inventory-sa      payment-sa      monitoring-sa
             │                  │                  │
      Dedicated Identity  Dedicated Identity  Dedicated Identity
```

- B. monitoring-sa
- C. default

# Lab Summary

In this lab, you strengthened workload authentication by replacing the default Service Account with dedicated identities for individual applications. You explored how Kubernetes authenticates workloads, inspected projected Service Account tokens, disabled unnecessary token mounting, and compared secure versus insecure authentication configurations.

You also reviewed RBAC permissions associated with Service Accounts and prepared the platform for cloud-native workload identity solutions such as **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)** on Amazon EKS, **Azure Workload Identity**, and **Google Workload Identity Federation**. These practices help reduce the attack surface, enforce least privilege, and improve the security and auditability of Kubernetes workloads in enterprise environments.

# Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has migrated over fifty business applications to Kubernetes.

Initially, every engineer was granted **cluster-admin** privileges to simplify the migration. As the platform expanded, the Cloud Security team identified several governance issues:

- Developers can delete production workloads.
- Security analysts can modify application deployments.
- Auditors have write access to cluster resources.
- Platform engineers share privileged Service Accounts.
- There is no formal RBAC design.

The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) has instructed the Cloud Security team to redesign access management according to the **Principle of Least Privilege**.

As the Kubernetes Security Engineer, your task is to implement a secure RBAC model that supports multiple business teams while ensuring users only receive the permissions required to perform their job functions.

---

# Learning Objectives

By completing this lab you will learn how to:

- Design enterprise RBAC
- Differentiate Roles and ClusterRoles
- Implement namespace-scoped permissions
- Configure cluster-wide permissions
- Create RoleBindings
- Create ClusterRoleBindings
- Validate permissions
- Troubleshoot RBAC issues
- Apply least privilege
- Implement separation of duties
- Perform RBAC security assessments

---

# Enterprise Architecture

```text
                    CloudNova Kubernetes Cluster

                         Kubernetes API Server
                                   │
                          Authentication
                                   │
                         Authorization (RBAC)
                                   │
      ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
      │              │              │              │
 Developers      Operations      Security      Auditors
      │              │              │              │
  Developer      Operations      Security      Read-Only
     Role            Role           Role       ClusterRole
      │              │              │              │
 RoleBinding    RoleBinding    RoleBinding  ClusterRoleBinding
      │              │              │              │
 Dedicated     Dedicated      Dedicated      Dedicated
ServiceAccount ServiceAccount ServiceAccount ServiceAccount
```

Mission Scenario

Section titled “Mission Scenario”

CloudNova Technologies has migrated over fifty business applications to Kubernetes.

Initially, every engineer was granted cluster-admin privileges to simplify the migration. As the platform expanded, the Cloud Security team identified several governance issues:

  • Developers can delete production workloads.
  • Security analysts can modify application deployments.
  • Auditors have write access to cluster resources.
  • Platform engineers share privileged Service Accounts.
  • There is no formal RBAC design.

The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) has instructed the Cloud Security team to redesign access management according to the Principle of Least Privilege.

As the Kubernetes Security Engineer, your task is to implement a secure RBAC model that supports multiple business teams while ensuring users only receive the permissions required to perform their job functions.

# Mission Scenario

CloudNova Technologies has modernised its application platform by migrating to **Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)**.

Historically, application teams embedded AWS Access Keys and Secret Access Keys inside:

- Kubernetes Secrets
- Environment Variables
- Configuration Files
- CI/CD Pipelines

A recent security assessment identified multiple risks:

- Long-lived AWS credentials stored inside containers
- Shared IAM users across applications
- Excessive AWS permissions
- Credential rotation challenges
- Poor auditability
- High risk of credential compromise

To address these issues, the Cloud Security Team has decided to implement **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)** using **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**.

Your task is to migrate workloads from static AWS credentials to short-lived federated identities while enforcing least privilege and improving the security posture of the Kubernetes platform.

---

By completing this lab, you will learn how to:

- Understand Kubernetes authentication
- Understand OpenID Connect (OIDC)
- Understand workload identity federation
- Configure an OIDC provider for Amazon EKS

- Create IAM roles for Kubernetes workloads
- Configure IAM trust policies
- Associate IAM roles with Service Accounts
- Validate AWS authentication from Pods
- Eliminate long-lived AWS credentials
- Troubleshoot IRSA authentication
- Perform an enterprise authentication assessment

# Enterprise Background

Traditional Kubernetes applications authenticate to AWS using long-lived IAM user credentials.

Example:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID

AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

Problems include:

- Credentials can be stolen.
- Manual rotation is required.
- Secrets are copied between environments.
- Difficult to audit.
- Broad permissions are common.

IRSA removes these risks by issuing **temporary credentials** through AWS Security Token Service (STS).

---

# Authentication Flow

```text
Application Pod

↓

Service Account

↓

OIDC Token

↓

Amazon STS

↓

IAM Role

↓

Temporary Credentials

↓

AWS Services
```

```bash
kubectl cluster-info

kubectl get nodes
```

```bash
aws iam list-open-id-connect-providers
```

Describe the EKS cluster.

```bash
aws eks describe-cluster \
--name <cluster-name>
```

If the OIDC provider is not associated, enable it using:

```bash
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider \
--cluster <cluster-name> \
--approve
```

Verify the provider has been created successfully.

# Lab Summary

In this lab, you implemented secure workload authentication for Amazon EKS using **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** and **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)**. You enabled an OIDC identity provider, created least-privilege IAM policies and roles, configured trust relationships, and associated an IAM role with a Kubernetes Service Account.

You validated that workloads received temporary AWS credentials from AWS Security Token Service (STS) without storing long-lived access keys inside containers or Kubernetes Secrets. By replacing static credentials with federated workload identities, you significantly reduced credential management overhead, improved auditability, and strengthened the overall security posture of the Kubernetes environment.

These authentication patterns are considered AWS best practice and are widely adopted in production Amazon EKS environments to securely integrate Kubernetes workloads with AWS services.

Lab Summary

Section titled “Lab Summary”

In this lab, you implemented secure workload authentication for Amazon EKS using OpenID Connect (OIDC) and IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA). You enabled an OIDC identity provider, created least-privilege IAM policies and roles, configured trust relationships, and associated an IAM role with a Kubernetes Service Account.

You validated that workloads received temporary AWS credentials from AWS Security Token Service (STS) without storing long-lived access keys inside containers or Kubernetes Secrets. By replacing static credentials with federated workload identities, you significantly reduced credential management overhead, improved auditability, and strengthened the overall security posture of the Kubernetes environment.

These authentication patterns are considered AWS best practice and are widely adopted in production Amazon EKS environments to securely integrate Kubernetes workloads with AWS services.

Why should wildcard (`*`) permissions generally be avoided?

- A. They reduce cluster performance.
- B. They violate the principle of least privilege by granting broad access.

- D. They disable Kubernetes authentication.

**Answer:** **B**

- D. It automatically encrypts Kubernetes Secrets.

  • D. They disable Kubernetes authentication.

Answer: B

Question 4

Section titled “Question 4”

What is the primary benefit of IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) on Amazon EKS?

  • A. It increases Pod scheduling speed.
  • B. It replaces RBAC completely.
  • C. It provides temporary AWS credentials without storing long-lived access keys.
  • D. It automatically encrypts Kubernetes Secrets.

Answer: C

Question 5

Section titled “Question 5”

Which finding should normally be considered the highest priority during an identity audit?

  • A. Missing labels on Namespaces
  • B. An unused ConfigMap
  • C. Broad use of the cluster-admin role without business justification
  • D. An old ReplicaSet

Answer: C

# Purpose

This runbook provides a standard operational procedure for validating the health and security of Kubernetes identity and access management.

It is designed to be executed:

- Daily operational checks
- Weekly security reviews
- Before production deployments
- Before change windows
- Before compliance audits
- After security incidents

The objective is to ensure that authentication, authorisation, Service Accounts, RBAC, and workload identities remain secure and compliant with enterprise standards.

---

# Scenario

CloudNova Technologies operates several production Kubernetes clusters supporting critical customer applications.

Before approving daily production operations, the Cloud Security Operations team performs an Identity & Access Health Assessment to ensure:

- Authentication services are functioning correctly.
- Service Accounts remain compliant.
- RBAC permissions have not drifted.
- No excessive privileges have been introduced.
- Workload identities are operating correctly.
- Cloud identity integrations remain healthy.

You have been assigned today's operational assessment.

# Objectives

Validate:

- Cluster authentication
- Service Accounts
- RBAC
- Roles
- ClusterRoles
- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoleBindings
- Namespace isolation
- Workload identities
- OIDC
- IRSA / Workload Identity
- Least Privilege
- Identity governance

# Success Criteria

The assessment is successful when:

- Authentication is operational.
- No excessive privileges exist.
- Service Accounts follow standards.
- No unexpected cluster-admin assignments exist.
- RBAC is functioning correctly.
- Workload identities authenticate successfully.
- Cloud identity integrations are healthy.

# Phase 1 — Verify Cluster Connectivity

Confirm cluster access.

```bash
kubectl cluster-info
```

Expected

```text
Kubernetes control plane is running
```

---

Review cluster version.

```bash
kubectl version
```

- Client Version
- Server Version

---

Review current context.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
```

Confirm the correct production or assessment cluster is selected.

# Phase 2 — Verify Authentication

Confirm Kubernetes API access.

```bash
kubectl auth whoami
```

Verify:

- Username
- Groups
- Authentication method

Expected Outcome:

Authenticated identity matches the approved operational account.

---

# Phase 3 — Review Service Accounts

List all Service Accounts.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A
```

Review:

- Namespace
- Age
- Naming convention

Questions:

- Are dedicated Service Accounts used?
- Are default Service Accounts still active?
- Are obsolete Service Accounts present?

---

Inspect one Service Account.

```bash
kubectl describe sa <service-account> -n <namespace>
```

Verify:

- Secrets
- Annotations
- Labels
- Token configuration

---

# Phase 4 — Review Default Service Accounts

Identify workloads using the default Service Account.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A \
-o=jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{" "}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.serviceAccountName}{"\n"}{end}'
```

Review:

- Production workloads
- Shared identities
- Default Service Account usage

Expected:

Production workloads should use dedicated Service Accounts.

---

# Phase 5 — Validate Token Configuration

Inspect a running Pod.

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
```

Review:

```text
Service Account

Automount Token

Projected Volume
```

Confirm:

- Only workloads requiring Kubernetes API access have authentication tokens.
- `automountServiceAccountToken` is disabled where appropriate.

---

# Phase 6 — Review RBAC Objects

Inventory Roles.

```bash
kubectl get roles -A
```

Inventory ClusterRoles.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles
```

Review:

- Number of custom Roles
- Number of ClusterRoles
- Naming standards
- Wildcard permissions

---

# Phase 7 — Review RoleBindings

List RoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl get rolebindings -A
```

Inspect one RoleBinding.

```bash
kubectl describe rolebinding <rolebinding-name> -n <namespace>
```

Verify:

- Correct Service Account
- Correct Role
- Namespace alignment

---

# Phase 8 — Review ClusterRoleBindings

List ClusterRoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

Review:

- cluster-admin assignments
- Platform administrators
- Security administrators
- Auditor access

Questions:

- Is access justified?
- Is approval documented?
- Are any bindings obsolete?

---

# Phase 9 — Validate Least Privilege

Perform permission validation.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i get pods

kubectl auth can-i get secrets

kubectl auth can-i create deployments

kubectl auth can-i delete namespaces

kubectl auth can-i list nodes
```

Review:

- Expected permissions
- Unexpected permissions
- Permission denials

---

# Phase 10 — Review Workload Identity

Review Pods.

```bash
kubectl get pods -A
```

Inspect workloads.

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
```

Confirm:

- Dedicated Service Account
- Namespace isolation
- Token configuration
- Identity annotations

---

# Phase 11 — Review Cloud Identity Integration

## Amazon EKS

Verify OIDC provider.

```bash
aws eks describe-cluster \
--name <cluster-name>
```

Review:

- OIDC enabled
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
- IAM role annotations

---

## Azure AKS

Review:

- Azure Workload Identity
- Managed Identity configuration
- Federated Credentials

---

## Google GKE

Review:

- Workload Identity
- IAM bindings
- Kubernetes Service Account mapping

# Phase 12 — Review Authentication Logs

Review:

- Failed authentication
- Failed authorisation
- RBAC denials
- Token failures
- OIDC failures

Cloud integrations:

- Amazon CloudTrail
- Azure Activity Logs
- Google Cloud Audit Logs

# Phase 13 — Identity Governance Review

Confirm:

- Naming standards
- Identity ownership
- Service Account lifecycle
- Documentation
- Approval process
- Quarterly access reviews

---

# Phase 14 — Compliance Review

Assess alignment with:

- Principle of Least Privilege

| Control | Status |
|----------|--------|

| Default Service Accounts Avoided | ☐ |

# Risk Classification

## Critical

Examples:

- Authentication failure
- API Server authentication unavailable
- Multiple unauthorised cluster-admin assignments
- Compromised Service Account
- OIDC provider unavailable

Immediate escalation required.

---

## High

Examples:

- Shared Service Accounts
- Wildcard RBAC permissions
- Production workloads using default Service Accounts
- Missing IRSA or Workload Identity
- Excessive ClusterRoleBindings

---

## Medium

Examples:

- Unused Roles
- Duplicate Service Accounts
- Missing documentation
- Inconsistent naming standards

---

## Low

Examples:

- Minor documentation updates
- Legacy RoleBindings
- Obsolete annotations

Capture evidence for:

- Authentication status
- Service Accounts
- Roles
- ClusterRoles

- ClusterRoleBindings

- Identity health checklist
- Assessment report

---

# Operational Best Practices

Always:

- Use dedicated Service Accounts for each workload.
- Avoid using the default Service Account in production.
- Apply the Principle of Least Privilege.
- Review cluster-admin assignments regularly.
- Remove unused RBAC objects.
- Use workload identity federation instead of long-lived credentials.
- Enable audit logging for authentication and authorisation events.
- Perform quarterly identity reviews and immediate reviews after major platform changes.

---

# Troubleshooting Quick Reference

| Issue | Investigation |
|--------|---------------|
| Authentication failures | `kubectl auth whoami`, API Server logs |
| `Forbidden` errors | `kubectl auth can-i`, RoleBindings |
| Unexpected permissions | Review Roles and ClusterRoles |
| Missing access | Verify RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding |
| Service Account issues | `kubectl describe sa` |
| Token not mounted | Review `automountServiceAccountToken` |
| IRSA authentication failure | Verify OIDC provider, IAM Role, trust policy, Service Account annotation |
| Workload Identity failure | Review cloud identity integration and federated credentials |

# Purpose

This runbook provides a structured methodology for reviewing Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) within an enterprise environment.

It enables security engineers to validate that access controls are correctly implemented, follow the Principle of Least Privilege, and comply with organisational security policies before production workloads are approved.

---

# Scenario

CloudNova Technologies operates multiple Kubernetes clusters hosting mission-critical applications across development, testing, and production environments.

During a quarterly governance review, the Cloud Security team must validate that RBAC permissions remain appropriate and that no excessive privileges have been introduced through operational changes.

You have been assigned to conduct the Enterprise RBAC Review and produce a formal assessment report for the Change Advisory Board (CAB).

---

# Review Objectives

Review the following areas:

- Service Accounts
- Roles
- ClusterRoles
- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoleBindings
- Namespace isolation
- Administrative access
- Least privilege
- Separation of duties
- Identity governance
- Compliance
- Production readiness

---

# Success Criteria

The review is considered successful when:

- RBAC follows least privilege.
- No unnecessary cluster-admin assignments exist.
- Namespace boundaries are enforced.
- Service Accounts are dedicated to individual workloads.
- Administrative access is justified and documented.
- RBAC complies with enterprise standards.

---

# Enterprise RBAC Architecture

```text
                   Kubernetes API Server
                            │
                   Authentication
                            │
                   Authorization (RBAC)
                            │
      ┌─────────────┬─────────────┬─────────────┐
      │             │             │
   Developers   Operations   Security Team
      │             │             │
     Roles         Roles         Roles
      │             │             │
 RoleBindings   RoleBindings   RoleBindings
      │             │             │
 Dedicated      Dedicated      Dedicated
ServiceAccount ServiceAccount ServiceAccount

                │
                ▼

        Cluster Administrators
                │
         ClusterRoleBinding
                │
          cluster-admin
```

# Phase 1 — Verify Cluster Access

Verify cluster connectivity.

```bash
kubectl cluster-info
```

Verify current context.

```bash
kubectl config current-context
```

Review Kubernetes version.

```bash
kubectl version
```

Record:

- Cluster Name
- Kubernetes Version
- Cloud Provider
- Reviewer
- Review Date

---

# Phase 2 — Inventory RBAC Resources

List all RBAC resources.

```bash
kubectl get roles -A

kubectl get clusterroles

kubectl get rolebindings -A

kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

Document:

- Total Roles
- Total ClusterRoles
- Total RoleBindings
- Total ClusterRoleBindings

---

# Phase 3 — Review Service Accounts

List Service Accounts.

```bash
kubectl get serviceaccounts -A
```

Review:

- Dedicated Service Accounts
- Shared Service Accounts
- Default Service Accounts
- Naming conventions
- Namespace ownership

Questions:

- Is each application using its own identity?
- Are default Service Accounts used in production?
- Are obsolete Service Accounts present?

---

# Phase 4 — Review Namespace Isolation

Review namespaces.

```bash
kubectl get namespaces --show-labels
```

Confirm:

- Production
- Development
- Testing
- Monitoring
- Security

Review Role assignments within each namespace.

Verify:

- No cross-namespace privilege escalation
- Environment separation
- Ownership labels

---

# Phase 5 — Review Roles

Inventory Roles.

```bash
kubectl get roles -A
```

Inspect each Role.

```bash
kubectl describe role <role-name> \
-n <namespace>
```

Review:

- API Groups
- Resources
- Verbs
- Business purpose

Identify:

- Wildcard (`*`) permissions
- Duplicate Roles
- Excessive write permissions
- Unused Roles

---

# Phase 6 — Review ClusterRoles

List ClusterRoles.

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles
```

Inspect critical ClusterRoles.

```bash
kubectl describe clusterrole cluster-admin

kubectl describe clusterrole admin

kubectl describe clusterrole edit

kubectl describe clusterrole view
```

Review custom ClusterRoles.

Confirm:

- Business justification
- Scope
- Principle of Least Privilege
- Documentation

---

# Phase 7 — Review RoleBindings

Inventory RoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl get rolebindings -A
```

Inspect bindings.

```bash
kubectl describe rolebinding <binding-name> \
-n <namespace>
```

Verify:

- Correct namespace
- Correct Role
- Correct Service Account
- No orphaned bindings

---

# Phase 8 — Review ClusterRoleBindings

List ClusterRoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

Inspect privileged bindings.

Review:

- cluster-admin
- admin
- Custom administrators

Questions:

- Is access approved?
- Is the business justification documented?
- Is the assignment temporary or permanent?
- Has the access been reviewed recently?

---

# Phase 9 — Review Administrative Access

Identify all identities with elevated privileges.

# Risk Classification

## Critical

Examples:

- Unauthorised cluster-admin assignments
- Wildcard permissions on privileged Roles
- Public administrative identities
- Shared administrator Service Accounts
- Uncontrolled ClusterRoleBindings

Immediate remediation required.

---

## High

Examples:

- Excessive write permissions
- Production workloads using the default Service Account
- Missing namespace isolation
- Broad custom ClusterRoles
- Unapproved administrative access

---

## Medium

Examples:

- Duplicate Roles
- Inconsistent naming
- Unused RoleBindings
- Missing documentation

---

## Low

Examples:

- Legacy RBAC objects
- Minor governance gaps
- Documentation improvements

# Recommendations

Prioritise remediation in the following order:

1. Remove unnecessary `cluster-admin` assignments.
2. Replace shared identities with dedicated Service Accounts.
3. Eliminate wildcard (`*`) permissions.
4. Enforce namespace isolation.
5. Adopt workload identity federation (IRSA, Azure Workload Identity, GKE Workload Identity).
6. Conduct quarterly RBAC reviews.
7. Automate RBAC compliance checks.
8. Maintain complete RBAC documentation.

- Use dedicated Service Accounts for every workload.
- Restrict the use of the `cluster-admin` role.

# Purpose

This runbook provides a structured methodology for investigating privileged access within Kubernetes environments.

The objective is to determine:

- Who has privileged access
- Why privileged access exists
- Whether the access is authorised
- Whether privilege escalation has occurred
- Whether administrative access has been abused
- What remediation actions are required

This runbook is typically used during:

- Security incidents
- Insider threat investigations
- Compliance audits
- Production security reviews
- Privileged access reviews
- Red Team exercises

---

# Incident Scenario

CloudNova Technologies' Security Operations Centre (SOC) receives an alert indicating that a Kubernetes Service Account successfully listed Kubernetes Secrets across multiple namespaces.

Initial investigation reveals that the workload was never intended to have administrative permissions.

The CISO requests an immediate privileged access investigation to determine:

- How the workload obtained elevated privileges
- Whether additional identities have excessive permissions
- Whether privilege escalation has occurred
- Whether sensitive data has been exposed
- Whether production workloads remain secure

You have been assigned as the Kubernetes Security Engineer responsible for the investigation.

---

# Investigation Objectives

Determine:

- Who has privileged access
- Which identities are affected
- Which RBAC objects grant elevated permissions
- Whether privilege escalation occurred
- Whether sensitive resources were accessed
- Whether cloud identities were abused
- Whether remediation is required

# Investigation Preparation

Collect:

- Incident ticket number
- Cluster name
- Namespace
- Affected workload
- Service Account
- Username (if applicable)
- Timestamp
- Alert source
- Cloud provider
- Audit logs

---

# Phase 1 — Verify Cluster Access

Confirm access to the affected cluster.

```bash
kubectl cluster-info

kubectl config current-context
```

Record:

- Cluster Name
- Kubernetes Version
- Region
- Reviewer

---

# Phase 2 — Identify the Affected Identity

Determine which identity triggered the alert.

Review:

```bash
kubectl get pods -A
```

Inspect the affected Pod.

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
```

Identify:

- Namespace
- Service Account
- Deployment
- Node
- Labels
- Owner

---

# Phase 3 — Review Service Account

Inspect the Service Account.

```bash
kubectl describe serviceaccount <service-account> \
-n <namespace>
```

Review:

- Labels
- Annotations
- Secrets
- Token configuration
- IAM annotations
- Workload identity configuration

Questions:

- Is it a dedicated Service Account?
- Is it shared?
- Is it the default Service Account?
- Does it require elevated permissions?

---

# Phase 4 — Review Roles

Identify Roles associated with the Service Account.

```bash
kubectl get rolebindings -A
```

Inspect relevant RoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl describe rolebinding <binding-name> \
-n <namespace>
```

Review:

- Role name
- Resources
- Verbs
- Namespace

Look for:

- Secret access
- Pod creation
- Exec permissions
- RBAC modification
- Wildcard permissions

---

# Phase 5 — Review ClusterRoleBindings

List ClusterRoleBindings.

```bash
kubectl get clusterrolebindings
```

Inspect privileged bindings.

```bash
kubectl describe clusterrolebinding <binding-name>
```

Review:

- cluster-admin
- admin
- Custom administrative roles
- Platform administrator groups

Questions:

- Does the identity inherit cluster-wide permissions?
- Was the assignment approved?
- Is the assignment temporary?

---

# Phase 6 — Validate Effective Permissions

Determine what the affected identity can perform.

Examples:

```bash
kubectl auth can-i get secrets \
--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>

kubectl auth can-i create pods \
--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>

kubectl auth can-i create clusterrolebindings \
--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>

kubectl auth can-i impersonate users \
--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>
```

Document:

- Allowed actions
- Denied actions
- Unexpected privileges

---

# Phase 7 — Review Privilege Escalation Opportunities

Investigate whether the identity can:

- Create Pods
- Mount Secrets
- Mount Service Account tokens
- Modify Roles
- Modify ClusterRoles
- Create RoleBindings
- Create ClusterRoleBindings
- Use `hostPath` volumes
- Create privileged containers
- Access Nodes
- Use `kubectl exec`

Classify each finding.

---

# Phase 8 — Review Authentication Logs

Review Kubernetes audit logs.

Look for:

- Authentication events
- Failed logins
- Successful logins
- Secret access
- Pod creation
- RBAC modifications
- Namespace access

Review cloud audit logs:

## Amazon EKS

- CloudTrail
- STS AssumeRole events
- IAM activity

## Azure AKS

- Azure Activity Logs
- Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs

## Google GKE

- Cloud Audit Logs
- IAM Audit Logs

---

# Phase 9 — Review Workload Identity

Determine whether the workload uses:

- IRSA (Amazon EKS)
- Azure Workload Identity
- Google Workload Identity
- Static credentials
- Kubernetes Secrets

Inspect the Pod.

```bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>
```

Review annotations and projected identity tokens.

---

# Phase 10 — Review Sensitive Resource Access

Determine whether the identity accessed:

- Secrets
- ConfigMaps
- Persistent Volumes
- Nodes
- Deployments
- Namespaces
- ClusterRoles
- Admission Controllers

Assess potential impact.

---

# Phase 11 — Identify Root Cause

Determine whether elevated access resulted from:

- Incorrect Role
- Incorrect ClusterRole
- Misconfigured RoleBinding
- Excessive ClusterRoleBinding
- Shared Service Account
- Default Service Account
- Wildcard permissions
- Temporary access not removed
- Manual configuration error
- CI/CD deployment error

Document the root cause.

---

# Phase 12 — Containment

If unauthorised access is confirmed:

Immediate actions may include:

- Remove RoleBinding
- Remove ClusterRoleBinding
- Scale down the affected Deployment
- Disable compromised Service Account
- Rotate credentials
- Revoke cloud IAM role
- Block affected namespace
- Preserve forensic evidence

Ensure containment actions follow organisational incident response procedures.

---

# Phase 13 — Remediation

Recommended remediation actions:

- Remove unnecessary `cluster-admin` access.
- Replace shared Service Accounts with dedicated identities.
- Remove wildcard permissions.
- Implement least privilege.
- Enable workload identity federation (IRSA / Azure Workload Identity / GKE Workload Identity).
- Introduce approval workflows for privileged access.
- Schedule periodic RBAC reviews.
- Automate RBAC drift detection.

---

# Phase 14 — Risk Assessment

| Finding | Risk | Severity | Recommendation |
|----------|------|----------|----------------|
| Excessive ClusterRoleBinding | Full cluster compromise | Critical | Remove immediately |
| Shared Service Account | Lateral movement | High | Create dedicated identities |
| Wildcard permissions | Privilege escalation | High | Restrict permissions |
| Default Service Account in production | Identity misuse | High | Replace with dedicated Service Account |
| Missing workload identity | Credential exposure | Medium | Implement IRSA or equivalent |

---

# Phase 15 — Compliance Assessment

Assess alignment with:

- CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework
- ISO/IEC 27001
- Zero Trust Architecture
- Principle of Least Privilege
- Internal Identity Governance Policies

# Operational Best Practices

- Review privileged access quarterly.
- Use dedicated Service Accounts for every workload.
- Restrict `cluster-admin` assignments to a minimal number of authorised administrators.
- Enable Kubernetes audit logging.
- Monitor RBAC changes in real time.
- Use workload identity federation instead of long-lived credentials.
- Enforce separation of duties between development, operations, and security teams.
- Integrate Kubernetes audit logs with the enterprise SIEM for continuous monitoring.

# Lesson 01 — Kubernetes Networking

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand Kubernetes networking fundamentals
- Learn the Kubernetes networking model
- Understand Pod-to-Pod communication
- Explore Kubernetes Services
- Learn ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Services
- Understand DNS in Kubernetes
- Learn Amazon EKS networking
- Understand enterprise Kubernetes networking architecture
- Apply networking security best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Modern applications are no longer built as a single server.

Instead, applications consist of hundreds or even thousands of containers communicating across the network.

For example, an online banking application may include:

- Frontend Web Application
- Authentication Service
- User Service
- Payment Service
- Notification Service
- Database
- Monitoring Components

Each component runs as an independent Kubernetes workload.

Without an efficient networking model:

- Applications cannot communicate.
- Services become unavailable.
- Security controls cannot be enforced.
- Scaling becomes difficult.

Understanding Kubernetes networking is one of the most important skills for a Cloud Security Engineer because almost every security control—such as Network Policies, Service Mesh, Zero Trust, and Ingress Security—depends on a solid understanding of networking fundamentals.

---

# What is Kubernetes Networking?

Kubernetes networking is the system that enables communication between:

- Pods
- Services
- Nodes
- External clients
- Cloud services

Unlike traditional virtual machines, every Pod receives its own IP address.

This means every workload can communicate directly without requiring Network Address Translation (NAT) between Pods.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Model

Kubernetes follows a simple networking model based on four core principles.

### Principle 1

Every Pod receives its own unique IP address.

### Principle 2

Pods can communicate with other Pods without NAT.

### Principle 3

Nodes can communicate with all Pods.

### Principle 4

Applications should not need to know where Pods are running.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Architecture

```text
                     Internet
                         │
                         ▼
                Load Balancer
                         │
                         ▼
                  Kubernetes Service
                         │
      ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
      ▼                  ▼                  ▼
   Pod A              Pod B              Pod C
      │                  │                  │
      └────────── Kubernetes Network ───────┘
```

Applications communicate using Kubernetes Services rather than directly connecting to individual Pods.

---

# Every Pod Gets an IP Address

Unlike Docker networking, Kubernetes assigns every Pod its own IP address.

Example:

| Pod | IP Address |
|------|------------|
| Frontend | 10.244.1.5 |
| API | 10.244.2.9 |
| Database | 10.244.3.15 |

Every Pod behaves like an independent host on the network.

---

# Pod-to-Pod Communication

Pods communicate directly using IP addresses.

```text
Frontend Pod

↓

API Pod

↓

Database Pod
```

The Kubernetes networking model ensures communication works even if Pods are running on different worker nodes.

---

# Cross-Node Communication

Pods often run on different worker nodes.

Example:

```text
Worker Node 1

└── Frontend Pod

↓

Worker Node 2

└── API Pod

↓

Worker Node 3

└── Database Pod
```

The Container Network Interface (CNI) ensures traffic is routed correctly across nodes.

---

# Kubernetes Services

Pods are temporary.

When a Pod is restarted:

- Its IP address changes.
- Clients cannot rely on Pod IP addresses.

Kubernetes Services provide a stable network endpoint.

```text
Client

↓

Service

↓

Pod 1

Pod 2

Pod 3
```

Applications communicate with the Service instead of individual Pods.

---

# Why Services are Important

Without Services:

```text
Application

↓

Pod IP

↓

Pod Deleted

↓

Application Fails
```

With Services:

```text
Application

↓

Service

↓

New Pod

↓

Application Continues
```

Services provide stability despite changing Pod IP addresses.

---

# Types of Kubernetes Services

Kubernetes supports several Service types.

| Service Type | Purpose |
|--------------|----------|
| ClusterIP | Internal communication |
| NodePort | External access via Node |
| LoadBalancer | Cloud Load Balancer |
| ExternalName | External DNS mapping |

Each Service type addresses different networking requirements.

---

# ClusterIP

ClusterIP is the default Service type.

```text
Frontend

↓

ClusterIP Service

↓

Backend Pods
```

Characteristics:

- Internal communication only
- Not accessible from the Internet
- Most commonly used Service type

---

# NodePort

NodePort exposes an application using a port on every Kubernetes node.

```text
Internet

↓

Worker Node

↓

NodePort

↓

Pods
```

Although useful for testing, NodePort is rarely recommended for production internet-facing workloads.

---

# LoadBalancer

Cloud providers automatically provision a load balancer.

Example on Amazon EKS:

```text
Internet

↓

AWS Elastic Load Balancer

↓

Kubernetes Service

↓

Pods
```

Benefits:

- High availability
- Automatic scaling
- Native AWS integration
- Health checks

---

# ExternalName

ExternalName maps a Kubernetes Service to an external DNS name.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

ExternalName Service

↓

database.company.com
```

This allows workloads to access external services using Kubernetes-native service discovery.

---

# Kubernetes DNS

Kubernetes includes an internal DNS service (CoreDNS).

Instead of using IP addresses:

```text
payment-service

↓

DNS

↓

10.96.20.15
```

Applications communicate using service names.

Example:

```text
payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local
```

DNS simplifies service discovery and improves application portability.

---

# Service Discovery

Applications automatically discover other services.

```text
Frontend

↓

user-service

↓

payment-service

↓

notification-service
```

Developers do not need to hardcode IP addresses.

---

# Amazon EKS Networking

Amazon EKS uses the **Amazon VPC CNI** plugin.

Unlike many Kubernetes distributions, Pods receive real IP addresses from the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).

```text
Amazon VPC

↓

Worker Node

↓

Elastic Network Interface (ENI)

↓

Pod IP Addresses
```

This enables Pods to communicate directly with other AWS resources within the VPC.

---

# Amazon VPC CNI

The Amazon VPC CNI provides:

- Native VPC networking
- Direct Pod-to-VPC communication
- High performance
- Security Group integration
- Simplified routing

This architecture is one of the reasons Amazon EKS integrates seamlessly with AWS networking services.

---

# Enterprise Kubernetes Networking

Enterprise networking typically includes:

```text
Internet

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

Ingress Controller

↓

Kubernetes Services

↓

Pods

↓

Databases

↓

AWS Services
```

Multiple networking layers work together to provide availability and security.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global retail organisation operates a production Amazon EKS cluster.

Traffic flow:

```text
Customer

↓

Amazon CloudFront

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

NGINX Ingress Controller

↓

Frontend Service

↓

Frontend Pods

↓

API Service

↓

API Pods

↓

Database
```

This architecture provides:

- High availability
- Scalability
- Centralised routing
- Secure external access

---

# Common Networking Challenges

Cloud Security Engineers commonly encounter:

- Pod communication failures
- Incorrect Service configuration
- DNS resolution issues
- Load Balancer misconfiguration
- CNI failures
- IP address exhaustion
- Cross-node routing problems
- Incorrect security groups
- Misconfigured Ingress
- Network latency

Understanding the networking model helps diagnose these issues quickly.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security and platform teams should monitor:

- Network latency
- Service availability
- DNS failures
- Load Balancer health
- Pod connectivity
- CNI status
- Packet loss
- Network throughput
- Failed service discovery
- VPC networking events

Continuous monitoring ensures network performance and reliability.

---

# Networking Security Considerations

Although Kubernetes networking enables communication, unrestricted communication creates security risks.

Potential risks include:

- Unrestricted Pod-to-Pod communication
- Lateral movement
- Unauthorised service access
- Exposed applications
- Misconfigured Load Balancers
- DNS spoofing
- Traffic interception

These risks are addressed in later lessons using:

- Network Policies
- Service Mesh
- Zero Trust Networking
- Ingress Security
- Egress Controls

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Understand the Kubernetes networking model before implementing security controls.
- Use Kubernetes Services instead of Pod IP addresses.
- Use DNS-based service discovery.
- Deploy production applications behind LoadBalancers and Ingress Controllers.
- Monitor networking health continuously.
- Understand how Amazon VPC CNI allocates Pod IP addresses.
- Avoid exposing applications directly through NodePort in production.
- Design networking with scalability and security in mind.

Strong networking fundamentals are essential for building secure and resilient Kubernetes platforms.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A financial services company deploys a new microservice architecture on Amazon EKS.

Initially, developers connect services directly using Pod IP addresses.

When Pods are rescheduled during an update, IP addresses change and communication between services fails, causing an outage.

The platform team redesigns the architecture by introducing:

- Kubernetes Services
- CoreDNS service discovery
- Application Load Balancers
- Ingress Controllers

The applications now communicate using stable service names rather than dynamic Pod IP addresses, improving reliability and simplifying operations.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- Kubernetes networking fundamentals
- The Kubernetes networking model
- Pod-to-Pod communication
- Cross-node networking
- Kubernetes Services
- ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName Services
- CoreDNS and service discovery
- Amazon EKS networking using the Amazon VPC CNI
- Enterprise Kubernetes networking architecture
- Networking best practices

Kubernetes networking forms the foundation for every advanced networking security control. Understanding how workloads communicate is essential before implementing Network Policies, Zero Trust Networking, Service Mesh and enterprise security architectures.

# Lesson 02 — CNI Plugins

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin is
- Learn why Kubernetes requires a CNI plugin
- Understand how CNI plugins work
- Explore the Amazon VPC CNI plugin
- Compare Calico, Cilium, Flannel and Weave Net
- Learn enterprise CNI deployment models
- Understand CNI security considerations
- Apply networking best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Kubernetes schedules Pods, but it **does not provide networking by itself**.

When a new Pod starts, Kubernetes must answer several networking questions:

- How does the Pod get an IP address?
- How does it communicate with other Pods?
- How does it communicate across worker nodes?
- How does it reach AWS services?
- How can traffic be secured?

These tasks are performed by a **Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin**.

Without a CNI plugin:

- Pods cannot communicate.
- Services will not function.
- DNS will fail.
- Network Policies cannot be enforced.
- Kubernetes clusters become unusable.

Every Kubernetes cluster requires a CNI plugin.

---

# What is a CNI Plugin?

A **Container Network Interface (CNI)** plugin is software responsible for configuring networking for Pods.

It performs tasks such as:

- Assigning IP addresses
- Configuring virtual interfaces
- Connecting Pods to the network
- Routing traffic
- Enforcing network policies
- Integrating with cloud networking

Think of the CNI as the networking engine of Kubernetes.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Without a CNI

```text
Pod Created

↓

No IP Address

↓

No Routing

↓

No Communication

↓

Application Failure
```

Without a CNI plugin, Pods cannot communicate with each other or the outside world.

---

# Kubernetes Networking With a CNI

```text
Pod Created

↓

CNI Plugin

↓

Assign IP Address

↓

Configure Network Interface

↓

Update Routing

↓

Pod Ready
```

The CNI plugin automatically prepares the Pod for communication.

---

# CNI Workflow

When Kubernetes creates a Pod:

```text
kubectl apply

↓

Scheduler

↓

Worker Node

↓

Container Runtime

↓

CNI Plugin

↓

Network Interface

↓

Pod Receives IP

↓

Application Starts
```

Networking is configured before the Pod begins serving traffic.

---

# Responsibilities of a CNI Plugin

A CNI plugin is responsible for:

- Pod IP allocation
- Network interface creation
- Route configuration
- Cross-node networking
- Service connectivity
- DNS connectivity
- Network Policy enforcement (depending on the plugin)
- Cloud networking integration

These capabilities ensure workloads can communicate securely and reliably.

---

# Popular Kubernetes CNI Plugins

| CNI Plugin | Primary Use Case |
|------------|------------------|
| Amazon VPC CNI | Amazon EKS |
| Calico | Security and Network Policies |
| Cilium | eBPF-based networking and security |
| Flannel | Simple overlay networking |
| Weave Net | Easy-to-deploy networking |
| Antrea | Open vSwitch-based networking |

Each plugin has different strengths depending on the environment.

---

# Amazon VPC CNI

Amazon EKS uses the **Amazon VPC CNI** by default.

Architecture:

```text
Amazon VPC

↓

Elastic Network Interface (ENI)

↓

Worker Node

↓

Pod IP Address
```

Unlike overlay networks, Pods receive real IP addresses from the VPC subnet.

---

# Amazon VPC CNI Features

The Amazon VPC CNI provides:

- Native AWS networking
- VPC IP addresses for Pods
- High performance
- Low latency
- Security Group integration
- Direct communication with AWS services
- Native routing

This makes it the preferred choice for Amazon EKS.

---

# Amazon VPC CNI Architecture

```text
Amazon VPC

↓

Subnet

↓

Elastic Network Interface

↓

Worker Node

↓

Pod 1

Pod 2

Pod 3
```

Each Pod receives a routable IP address from the VPC.

---

# Calico

Calico is one of the most popular enterprise CNI solutions.

Key capabilities include:

- Layer 3 networking
- Network Policies
- Global Network Policies
- BGP routing
- IP-in-IP encapsulation
- VXLAN support
- Security enforcement

Calico is widely adopted in enterprise Kubernetes environments.

---

# Calico Architecture

```text
Pods

↓

Calico

↓

Policy Engine

↓

Routing

↓

Cluster Network
```

Calico is particularly well known for its powerful network policy capabilities.

---

# Cilium

Cilium is a modern CNI built on **eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter)**.

Capabilities include:

- High-performance networking
- Layer 7 visibility
- Identity-based security
- Service Mesh integration
- Network Policies
- Observability
- Load balancing

Cilium is increasingly popular in cloud-native enterprise environments.

---

# Cilium Architecture

```text
Pods

↓

eBPF

↓

Kernel Networking

↓

AWS Network
```

By operating within the Linux kernel, Cilium provides excellent performance and deep visibility into network traffic.

---

# Flannel

Flannel is a lightweight overlay networking solution.

Features include:

- Simple deployment
- VXLAN networking
- Basic routing
- Minimal configuration

Flannel is commonly used in:

- Learning environments
- Development clusters
- Small production deployments

It does not provide advanced security features such as Network Policy enforcement.

---

# Weave Net

Weave Net simplifies Kubernetes networking.

Features include:

- Automatic peer discovery
- Overlay networking
- Encrypted traffic
- Easy deployment

Weave Net is often chosen for environments where operational simplicity is a priority.

---

# CNI Comparison

| Feature | Amazon VPC CNI | Calico | Cilium | Flannel | Weave Net |
|----------|----------------|---------|---------|----------|------------|
| Amazon EKS Support | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Native VPC Networking | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Network Policies | Limited* | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | Basic |
| eBPF Support | ❌ | Partial | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| High Performance | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | Moderate | Moderate |
| Enterprise Security | Good | Excellent | Excellent | Basic | Good |

> *Amazon VPC CNI supports Kubernetes Network Policies when used with the Amazon VPC CNI Network Policy feature, though many organisations still combine it with solutions such as Calico or Cilium for advanced policy management.

---

# Choosing the Right CNI

Selection depends on business requirements.

| Requirement | Recommended CNI |
|-------------|-----------------|
| Amazon EKS | Amazon VPC CNI |
| Advanced Network Policies | Calico |
| High-performance Security | Cilium |
| Learning Kubernetes | Flannel |
| Simple Networking | Weave Net |

Enterprise organisations often prioritise security, scalability and observability when selecting a CNI.

---

# Enterprise Networking Architecture

```text
Internet

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Amazon VPC CNI

↓

Pods

↓

AWS Services
```

The CNI integrates Kubernetes networking with the AWS infrastructure.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational retailer operates several production Amazon EKS clusters.

Networking architecture:

```text
Amazon VPC

↓

Amazon VPC CNI

↓

Worker Nodes

↓

Frontend Pods

↓

API Pods

↓

Payment Pods

↓

Amazon RDS

↓

Amazon S3
```

Security controls include:

- Security Groups
- Network Policies
- AWS WAF
- AWS Shield
- Amazon GuardDuty
- AWS CloudTrail

This architecture delivers secure and scalable networking for business-critical applications.

---

# Common CNI Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Missing Network Policies
- IP address exhaustion
- Overlapping CIDR ranges
- Misconfigured routing
- Unrestricted Pod communication
- Excessive Security Group permissions
- CNI version vulnerabilities
- Incorrect subnet configuration
- Insecure overlay networking
- Lack of network monitoring

These issues can lead to outages, performance problems and security incidents.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security and platform teams should monitor:

- CNI health
- Pod IP allocation
- IP exhaustion
- Routing failures
- Network latency
- Packet loss
- Security Group changes
- Network Policy violations
- Cross-node communication
- Plugin version updates

Continuous monitoring ensures that networking remains healthy and secure.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use the Amazon VPC CNI for Amazon EKS unless there is a specific requirement for an alternative.
- Keep CNI plugins updated to the latest supported version.
- Plan VPC and subnet CIDR ranges carefully to avoid IP exhaustion.
- Monitor CNI health and networking metrics continuously.
- Implement Network Policies to restrict Pod communication.
- Integrate CNI networking with AWS Security Groups where appropriate.
- Regularly review routing and subnet configurations.
- Test networking after cluster upgrades.
- Avoid unnecessary overlay networking in Amazon EKS.
- Design networking for scalability, resilience and security.

Selecting the right CNI plugin is fundamental to building a secure, high-performing Kubernetes platform.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A company deploys a large Amazon EKS cluster with insufficient subnet capacity.

As the number of Pods increases, the Amazon VPC CNI cannot allocate additional IP addresses.

Symptoms include:

- Pods stuck in the **Pending** state
- Failed application deployments
- Service outages
- Scaling failures

The platform team resolves the issue by:

- Expanding VPC subnet CIDR ranges
- Implementing secondary CIDR blocks
- Monitoring IP utilisation
- Updating CNI configuration

The cluster can now scale reliably while maintaining secure networking.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin is
- Why Kubernetes requires a CNI plugin
- How Pods receive IP addresses
- The responsibilities of a CNI plugin
- The features of Amazon VPC CNI
- The capabilities of Calico, Cilium, Flannel and Weave Net
- Enterprise CNI deployment models
- Common networking risks and best practices

CNI plugins provide the networking foundation for Kubernetes. Every Pod, Service, Network Policy and cloud integration depends on a correctly configured CNI. Understanding how these plugins work is essential before implementing advanced networking security controls.

# Lesson 03 — Network Policies

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what Kubernetes Network Policies are

---

# Why This Matters

By default, Kubernetes networking is **highly permissive**.

This means:

- Every Pod can communicate with every other Pod.
- Applications can freely communicate across Namespaces.
- Malware can move laterally.
- Attackers can discover internal services.
- Sensitive applications become exposed.

Imagine an attacker compromises a web application.

Without Network Policies, the attacker may be able to:

- Access databases
- Scan the Kubernetes cluster
- Discover APIs
- Reach monitoring systems
- Attack internal services

Network Policies help prevent this by enforcing **least privilege networking**.

---

# What are Network Policies?

A **Network Policy** is a Kubernetes resource that controls how Pods communicate with:

- Other Pods
- Namespaces
- External networks (depending on the CNI)

Rather than allowing unrestricted communication, Network Policies specify exactly **who can communicate with whom**.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Without Network Policies

```text
Frontend Pod

↓

API Pod

↓

Database Pod

↓

Monitoring

↓

Logging

↓

Every Pod
```

Every workload can communicate freely.

This increases the attack surface.

---

# Kubernetes Networking With Network Policies

```text
Frontend Pod

↓

API Pod

↓

Database Pod

✗

Monitoring

✗

Logging
```

Only authorised communication is allowed.

Everything else is denied.

---

# Default Kubernetes Behaviour

Without Network Policies:

```text
Pod A

↓

Pod B

↓

Allowed
```

```text
Pod A

↓

Database

↓

Allowed
```

```text
Pod A

↓

Monitoring

↓

Allowed
```

Everything is allowed by default.

---

# Zero Trust Networking

Network Policies support a **Zero Trust** model.

Zero Trust assumes:

> Never trust network traffic simply because it originates inside the Kubernetes cluster.

Every communication request should be explicitly authorised.

```text
Request

↓

Evaluate Policy

↓

Allow

or

Deny
```

---

# Micro-Segmentation

Micro-segmentation divides applications into secure network zones.

Example:

```text
Frontend

↓

API

↓

Database
```

Blocked:

```text
Frontend

↓

Database

✗ Denied
```

Only required communication paths are permitted.

---

# Network Policy Components

A Network Policy consists of:

- Pod Selector
- Policy Types
- Ingress Rules
- Egress Rules

Together they determine which traffic is permitted.

---

# Pod Selector

A Pod Selector identifies which Pods the policy applies to.

Example:

```text
Policy

↓

Frontend Pods
```

Only matching Pods are affected by the policy.

---

# Policy Types

Kubernetes supports two primary policy types.

| Policy Type | Controls |
|--------------|----------|
| Ingress | Incoming traffic |
| Egress | Outgoing traffic |

Policies may define either or both.

---

# Ingress Policies

Ingress policies control who can connect **to** a Pod.

Example:

```text
Frontend

↓

API

✓ Allowed

-------------------

Unknown Pod

↓

API

✗ Denied
```

Only approved sources can access the API.

---

# Egress Policies

Egress policies control where a Pod may connect.

Example:

```text
Application

↓

Amazon RDS

✓ Allowed

--------------------

Application

↓

Unknown Internet Host

✗ Denied
```

Restricting outbound communication reduces data exfiltration risks.

---

# Namespace Isolation

Network Policies can isolate entire Namespaces.

```text
Finance Namespace

↓

Finance Database

✓ Allowed

---------------------

HR Namespace

↓

Finance Database

✗ Denied
```

Namespaces become logical security boundaries.

---

# Label-Based Policies

Policies use Kubernetes labels rather than IP addresses.

Example:

```text
role=frontend

↓

Allowed

↓

role=api
```

Benefits include:

- Dynamic
- Scalable
- Cloud-native
- Easy to maintain

Labels continue to work even when Pods are recreated.

---

# Default Deny Policy

Enterprise clusters commonly begin with a **Default Deny** policy.

```text
Every Pod

↓

All Traffic

↓

Denied
```

Administrators then create explicit allow rules.

This is considered a security best practice.

---

# Example Network Policy Design

```text
Internet

↓

Ingress Controller

↓

Frontend

↓

API

↓

Database
```

Allowed:

- Ingress → Frontend
- Frontend → API
- API → Database

Blocked:

- Frontend → Database
- Database → Internet
- Monitoring → Database
- Unknown Pods → API

---

# Network Policies in Amazon EKS

Amazon EKS supports Kubernetes Network Policies when using compatible networking capabilities such as the Amazon VPC CNI Network Policy feature or CNIs like Calico or Cilium.

Example architecture:

```text
Amazon VPC

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Amazon VPC CNI

↓

Network Policies

↓

Pods
```

Network Policies provide fine-grained control over workload communication within the cluster.

---

# Enterprise Example

A healthcare provider operates an Amazon EKS cluster hosting several applications.

Architecture:

```text
Patient Portal

↓

Patient API

↓

Medical Database

↓

AWS Secrets Manager
```

Network Policies allow:

- Patient Portal → Patient API
- Patient API → Medical Database

Blocked:

- Patient Portal → Database
- Monitoring → Database
- Unauthorised Namespaces
- Unknown Pods

This design helps protect sensitive patient information.

---

# Common Network Policy Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- No Network Policies
- Missing default deny rules
- Overly broad allow rules
- Cross-namespace access
- Unrestricted egress traffic
- Incorrect Pod labels
- Missing Namespace isolation
- Policies that are never tested
- Overlapping policies
- Forgotten legacy policies

These weaknesses increase the risk of lateral movement within the cluster.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Network Policy changes
- Policy violations
- Blocked connections
- Cross-namespace traffic
- Unusual east-west communication
- Failed DNS requests
- Egress traffic
- New Namespaces
- Label changes
- Pod communication patterns

Observability platforms such as Amazon CloudWatch, GuardDuty, Calico Enterprise or Cilium Hubble can help visualise and monitor network traffic.

---

# Network Policy Design Strategy

A recommended enterprise approach:

```text
Step 1

↓

Create Default Deny

↓

Step 2

↓

Allow DNS

↓

Step 3

↓

Allow Required Services

↓

Step 4

↓

Restrict Egress

↓

Step 5

↓

Monitor

↓

Step 6

↓

Review Regularly
```

Policies should evolve alongside applications.

---

# Network Policies and Zero Trust

Zero Trust networking combines:

- Network Policies
- RBAC
- Service Accounts
- IRSA
- Pod Security Standards
- Service Mesh
- Identity-based access

Example:

```text
Identity

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorisation

↓

Network Policy

↓

Service

↓

Pod
```

Security is enforced at multiple layers.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Implement a default deny policy in every production Namespace.
- Allow only the minimum required ingress and egress traffic.
- Use labels rather than IP addresses.
- Isolate workloads using Namespaces and Network Policies.
- Restrict outbound internet access wherever possible.
- Review Network Policies whenever applications change.
- Test policies before deploying to production.
- Monitor blocked and unexpected traffic.
- Use compatible CNI plugins that support Network Policies.
- Follow Zero Trust networking principles.

Well-designed Network Policies significantly reduce the attack surface of Kubernetes clusters.

---

# Real-World Scenario

An e-commerce company deploys several microservices on Amazon EKS.

A vulnerable product catalogue service is compromised through a web application vulnerability.

Without Network Policies, the attacker:

- Scans the cluster
- Discovers internal APIs
- Connects directly to the payment database
- Attempts credential theft

Following the incident, the organisation implements:

- Default deny policies
- Namespace isolation
- Ingress and egress restrictions
- Label-based Network Policies
- Continuous traffic monitoring

When a similar attack occurs later, the compromised Pod cannot communicate beyond its authorised services, preventing lateral movement and reducing the impact of the attack.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What Kubernetes Network Policies are
- Why default Kubernetes networking is permissive
- How ingress and egress policies work
- The importance of micro-segmentation
- How Network Policies support Zero Trust
- Namespace isolation techniques
- Enterprise Network Policy design
- Common security risks and best practices

Network Policies are one of the most effective security controls available in Kubernetes. By explicitly defining which workloads may communicate, organisations can prevent lateral movement, enforce Zero Trust networking and significantly strengthen the security of Amazon EKS environments.

# Lesson 04 — Ingress Controllers

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what an Ingress Controller is
- Learn how Ingress differs from Kubernetes Services
- Understand HTTP and HTTPS routing
- Learn SSL/TLS termination
- Explore the AWS Load Balancer Controller
- Understand Amazon Application Load Balancers (ALB)
- Secure external application access
- Apply enterprise ingress security best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Modern Kubernetes applications are designed to be accessed by:

- Customers
- Employees
- Mobile applications
- APIs
- Business partners
- Third-party integrations

These applications require secure external access.

For example:

```text
Internet

↓

Online Banking Portal

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Without a secure ingress solution:

- Applications cannot be reached from the Internet.
- Traffic cannot be encrypted.
- SSL certificates cannot be managed efficiently.
- Routing becomes difficult.
- Security controls become inconsistent.

Ingress Controllers provide a secure and scalable way to expose Kubernetes applications to external users.

---

# What is an Ingress?

An **Ingress** is a Kubernetes resource that defines how external HTTP and HTTPS traffic reaches services inside the cluster.

Unlike a Service, an Ingress does not forward traffic itself.

Instead, it provides routing rules that are implemented by an **Ingress Controller**.

---

# What is an Ingress Controller?

An **Ingress Controller** is the component responsible for implementing Ingress rules.

It:

- Receives incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic
- Applies routing rules
- Terminates SSL/TLS
- Forwards requests to Kubernetes Services
- Performs health checks
- Supports load balancing

Think of it as the **reverse proxy** for your Kubernetes cluster.

---

# Kubernetes Networking Without an Ingress Controller

Without an Ingress Controller:

```text
Internet

↓

LoadBalancer Service

↓

Application A
```

```text
Internet

↓

LoadBalancer Service

↓

Application B
```

```text
Internet

↓

LoadBalancer Service

↓

Application C
```

Each application requires its own external Load Balancer.

Problems include:

- Increased cost
- Difficult certificate management
- Complex routing
- Operational overhead

---

# Kubernetes Networking With an Ingress Controller

```text
Internet

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

Ingress Controller

├── /app1

├── /app2

├── /api

└── /admin

↓

Kubernetes Services

↓

Pods
```

One entry point can securely expose multiple applications.

---

# Ingress vs Service

| Kubernetes Service | Kubernetes Ingress |
|---------------------|-------------------|
| Provides internal connectivity | Manages external HTTP/HTTPS access |
| Routes traffic to Pods | Routes traffic to Services |
| Works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) | Works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) |
| No URL-based routing | Supports path and host-based routing |
| No SSL termination | Supports SSL/TLS termination |

Ingress complements Kubernetes Services rather than replacing them.

---

# How an Ingress Controller Works

```text
Client Request

↓

Ingress Controller

↓

Routing Rules

↓

Kubernetes Service

↓

Pod
```

Applications never receive traffic directly from the Internet.

---

# Host-Based Routing

Host-based routing directs traffic based on the requested hostname.

Example:

```text
bank.company.com

↓

Banking Service

---------------------

api.company.com

↓

API Service

---------------------

admin.company.com

↓

Admin Portal
```

Multiple applications can share a single external Load Balancer.

---

# Path-Based Routing

Traffic can also be routed based on the URL path.

```text
company.com/app

↓

Frontend

---------------------

company.com/api

↓

API

---------------------

company.com/admin

↓

Admin Portal
```

This reduces infrastructure complexity while maintaining logical separation.

---

# SSL/TLS Termination

One of the primary responsibilities of an Ingress Controller is terminating encrypted HTTPS connections.

```text
Browser

↓

HTTPS

↓

Ingress Controller

↓

HTTP (Internal)

↓

Application
```

The controller decrypts incoming traffic before forwarding it to internal services.

In highly regulated environments, **end-to-end TLS** may also be implemented so that traffic remains encrypted all the way to the application.

---

# TLS Certificates

Ingress Controllers commonly use certificates issued by:

- AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
- Let's Encrypt
- DigiCert
- Entrust
- Internal Enterprise Certificate Authorities (CAs)

Certificates provide:

- Encryption
- Authentication
- Trust

Users can verify that they are communicating with the legitimate application.

---

# Amazon EKS Ingress Architecture

The recommended ingress architecture for Amazon EKS is:

```text
Internet

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

AWS Load Balancer Controller

↓

Ingress

↓

Kubernetes Services

↓

Pods
```

This architecture combines Kubernetes routing with native AWS networking and security services.

---

# AWS Load Balancer Controller

The **AWS Load Balancer Controller** is the recommended Ingress Controller for Amazon EKS.

It automatically provisions and manages:

- Application Load Balancers (ALBs)
- Network Load Balancers (NLBs)

Features include:

- Automatic ALB creation
- SSL termination
- Host-based routing
- Path-based routing
- Target Group management
- Native AWS integration

---

# Application Load Balancer (ALB)

Application Load Balancer operates at **OSI Layer 7**.

Capabilities include:

- HTTP routing
- HTTPS routing
- URL path routing
- Host-based routing
- Redirects
- WebSocket support
- Health checks

ALBs are ideal for web applications and REST APIs.

---

# Network Load Balancer (NLB)

Network Load Balancer operates at **OSI Layer 4**.

Capabilities include:

- TCP
- UDP
- TLS passthrough
- Very high throughput
- Low latency

NLBs are commonly used for non-HTTP applications and high-performance workloads.

---

# Ingress Security Architecture

```text
Internet

↓

AWS Shield

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

AWS Load Balancer Controller

↓

Ingress Rules

↓

Kubernetes Services

↓

Pods
```

Multiple layers of protection help defend against internet-based attacks.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational retail organisation hosts several applications on Amazon EKS.

Traffic flow:

```text
Customer

↓

Amazon CloudFront

↓

AWS WAF

↓

Application Load Balancer

↓

AWS Load Balancer Controller

↓

Ingress

↓

Frontend Service

↓

Frontend Pods

↓

API Service

↓

Payment Service
```

Benefits include:

- Centralised routing
- SSL termination
- High availability
- Automatic scaling
- Secure public access

---

# Common Ingress Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- HTTP instead of HTTPS
- Expired TLS certificates
- Public administrative endpoints
- Missing Web Application Firewall (WAF)
- Weak TLS versions
- Missing authentication
- Overly broad routing rules
- Misconfigured Load Balancers
- Open debugging endpoints
- Unrestricted internet exposure

These weaknesses increase the risk of application compromise.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- HTTPS certificate expiry
- Load Balancer health
- HTTP error rates
- 4xx and 5xx responses
- Blocked WAF requests
- Ingress configuration changes
- Unexpected routing changes
- DDoS events
- TLS handshake failures
- Application latency

Monitoring provides early warning of configuration errors and security threats.

---

# Ingress Security Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use HTTPS for all public applications.
- Manage certificates using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).
- Deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller in Amazon EKS.
- Protect internet-facing applications with AWS WAF.
- Enable AWS Shield for DDoS protection.
- Avoid exposing administrative interfaces publicly.
- Restrict access using authentication and authorisation controls.
- Use host-based and path-based routing to simplify application exposure.
- Keep Ingress Controller software up to date.
- Continuously monitor ingress traffic and security events.

A well-designed ingress architecture protects applications while providing scalability and operational simplicity.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A company exposes its internal Kubernetes dashboard directly through a public LoadBalancer Service without authentication.

An attacker discovers the endpoint through an internet scan.

Because there is:

- No authentication
- No TLS enforcement
- No WAF protection

the attacker gains administrative access to the cluster.

Following the incident, the company redesigns its ingress architecture by implementing:

- AWS Load Balancer Controller
- AWS WAF
- HTTPS with ACM certificates
- Private administrative endpoints
- Identity-based authentication
- Continuous monitoring

The Kubernetes dashboard is no longer publicly accessible, significantly reducing the attack surface.

Learning Objectives

Section titled “Learning Objectives”

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what an Ingress Controller is
  • Learn how Ingress differs from Kubernetes Services
  • Understand HTTP and HTTPS routing
  • Learn SSL/TLS termination
  • Explore the AWS Load Balancer Controller
