# Lesson 02 — Container Image Architecture

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what a container image is
- Learn how container images are built
- Understand image layers and Union File Systems
- Explore Dockerfile architecture
- Learn how container images are stored and distributed
- Understand how image architecture impacts security
- Apply enterprise container image best practices for Amazon EKS

---

# Why This Matters

Every container running in Kubernetes starts from a **container image**.

The image contains everything required to run an application, including:

- Operating system libraries
- Runtime environment
- Application code
- Configuration
- Dependencies
- Startup commands

If the image is poorly designed or contains vulnerabilities, every container created from it inherits those security weaknesses.

Understanding container image architecture is the first step toward building secure Kubernetes workloads.

---

# What is a Container Image?

A container image is an **immutable package** that contains everything an application needs to execute.

Unlike a virtual machine, a container image does not contain an entire operating system.

Instead, it shares the host kernel while packaging only the components required by the application.

```text
Container Image

├── Base Operating System

├── Runtime

├── Libraries

├── Dependencies

├── Application Code

└── Startup Configuration
```

Once built, the image should never be modified.

---

# Container Image vs Running Container

A container image is a **template**.

A running container is an **instance** of that template.

```text
Container Image

↓

Container

↓

Running Application
```

Think of it like this:

- Image = Blueprint
- Container = Building constructed from the blueprint

One image can create thousands of identical containers.

---

# Container Image Lifecycle

```text
Developer

↓

Source Code

↓

Dockerfile

↓

Build Image

↓

Image Scan

↓

Container Registry

↓

Deploy

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Running Container
```

Every stage should include security validation.

---

# Anatomy of a Container Image

A typical image contains several components.

```text
Container Image

├── Base Image

├── Package Manager

├── Runtime

├── Application Dependencies

├── Application Files

├── Configuration

└── Metadata
```

Each component contributes to the overall security posture.

---

# Understanding Image Layers

Container images are built using **layers**.

Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer.

```text
Application Layer

──────────────

Dependencies

──────────────

Runtime

──────────────

Base Image
```

When Kubernetes starts a container, these layers are combined into a single filesystem.

---

# Benefits of Layered Images

Layering provides several advantages.

- Faster image builds
- Efficient storage
- Layer reuse
- Faster downloads
- Reduced network usage
- Improved caching

If only the application code changes, Kubernetes reuses the existing lower layers.

---

# Union File System

Container runtimes use a **Union File System (UnionFS)** to combine multiple layers into one virtual filesystem.

```text
Application Layer

↓

Dependencies

↓

Runtime

↓

Base Image

↓

Unified Filesystem

↓

Running Container
```

Applications see a single filesystem even though it is built from multiple layers.

---

# Read-Only Image Layers

Image layers are **read-only**.

When a container starts:

```text
Read-Only Image

↓

Writable Container Layer

↓

Running Application
```

The writable layer exists only while the container is running.

Once the container is deleted, any changes in the writable layer are lost unless external storage is used.

---

# Base Images

Every container image starts with a base image.

Examples include:

- Amazon Linux
- Alpine Linux
- Ubuntu
- Debian
- Distroless Images

The security of the base image directly affects every application built on top of it.

---

# Choosing a Secure Base Image

Enterprise organizations prefer base images that are:

- Officially maintained
- Frequently updated
- Minimal
- Vulnerability scanned
- Digitally signed
- Supported by the vendor

Smaller images generally contain fewer packages and therefore a smaller attack surface.

---

# Dockerfile Architecture

A Dockerfile defines how a container image is built.

Typical workflow:

```text
Base Image

↓

Install Packages

↓

Copy Application

↓

Configure Runtime

↓

Define Startup Command

↓

Build Image
```

Every instruction creates a new image layer.

---

# Example Dockerfile

```dockerfile
FROM amazonlinux:2023

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN yum install -y python3

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

USER 1000

CMD ["python3", "app.py"]
```

Notice that the application runs as a non-root user rather than the default root account.

---

# Image Metadata

Every container image includes metadata such as:

- Image ID
- Digest
- Tags
- Labels
- Architecture
- Build information

Example:

```text
Image

↓

Digest

↓

sha256:xxxxxxxx
```

The image digest uniquely identifies the exact image contents.

---

# Image Tags vs Image Digests

| Image Tag | Image Digest |
|------------|--------------|
| Human-readable | Cryptographic identifier |
| Can change | Immutable |
| Example: `v1.2` | Example: `sha256:abc123...` |
| Convenient for developers | Best for production deployments |

Enterprise deployments often reference image digests to ensure the exact approved image is deployed.

---

# Container Registry

After an image is built, it is stored in a registry.

```text
Developer

↓

Build Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Container
```

Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) is the recommended private registry for Amazon EKS.

---

# Multi-Architecture Images

Modern container images can support multiple CPU architectures.

Example:

```text
Image Manifest

├── AMD64

├── ARM64

└── Other Architectures
```

The container runtime automatically pulls the correct image for the target node.

---

# Image Architecture and Security

Every additional package increases the attack surface.

Example:

```text
Large Image

↓

More Packages

↓

More Vulnerabilities

↓

Higher Risk
```

Instead:

```text
Minimal Image

↓

Fewer Packages

↓

Smaller Attack Surface

↓

Lower Risk
```

This is why minimal base images are recommended for production workloads.

---

# Amazon EKS Architecture

```text
Developer

↓

Git Repository

↓

Dockerfile

↓

Build Pipeline

↓

Image Scan

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Running Container
```

Container image architecture forms the foundation of every Kubernetes deployment.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global banking organization builds all production workloads using an enterprise image pipeline.

The pipeline automatically:

- Builds images from approved base images
- Removes unnecessary packages
- Scans for vulnerabilities
- Signs images
- Pushes approved images to Amazon ECR
- Rejects images that fail security policies

Application teams are prohibited from deploying public container images directly into production.

Every workload originates from an approved enterprise image.

---

# Common Image Architecture Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Large container images
- Outdated base images
- Unnecessary packages
- Images built as root
- Hardcoded secrets
- Missing metadata
- Public images without verification
- Excessive image layers
- Unpatched software
- Untrusted image sources

These weaknesses increase the likelihood of software supply chain attacks.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Base image updates
- Image build failures
- Image vulnerabilities
- Image digest changes
- Registry access logs
- Image signing validation
- Unauthorized image uploads
- CI/CD build events
- Image age
- Deployment source

Monitoring helps ensure only trusted images reach production.

---

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended implementation roadmap:

```text
Step 1

↓

Choose Approved Base Images

↓

Step 2

↓

Build Minimal Images

↓

Step 3

↓

Remove Unnecessary Packages

↓

Step 4

↓

Configure Non-Root User

↓

Step 5

↓

Scan Images

↓

Step 6

↓

Sign Images

↓

Step 7

↓

Store in Amazon ECR

↓

Step 8

↓

Deploy to Amazon EKS

↓

Step 9

↓

Continuously Monitor
```

This process reduces the attack surface while improving operational consistency.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use trusted and officially maintained base images.
- Prefer minimal or distroless images where appropriate.
- Keep images small to reduce vulnerabilities.
- Avoid installing unnecessary packages.
- Configure images to run as non-root users.
- Reference images by digest in production.
- Store production images in private registries such as Amazon ECR.
- Scan and sign every image before deployment.
- Continuously update base images with security patches.
- Automate image validation within CI/CD pipelines.

Secure image architecture is the foundation of a secure software supply chain.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A software company develops a new customer portal for Amazon EKS.

Initially, developers build the application using a large public Ubuntu image containing hundreds of unused packages.

During security scanning, the pipeline identifies multiple critical vulnerabilities inherited from the base image.

The team rebuilds the application using an approved minimal enterprise base image.

The new image:

- Removes unnecessary software
- Reduces the image size by more than half
- Contains significantly fewer vulnerabilities
- Runs as a non-root user
- Is digitally signed before being stored in Amazon ECR

When deployed, the application provides the same functionality while presenting a much smaller attack surface.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What a container image is
- How container images are built
- Image layers and Union File Systems
- Dockerfile architecture
- Image metadata, tags and digests
- Secure base image selection
- Amazon ECR image management
- Enterprise container image best practices

Container image architecture is the foundation of Kubernetes supply chain security. Well-designed images reduce vulnerabilities, improve consistency and support secure, repeatable deployments across Amazon EKS environments.

# Lesson 03 — Dockerfile Security Best Practices

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand why Dockerfile security is important
- Learn common Dockerfile security mistakes
- Build secure and minimal container images
- Configure non-root users
- Reduce the container attack surface
- Apply enterprise Dockerfile standards
- Follow secure image development practices for Amazon EKS

---

# Why This Matters

Every container image starts with a **Dockerfile**.

The Dockerfile defines:

- Base image
- Installed software
- Application files
- Runtime configuration
- Startup commands
- Default user

A poorly written Dockerfile can introduce vulnerabilities before the application is even deployed.

Since every container is built from the Dockerfile, insecure practices are replicated across every deployment.

For this reason, securing Dockerfiles is one of the earliest and most important steps in securing the software supply chain.

---

# What is a Dockerfile?

A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions used to build a container image.

Example build process:

```text
Dockerfile

↓

Docker Build

↓

Container Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Running Container
```

Every instruction creates a new image layer.

---

# Secure Dockerfile Principles

Enterprise Dockerfiles follow several core principles:

- Minimal attack surface
- Least privilege
- Immutable infrastructure
- Reproducible builds
- Trusted software
- Secure defaults

These principles reduce vulnerabilities while improving maintainability.

---

# Principle 1 — Use Trusted Base Images

Everything begins with the base image.

Instead of using random public images:

```dockerfile
FROM unknown/image
```

Use:

- Amazon Linux
- Alpine Linux
- Distroless Images
- Official vendor images

Example:

```dockerfile
FROM public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux:2023
```

Using trusted images reduces supply chain risk.

---

# Principle 2 — Keep Images Small

Large images contain:

- More software
- More libraries
- More packages
- More vulnerabilities

Example:

```text
Large Image

↓

More Packages

↓

Higher Attack Surface
```

Instead:

```text
Minimal Image

↓

Fewer Packages

↓

Lower Risk
```

Smaller images also build and deploy faster.

---

# Principle 3 — Pin Image Versions

Avoid using floating tags such as:

```dockerfile
FROM python:latest
```

Instead:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12
```

Even better:

```text
Use Image Digest

↓

sha256:xxxxxxxx
```

Pinned versions provide predictable and reproducible builds.

---

# Principle 4 — Run as a Non-Root User

Containers should never run as the default root user.

Instead:

```dockerfile
RUN useradd appuser

USER appuser
```

Benefits include:

- Reduced privilege escalation
- Lower container escape risk
- Improved compliance
- Better workload isolation

---

# Principle 5 — Install Only Required Packages

Avoid installing unnecessary software.

Poor practice:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get install -y \
vim \
curl \
net-tools \
telnet \
ftp
```

Better:

Install only the packages required by the application.

Every unnecessary package increases the attack surface.

---

# Principle 6 — Remove Package Cache

Package managers leave behind temporary files.

Example:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get clean
```

Removing temporary files:

- Reduces image size
- Removes unnecessary artifacts
- Improves efficiency

---

# Principle 7 — Use Multi-Stage Builds

Multi-stage builds separate:

- Build environment
- Runtime environment

Example:

```text
Builder Image

↓

Compile Application

↓

Copy Binary

↓

Minimal Runtime Image
```

The final image contains only the application—not build tools.

---

# Principle 8 — Avoid Hardcoded Secrets

Never include:

- Passwords
- API keys
- Tokens
- Certificates
- AWS credentials

Bad example:

```dockerfile
ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=xxxxxxxx
```

Instead, use:

- Kubernetes Secrets
- AWS Secrets Manager
- IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)

---

# Principle 9 — Copy Only Required Files

Avoid copying the entire project directory.

Poor practice:

```dockerfile
COPY . .
```

Better practice:

Copy only required application files.

This prevents accidental inclusion of:

- Source code
- Credentials
- Git history
- Documentation
- Temporary files

---

# Principle 10 — Use .dockerignore

The `.dockerignore` file excludes unnecessary files from the build.

Typical exclusions:

```text
.git

.env

node_modules

logs

tmp

*.pem

*.key

README.md
```

This reduces image size and prevents sensitive information from entering production images.

---

# Dockerfile Build Workflow

```text
Developer

↓

Dockerfile

↓

Secure Build

↓

Image Scan

↓

Image Signing

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Security validation should occur automatically during every build.

---

# Common Dockerfile Mistakes

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Running as root
- Using `latest` tags
- Large base images
- Hardcoded credentials
- Unnecessary software
- Public untrusted images
- Missing `.dockerignore`
- Missing version pinning
- Old package versions
- Images built without scanning

These weaknesses increase software supply chain risk.

---

# Secure Dockerfile Example

```dockerfile
FROM public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux:2023

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN yum install -y python3 && \
    pip3 install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY app.py .

RUN useradd appuser

USER appuser

CMD ["python3","app.py"]
```

This example demonstrates:

- Trusted base image
- Minimal package installation
- Non-root execution
- Simple application layout
- Predictable startup

---

```text
↓

Git Repository

↓

Dockerfile

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Image Build

Image Scan

Amazon ECR

Amazon EKS
```

Dockerfile security is enforced before images reach production.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational financial institution requires every Dockerfile to pass automated security validation.

The CI/CD pipeline verifies:

- Approved base image
- Version pinning
- Non-root user
- No hardcoded secrets
- Minimal packages
- Multi-stage build where applicable
- Vulnerability scan passed
- Image signed successfully

If any security requirement fails, the image is rejected automatically.

Developers receive immediate feedback and must correct the Dockerfile before deployment.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams monitor:

- Base image usage
- Dockerfile policy violations
- Hardcoded secrets
- Image size growth
- Package inventory
- Vulnerability scan results
- Image signing failures
- Build pipeline failures
- Registry uploads
- Deployment approvals

Monitoring ensures Dockerfiles remain compliant with enterprise standards.

---

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended rollout:

```text
Step 1

↓

Approve Base Images

↓

Step 2

↓

Create Dockerfile Standards

↓

Step 3

↓

Implement Multi-Stage Builds

↓

Step 4

↓

Require Non-Root Users

↓

Step 5

↓

Scan Images

↓

Step 6

↓

Sign Images

↓

Step 7

↓

Push to Amazon ECR

↓

Step 8

↓

Deploy to Amazon EKS

↓

Step 9

↓

Continuously Monitor
```

This approach embeds security into every image build.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use trusted and officially supported base images.
- Pin image versions or use image digests.
- Keep images as small as possible.
- Remove unnecessary software and build artifacts.
- Run applications as non-root users.
- Never hardcode credentials or secrets.
- Use `.dockerignore` to exclude unnecessary files.
- Use multi-stage builds whenever appropriate.
- Scan and sign every image before deployment.
- Automate Dockerfile validation within CI/CD pipelines.

Secure Dockerfiles provide the foundation for secure container images.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A software development team builds a new API service for Amazon EKS.

The initial Dockerfile:

- Uses `ubuntu:latest`
- Installs debugging tools
- Runs as root
- Copies the entire project directory
- Includes an `.env` file containing API keys

During the CI/CD process:

- Dockerfile policy validation detects the use of `latest`.
- Secret scanning identifies the exposed credentials.
- Image scanning reports unnecessary packages.
- The deployment is blocked.

The developers update the Dockerfile to:

- Use an approved Amazon Linux base image
- Pin the image version
- Exclude `.env` using `.dockerignore`
- Install only required packages
- Create a dedicated application user
- Run the container as non-root

The rebuilt image passes all security checks and is deployed successfully to Amazon EKS.

- The importance of trusted base images
- Running containers as non-root users
- Multi-stage builds and minimal images
- Secret management best practices
- CI/CD validation for Dockerfiles

A secure Dockerfile is the first building block of a secure container image. By following enterprise best practices, organizations can reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen their software supply chain and deploy hardened workloads into Amazon EKS with confidence.

# Lesson 04 — Base Image Security

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what a base image is
- Learn why base image security is critical
- Compare different types of base images
- Understand the security risks of outdated images
- Learn how enterprise organizations manage approved base images
- Secure container images for Amazon EKS
- Apply enterprise best practices for base image governance

---

# Why This Matters

Every container image begins with a **base image**.

The base image provides:

- Operating system libraries
- Package manager
- Runtime dependencies
- Core system utilities
- Default users and permissions

Every application built on top of that base image inherits its components and vulnerabilities.

If the base image contains outdated software or security flaws, every container built from it is also vulnerable.

Selecting a secure base image is one of the most important decisions in container security.

---

# What is a Base Image?

A base image is the **foundation** upon which all other image layers are built.

```text
Application Layer

↓

Dependencies

↓

Runtime

↓

Base Image
```

Everything above the base image depends on it.

---

# Container Image Architecture

```text
Application

↓

Libraries

↓

Runtime

↓

Operating System Components

↓

Base Image
```

The base image is responsible for providing the core operating system environment.

---

# Why Base Images Matter

A vulnerable base image creates risk for every workload.

Example:

```text
Outdated Base Image

↓

Known Vulnerability

↓

Application Image

↓

Production Container

↓

Security Risk
```

Even if the application code is secure, inherited vulnerabilities can still be exploited.

---

# Types of Base Images

Enterprise environments commonly use several categories of base images.

| Type | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| Official Images | Maintained by trusted vendors |
| Enterprise Images | Built and managed internally |
| Minimal Images | Contain only essential components |
| Distroless Images | Include only the application runtime |
| Community Images | Created by third parties |

The level of trust varies significantly between these image types.

---

# Official Images

Official images are published by software vendors or trusted organizations.

Examples include:

- Amazon Linux
- Ubuntu
- Debian
- Alpine Linux
- Red Hat Universal Base Image (UBI)

Benefits:

- Regular security updates
- Vendor support
- Better documentation
- Predictable release cycles

---

# Enterprise Base Images

Many organizations build their own approved base images.

Example:

```text
Amazon Linux

↓

Security Hardening

↓

Internal Packages

↓

Security Agents

↓

Enterprise Base Image
```

Application teams must use these approved images instead of downloading public images.

---

# Minimal Base Images

Minimal images remove unnecessary software.

Example:

```text
Traditional Image

↓

500 Packages

↓

Larger Attack Surface

-------------------------

Minimal Image

↓

80 Packages

↓

Smaller Attack Surface
```

Fewer packages generally mean fewer vulnerabilities.

---

# Distroless Images

Distroless images contain only:

- Application runtime
- Required libraries

They do **not** include:

- Shells
- Package managers
- Debugging tools

Benefits:

- Very small attack surface
- Fewer vulnerabilities
- Reduced exploitation opportunities

These images are well suited for production workloads where interactive debugging is not required.

---

# Risks of Community Images

Public community images may contain:

- Malware
- Backdoors
- Cryptocurrency miners
- Unpatched software
- Unknown maintainers
- Weak security practices

Enterprise organizations should avoid deploying unverified community images into production.

---

# Outdated Base Images

Old images often contain:

- Known CVEs
- Unsupported software
- Expired packages
- End-of-life operating systems

Example:

```text
Old Base Image

↓

Unpatched Vulnerability

↓

Container Compromise
```

Regular updates are essential.

---

# Base Image Lifecycle

```text
Vendor

↓

Security Updates

↓

Enterprise Validation

↓

Image Scan

↓

Approved Base Image

↓

Application Image

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Every update should be validated before production use.

---

# Base Image Hardening

Enterprise base images commonly include:

- Removed unnecessary packages
- Updated security patches
- Secure default configuration
- Non-root user support
- Security monitoring agents
- Approved certificates
- Logging configuration

These controls improve consistency across workloads.

---

# Image Inheritance

Every application inherits from its base image.

```text
Base Image

↓

Application A

↓

Application B

↓

Application C

↓

Production Containers
```

A vulnerability in the base image affects every dependent application.

---

# Base Image Security in Amazon EKS

```text
Developer

↓

Enterprise Base Image

↓

Dockerfile

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Image Scan

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Only approved base images should be allowed in production environments.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global insurance company supports more than **12,000 containers** across multiple Amazon EKS clusters.

Its security policy requires:

- Only approved enterprise base images
- Weekly vulnerability scanning
- Monthly base image updates
- Image signing
- Private Amazon ECR repositories
- Automatic rebuilds when critical vulnerabilities are identified

When a new OpenSSL vulnerability is disclosed, the platform team updates the enterprise base image.

All application images are automatically rebuilt using the patched base image and redeployed after security validation.

This centralized approach significantly reduces remediation time.

---

# Common Base Image Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Outdated operating systems
- End-of-life distributions
- Public unverified images
- Excessive software packages
- Missing security patches
- Images running as root
- Embedded credentials
- Weak image governance
- Missing image signing
- Inconsistent image versions

These issues increase software supply chain risk.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should continuously monitor:

- Base image versions
- New security advisories
- Vulnerability scan results
- Image age
- End-of-life operating systems
- Registry uploads
- Image signing validation
- Unauthorized image sources
- CI/CD build events
- Deployment compliance

Continuous monitoring helps ensure every workload uses approved and supported base images.

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended roadmap:

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use only approved and trusted base images.
- Prefer minimal or distroless images for production workloads.
- Regularly update base images with the latest security patches.
- Remove unnecessary software and packages.
- Avoid unverified public community images.
- Scan every base image for vulnerabilities.
- Digitally sign approved images.
- Store production images in private registries such as Amazon ECR.
- Automate base image validation within CI/CD pipelines.
- Continuously monitor for newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

A secure base image reduces risk before application code is even added.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A financial technology company builds hundreds of container images every week.

A newly disclosed vulnerability affects the version of OpenSSL included in the organization's enterprise base image.

Because every application inherits from that base image:

- The platform team patches the enterprise base image.
- A new version is scanned and digitally signed.
- CI/CD automatically rebuilds all dependent application images.
- Updated images are pushed to Amazon ECR.
- Amazon EKS rolling updates deploy the patched containers.

Within hours, hundreds of applications are protected without requiring individual development teams to manually patch their Dockerfiles.

# Lesson 05 — Image Vulnerability Scanning

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what Image Vulnerability Scanning is
- Learn how vulnerabilities enter container images
- Understand CVEs and CVSS severity ratings
- Explore image scanning tools and workflows
- Integrate vulnerability scanning into CI/CD pipelines
- Protect Amazon EKS workloads using automated image scanning
- Apply enterprise vulnerability management best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Every container image contains software components such as:

- Operating system packages
- Application frameworks
- Programming language runtimes
- Third-party libraries
- Open-source dependencies

These components may contain known security vulnerabilities.

If vulnerable images are deployed into production, attackers can exploit them to:

- Execute remote code
- Escalate privileges
- Steal sensitive data
- Compromise applications
- Move laterally across Kubernetes clusters

Image Vulnerability Scanning helps identify these risks before containers reach production.

---

# What is Image Vulnerability Scanning?

Image Vulnerability Scanning is the process of analysing a container image to identify known security vulnerabilities.

The scanner examines:

- Operating system packages
- Installed libraries
- Programming language dependencies
- Application frameworks
- Configuration issues

The results are compared against vulnerability databases to identify known security issues.

---

# Image Scanning Lifecycle

```text
Developer

↓

Dockerfile

↓

Build Image

↓

Image Scan

↓

Security Policy

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Images should be scanned before they are stored or deployed.

---

# How Vulnerabilities Enter Images

Vulnerabilities rarely originate from the application itself.

Most are inherited from dependencies.

```text
Base Image

↓

Operating System Packages

↓

Application Libraries

↓

Third-Party Dependencies

↓

Container Image

↓

Production
```

Every layer of the image should be assessed.

---

# What is a CVE?

A **Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)** identifier uniquely identifies a publicly disclosed security vulnerability.

Example:

```text
CVE-2025-12345
```

Each CVE contains information about:

- Affected software
- Severity
- Exploitation details
- Available patches
- Mitigation guidance

---

# CVSS Severity Ratings

Most scanners classify vulnerabilities using the **Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).**

| Severity | Typical CVSS Score |
|-----------|-------------------:|
| Critical | 9.0 – 10.0 |
| High | 7.0 – 8.9 |
| Medium | 4.0 – 6.9 |
| Low | 0.1 – 3.9 |

Enterprise security teams often block deployments containing Critical or High vulnerabilities.

---

# What Does a Scanner Check?

A vulnerability scanner analyses:

- Base operating system
- Installed packages
- Programming language libraries
- Open-source dependencies
- Known CVEs
- Configuration issues
- Unsupported software versions

Scanning provides visibility into inherited risks.

---

# Example Scan Results

```text
Image

↓

Scan Complete

↓

Critical : 1

High : 3

Medium : 8

Low : 15
```

Security teams prioritize remediation based on severity and business impact.

---

# Types of Image Vulnerabilities

Common findings include:

- Remote Code Execution (RCE)
- Privilege Escalation
- Buffer Overflows
- Authentication Bypass
- SQL Injection libraries
- Outdated OpenSSL
- Vulnerable Log4j versions
- Weak cryptographic libraries

Early detection significantly reduces organizational risk.

---

# Image Scanning Tools

Enterprise organizations use a variety of scanning solutions.

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| Amazon ECR Enhanced Scanning | Native AWS image vulnerability scanning |
| Amazon Inspector | Continuous vulnerability assessment |
| Trivy | Open-source image scanner |
| Grype | Open-source vulnerability scanner |
| Snyk Container | Developer-focused image scanning |
| Aqua Security | Enterprise container security |
| Prisma Cloud | Cloud-native security platform |
| Sysdig Secure | Image and runtime security |

Many organizations use multiple tools for layered security.

---

# Amazon ECR Enhanced Scanning

Amazon ECR provides integrated vulnerability scanning.

Features include:

- Continuous image scanning
- CVE detection
- Severity classification
- Integration with Amazon Inspector
- Automatic notifications
- Centralized findings

This enables organizations to monitor images throughout their lifecycle.

---

# Amazon Inspector

Amazon Inspector continuously evaluates:

- Container images
- EC2 instances
- Lambda functions

For container images, Inspector:

- Identifies new vulnerabilities
- Updates findings automatically
- Prioritizes risks
- Integrates with AWS Security Hub

Images continue to be assessed even after they have been stored in Amazon ECR.

---

# CI/CD Image Scanning

Scanning should occur automatically during builds.

```text
Developer

↓

Git Push

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Build Image

↓

Image Scan

↓

Pass

↓

Amazon ECR

--------------------

Fail

↓

Deployment Blocked
```

Only approved images should proceed to production.

---

# Shift-Left Security

Image scanning supports the **Shift-Left** security model.

```text
Develop

↓

Build

↓

Scan

↓

Fix

↓

Deploy
```

The earlier vulnerabilities are discovered, the less expensive they are to remediate.

---

# Vulnerability Remediation

When vulnerabilities are identified:

```text
Scanner

↓

Report Generated

↓

Developer

↓

Update Packages

↓

Rebuild Image

↓

Rescan

↓

Deploy
```

Images should always be rescanned after remediation.

---

# Continuous Scanning

Security does not stop after deployment.

New CVEs are discovered every day.

```text
Stored Image

↓

New CVE Published

↓

Automatic Rescan

↓

Security Alert
```

Continuous scanning identifies newly discovered vulnerabilities affecting previously approved images.

---

# Enterprise Amazon EKS Architecture

```text
Developer

↓

Git Repository

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Build Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon Inspector

↓

AWS Security Hub

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Security findings become part of the organization's continuous compliance programme.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational healthcare provider maintains thousands of container images in Amazon ECR.

Every image must:

- Pass vulnerability scanning
- Contain no Critical vulnerabilities
- Be digitally signed
- Use approved base images
- Meet internal compliance requirements

One morning, Amazon Inspector identifies a newly published Critical OpenSSL vulnerability affecting several production images.

The platform team:

- Rebuilds the affected images
- Applies the patched OpenSSL package
- Rescans the images
- Pushes the updated images to Amazon ECR
- Deploys the patched containers using Amazon EKS rolling updates

Within hours, the organization eliminates the vulnerability across hundreds of workloads.

---

# Common Vulnerability Scanning Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently discover:

- Images never scanned
- Outdated base images
- Ignored Critical CVEs
- Unsupported operating systems
- Missing dependency updates
- Manual scanning processes
- Missing CI/CD integration
- Inconsistent scanner configuration
- Images deployed despite High severity findings
- Lack of continuous scanning

These weaknesses significantly increase software supply chain risk.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Critical vulnerabilities
- High severity vulnerabilities
- Newly disclosed CVEs
- Base image updates
- Scan failures
- Image age
- Registry activity
- Inspector findings
- Security Hub findings
- Compliance dashboards

Continuous monitoring helps ensure vulnerabilities are identified and remediated quickly.

---

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended rollout:

```text
Step 1

↓

Approve Base Images

↓

Step 2

↓

Integrate Image Scanning

↓

Step 3

↓

Configure Scan Policies

↓

Step 4

↓

Block Critical Findings

↓

Step 5

↓

Store Images in Amazon ECR

↓

Step 6

↓

Enable Amazon Inspector

↓

Step 7

↓

Monitor Security Hub

↓

Step 8

↓

Continuously Patch & Rebuild
```

This approach embeds vulnerability management into the software delivery process.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Scan every image before deployment.
- Enable continuous scanning for stored images.
- Prioritize Critical and High severity vulnerabilities.
- Keep base images regularly updated.
- Automate vulnerability scanning in CI/CD pipelines.
- Never deploy images with unapproved Critical vulnerabilities.
- Integrate Amazon Inspector with Amazon ECR and AWS Security Hub.
- Regularly rebuild images using updated dependencies.
- Monitor newly disclosed CVEs continuously.
- Combine image scanning with image signing and runtime security.

Image Vulnerability Scanning is a fundamental component of secure container supply chains.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A software company deploys a customer portal on Amazon EKS.

Several weeks after deployment, a Critical vulnerability is disclosed in a widely used OpenSSL library.

Because Amazon Inspector continuously scans Amazon ECR repositories:

- The affected image is automatically identified.
- Security Hub creates a new finding.
- The platform team receives an alert.
- Developers rebuild the image using the patched library.
- The new image passes vulnerability scanning.
- Amazon EKS performs a rolling deployment of the updated containers.

The vulnerability is remediated before attackers can exploit it.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What Image Vulnerability Scanning is
- How vulnerabilities enter container images
- CVEs and CVSS severity ratings
- Enterprise image scanning tools
- Amazon ECR Enhanced Scanning and Amazon Inspector
- CI/CD integration
- Continuous vulnerability management
- Best practices for Amazon EKS

Image Vulnerability Scanning enables organizations to identify and remediate known security vulnerabilities before they become production incidents. Combined with secure Dockerfiles, trusted base images, image signing and runtime protection, it forms a critical component of Kubernetes supply chain security.

# Lesson 06 — Image Signing & Verification

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what Image Signing is
- Learn why image signing is critical for supply chain security
- Understand digital signatures and cryptographic verification
- Explore image signing technologies
- Learn how Amazon EKS verifies trusted images
- Integrate image signing into CI/CD pipelines
- Apply enterprise image trust best practices

---

# Why This Matters

Building a secure container image is only part of the security journey.

Organizations must also answer critical questions:

- Was this image created by our organization?
- Has the image been modified?
- Has the image been replaced by an attacker?
- Can this image be trusted?
- Is this the exact image that passed security validation?

Without verification, attackers may introduce:

- Malicious container images
- Backdoored software
- Trojanized dependencies
- Fake application updates
- Supply chain attacks

Image Signing ensures only trusted images are deployed into production.

---

# What is Image Signing?

Image Signing is the process of digitally signing a container image using cryptographic keys.

The signature proves:

- Who created the image
- That the image has not been modified
- That the image is authentic
- That the image can be trusted

Unlike image scanning, which identifies vulnerabilities, image signing establishes **trust**.

---

# Image Signing Workflow

```text
Developer

↓

Build Image

↓

Security Scan

↓

Digitally Sign Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Verify Signature

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Deploy Container
```

Only trusted images are allowed into production.

---

# Why Image Signing Matters

Without image signing:

```text
Attacker

↓

Uploads Fake Image

↓

Registry

↓

Production Deployment
```

With image signing:

```text
Fake Image

↓

Signature Validation

↓

Verification Failed

↓

Deployment Blocked
```

Digital signatures help prevent unauthorized or tampered images from being deployed.

---

# Digital Signatures

A digital signature uses cryptography to verify authenticity and integrity.

The process uses:

- Private Key
- Public Key

```text
Private Key

↓

Sign Image

↓

Digital Signature

↓

Public Key

↓

Verify Image
```

Only the holder of the private key can create a valid signature.

---

# Public Key Cryptography

Image signing relies on asymmetric cryptography.

| Private Key | Public Key |
|-------------|------------|
| Secret | Shared |
| Creates signatures | Verifies signatures |
| Stored securely | Distributed to verifiers |

If the image changes after signing, verification fails.

---

# Image Integrity

Image signing protects image integrity.

```text
Original Image

↓

Sign Image

↓

Store Signature

↓

Image Modified?

↓

Yes

↓

Verification Failed
```

Even a single modified byte invalidates the signature.

---

# Image Authenticity

Image verification confirms:

```text
Trusted Publisher

↓

Signed Image

↓

Registry

↓

Verification

↓

Deployment Approved
```

The organization knows exactly who produced the image.

---

# Image Signing Lifecycle

```text
Developer

↓

Source Code

↓

Build Image

↓

Scan Image

↓

Sign Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Admission Policy

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Signing should occur only after the image successfully passes security validation.

---

# Common Image Signing Technologies

Enterprise organizations commonly use:

| Technology | Purpose |
|------------|---------|
| Cosign | Container image signing and verification |
| Sigstore | Open-source signing infrastructure |
| Notation | OCI image signing standard |
| AWS Signer | Managed code signing service (for supported workloads and integrations) |
| in-toto | Supply chain integrity metadata |
| The Update Framework (TUF) | Secure software update framework |

Cosign has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for Kubernetes image signing.

---

# Cosign

Cosign is an open-source image signing tool developed as part of the Sigstore project.

Features include:

- Image signing
- Signature verification
- Keyless signing support
- OCI registry integration
- Supply chain security
- Kubernetes policy integration

Many enterprise Kubernetes platforms use Cosign as part of their CI/CD pipelines.

---

# Sigstore

Sigstore provides a secure ecosystem for software signing.

Components include:

- Cosign
- Fulcio (certificate authority)
- Rekor (transparency log)

Benefits:

- Open source
- Transparent verification
- Supply chain integrity
- Simplified key management

---

# Image Verification

Before deployment:

```text
Container Image

↓

Verify Signature

↓

Trusted?

↓

Yes

↓

Deploy

-------------------

No

↓

Reject Deployment
```

Verification ensures only approved images reach production.

---

# Admission Controllers

Image verification is commonly enforced using admission policies.

```text
Developer

↓

Deploy Image

↓

Admission Controller

↓

Verify Signature

↓

Approved

or

Rejected
```

Unsigned or untrusted images are blocked automatically.

---

# Image Signing in Amazon EKS

```text
Developer

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Image Scan

↓

Cosign Sign

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Admission Policy

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Running Container
```

Image trust becomes an automated part of the deployment process.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational banking organization deploys all workloads through a centralized CI/CD platform.

The pipeline automatically:

- Builds the image
- Performs vulnerability scanning
- Executes compliance checks
- Signs the image using Cosign
- Stores the image in Amazon ECR

When developers deploy an application:

- The admission controller verifies the signature.
- Only images signed by the organization's trusted signing key are accepted.
- Unsigned or externally signed images are rejected.

This ensures every workload running in production is both approved and traceable.

---

# Common Image Signing Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Unsigned production images
- Shared signing keys
- Private keys stored in source code
- Missing signature verification
- Public images without validation
- Weak admission policies
- Untrusted registries
- Expired signing certificates
- Missing audit trails
- Manual deployment bypasses

These weaknesses reduce trust in the software supply chain.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Image signing failures
- Signature verification failures
- Admission controller denials
- Registry activity
- Signing key usage
- Certificate expiration
- Unauthorized image uploads
- CI/CD pipeline events
- Security policy violations
- Deployment approvals

Monitoring helps ensure that only trusted images are deployed.

---

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended rollout:

```text
Step 1

↓

Approve Base Images

↓

Step 2

↓

Build Container Images

↓

Step 3

↓

Perform Vulnerability Scanning

↓

Step 4

↓

Digitally Sign Images

↓

Step 5

↓

Push to Amazon ECR

↓

Step 6

↓

Enable Signature Verification

↓

Step 7

↓

Enforce Admission Policies

↓

Step 8

↓

Continuously Monitor
```

This process establishes a trusted software supply chain.

---

# Image Signing vs Image Scanning

| Image Scanning | Image Signing |
|----------------|---------------|
| Finds vulnerabilities | Verifies authenticity |
| Detects CVEs | Confirms trusted publisher |
| Identifies outdated software | Detects image tampering |
| Improves security posture | Establishes deployment trust |
| Should occur before deployment | Should occur after successful scanning |

Enterprise environments require **both** scanning and signing.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Sign every production container image.
- Scan images before signing them.
- Store signing keys securely using enterprise key management solutions.
- Never commit private signing keys to source code.
- Verify image signatures before deployment.
- Use admission policies to block unsigned images.
- Store images in trusted private registries such as Amazon ECR.
- Rotate signing keys regularly.
- Audit image signing and verification events.
- Integrate image signing into CI/CD pipelines.

Image signing establishes trust throughout the software supply chain and helps prevent unauthorized software from entering production.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A technology company manages multiple Amazon EKS production clusters.

An attacker gains access to a developer's workstation and attempts to upload a modified container image containing a hidden cryptocurrency miner.

The attacker pushes the image to the organization's registry.

When the deployment begins:

- The admission controller requests signature verification.
- The image has no valid enterprise signature.
- Verification fails.
- Kubernetes rejects the deployment.
- Security teams receive an alert.
- The malicious image never reaches production.

Because image signing and verification were enforced, the attempted supply chain attack is stopped before any workloads are affected.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- What Image Signing is
- Why digital signatures are important
- How public/private key cryptography supports image trust
- Image authenticity and integrity
- Cosign, Sigstore and enterprise signing technologies
- Admission controller verification
- Amazon EKS image trust architecture
- Best practices for software supply chain security

Image Signing & Verification are critical components of modern Kubernetes supply chain security. By combining vulnerability scanning, cryptographic signatures, admission policy enforcement and continuous monitoring, organizations can ensure that only trusted, approved and untampered container images are deployed into Amazon EKS production environments.

# Lesson 07 — Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand what a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is
- Learn why SBOMs are important for container security
- Understand the components of an SBOM
- Explore SBOM standards and formats
- Learn how SBOMs improve vulnerability management
- Integrate SBOM generation into CI/CD pipelines
- Apply enterprise SBOM best practices for Amazon EKS

---

# Why This Matters

Modern applications rarely consist of only custom-written code.

Instead, they contain:

- Open-source libraries
- Programming language packages
- Operating system packages
- Frameworks
- Third-party dependencies
- Container base images

A single container image may contain **hundreds or even thousands of software components**.

Without visibility into these components, organizations cannot quickly answer questions such as:

- Which applications use Log4j?
- Which containers contain vulnerable OpenSSL versions?
- Which workloads are affected by a newly disclosed CVE?
- Are we using approved software components?

An **SBOM** provides this visibility.

---

# What is an SBOM?

A **Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)** is a complete inventory of every software component included in an application or container image.

Think of it as an ingredient list on a food product.

```text
Container Image

↓

Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

├── Base Image

├── Operating System Packages

├── Runtime

├── Libraries

├── Open Source Dependencies

├── Application Packages

└── Versions
```

An SBOM provides complete transparency into what is inside an image.

---

# Why SBOMs Matter

Without an SBOM:

```text
Critical CVE Published

↓

Which Applications Are Affected?

↓

Unknown

↓

Slow Response
```

With an SBOM:

```text
Critical CVE Published

↓

Search SBOM

↓

Identify Affected Images

↓

Patch Quickly
```

SBOMs dramatically reduce incident response time.

---

# What Information Does an SBOM Contain?

An enterprise SBOM typically includes:

- Software name
- Component version
- Supplier or vendor
- Package manager
- License information
- Hash values
- Dependency relationships
- Component type
- Image digest
- Build metadata

This information helps organizations understand exactly what has been deployed.

---

# SBOM Example

```text
Application

↓

Python 3.12

↓

Flask 3.0.2

↓

Requests 2.32

↓

OpenSSL 3.x

↓

Amazon Linux 2023
```

Every component is recorded with its version.

---

# Direct vs Indirect Dependencies

Applications contain both direct and indirect dependencies.

```text
Application

├── Direct Library A

│
```

# Enterprise Example

A multinational healthcare provider operates over **20,000 containerized workloads** on Amazon EKS.

A Critical vulnerability is disclosed in a widely used JSON parsing library.

Because every image includes an SBOM:

- They identify every affected application within minutes.
- Development teams rebuild only the impacted images.
- Updated images are rescanned, signed and deployed.

# SBOM vs Image Scanning

| SBOM | Image Scanning |
|------|----------------|
| Lists all software components | Identifies known vulnerabilities |
| Provides software inventory | Detects CVEs |
| Supports compliance | Supports remediation |
| Enables dependency analysis | Enables risk prioritization |
| Improves supply chain transparency | Improves security posture |

Both capabilities complement each other and should be implemented together.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Generate an SBOM for every production image.
- Automate SBOM generation in CI/CD pipelines.
- Store SBOMs alongside container images.
- Use standardized formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
- Link SBOMs to image digests and signatures.
- Continuously update SBOMs whenever images are rebuilt.
- Combine SBOMs with vulnerability scanning and image signing.
- Monitor software inventory for newly disclosed CVEs.
- Track third-party software and license obligations.
- Use SBOMs to accelerate incident response and compliance activities.

SBOMs provide the visibility needed to secure modern software supply chains.

---

A global e-commerce company receives an urgent advisory about a newly discovered vulnerability in an open-source compression library.

Without an SBOM, engineers would need to inspect hundreds of repositories and thousands of container images manually.

Instead:

- The security team searches the centralized SBOM repository.
- All affected container images are identified within minutes.
- Developers rebuild the images using updated libraries.
- The new images are scanned, signed and redeployed through Amazon EKS.

The organization reduces remediation time from several days to just a few hours.

# Why This Matters

Modern applications are built using numerous tools and services.

A typical build pipeline includes:

- Source code repositories
- CI/CD platforms
- Package managers
- Build servers
- Container registries
- Deployment pipelines
- Kubernetes clusters

If any stage of this pipeline is compromised, attackers can inject malicious software into production.

Recent attacks on software supply chains have demonstrated that compromising the build process can impact thousands of organizations simultaneously.

Supply chain security frameworks help establish trust across the entire software development lifecycle.

---

# What is Software Supply Chain Security?

Software Supply Chain Security ensures that every component involved in creating and deploying software is trustworthy.

```text
Source Code

↓

Build

↓

Test

↓

Package

↓

Container Image

↓

Registry

↓

Deployment

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Every stage must be protected against tampering.

---

# What is SLSA?

**SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts)** is a security framework developed to improve software build integrity and reduce supply chain attacks.

Its objectives include:

- Prevent build tampering
- Improve build integrity
- Generate provenance
- Secure CI/CD pipelines
- Verify software authenticity
- Establish deployment trust

SLSA provides a maturity model that organizations can progressively adopt.

---

# SLSA Goals

SLSA focuses on four key goals.

```text
Source Integrity

↓

Build Integrity

↓

Artifact Integrity

↓

Deployment Trust
```

Together, these controls reduce the likelihood of malicious software entering production.

---

# SLSA Levels

SLSA defines increasing levels of security maturity.

| Level | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Level 1 | Basic build process and provenance generation |
| Level 2 | Hosted build services with authenticated source control |
| Level 3 | Hardened build platform with stronger isolation |
| Level 4 | Highest assurance with reproducible and verifiable builds |

Higher levels provide stronger protection against sophisticated supply chain attacks.

---

# What is Provenance?

**Provenance** is a verifiable record describing how software was produced.

It answers questions such as:

- Who built the software?
- Which source code was used?
- Which build system created it?
- Which dependencies were included?
- Which compiler version was used?
- Which security checks were performed?

Provenance creates an auditable history for every software artifact.

---

# Provenance Example

```text
Application

↓

Git Commit

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Build Server

↓

Image Digest

↓

Digital Signature

↓

Deployment
```

Every step is recorded and can be verified.

---

# What is in-toto?

**in-toto** is an open-source framework that protects software supply chains by recording and verifying every step in the build pipeline.

It creates cryptographically signed metadata describing:

- Build steps
- Developers
- Build systems
- Artifacts
- Dependencies
- Validation checks

This metadata helps ensure no unauthorized modifications occur during the software lifecycle.

---

# How in-toto Works

```text
Developer

↓

Build Step

↓

Signed Metadata

↓

Test Step

↓

Signed Metadata

↓

Package Step

↓

Signed Metadata

↓

Deploy
```

Each stage signs its work, creating a verifiable chain of trust.

---

# Chain of Trust

A secure software supply chain establishes a continuous chain of trust.

```text
Source Code

↓

Authenticated Commit

↓

Verified Build

↓

Signed Image

↓

Verified Registry

↓

Admission Controller

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Breaking the chain results in deployment failure.

---

# Supply Chain Attack Example

Without supply chain protection:

```text
Attacker

↓

Compromised Build Server

↓

Malicious Container Image

↓

Production Deployment
```

The malicious software reaches production unnoticed.

---

# Protected Build Pipeline

With SLSA and in-toto:

```text
Attacker

↓

Attempts Modification

↓

Metadata Verification

↓

Integrity Check Failed

↓

Deployment Blocked
```

Unauthorized changes are detected before deployment.

---

```text
Developer

↓

Git Repository

↓

Authenticated Commit

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Build Provenance

↓

SBOM Generation

Image Scanning

↓

Image Signing

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Admission Verification

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Every stage contributes to software trust.

---

# SLSA + SBOM + Image Signing

Modern supply chain security combines several technologies.

| Technology | Purpose |
|------------|---------|
| SBOM | Software inventory |
| Image Scanning | Vulnerability detection |
| Image Signing | Authenticity verification |
| Provenance | Build history |
| SLSA | Secure build framework |
| in-toto | Pipeline integrity verification |

Together, these controls provide defense in depth.

---

# Enterprise Example

A global financial institution builds over **5,000 container images** every month.

To secure its software supply chain, the organization implements:

- Git commit signing
- Protected source repositories
- SLSA-compliant build pipelines
- Automated SBOM generation
- Continuous vulnerability scanning
- Cosign image signing
- in-toto build metadata
- Admission controller verification
- Private Amazon ECR repositories

When an attacker attempts to modify an artifact during the build process, the generated provenance no longer matches the expected metadata.

The deployment is automatically rejected, and the security team receives an alert before the image reaches Amazon EKS.

---

# Common Supply Chain Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently encounter:

- Unverified source code
- Manual build processes
- Shared CI/CD credentials
- Missing provenance
- Unsigned artifacts
- Untrusted dependencies
- Weak build server security
- Incomplete audit trails
- Missing artifact verification
- Public dependency confusion attacks

These weaknesses increase the risk of software compromise.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Build pipeline integrity
- Provenance generation
- Build failures
- Artifact verification failures
- Admission controller denials
- Unauthorized source code changes
- Image signing events
- Dependency updates
- SBOM generation status
- CI/CD audit logs

Monitoring provides visibility into the health of the software supply chain.


---

# SLSA vs in-toto

| SLSA | in-toto |
|------|----------|
| Security framework | Security implementation framework |
| Defines maturity levels | Records build steps |
| Focuses on build integrity | Focuses on artifact verification |
| Provides best practices | Generates signed metadata |
| Guides enterprise adoption | Enables cryptographic verification |

They complement each other rather than compete.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Protect source code repositories with strong authentication.
- Automate builds using trusted CI/CD systems.
- Generate provenance for every build.
- Produce SBOMs for all production images.
- Scan images before deployment.
- Sign images using trusted signing keys.
- Verify signatures and provenance during deployment.
- Implement admission policies that enforce trusted artifacts.
- Regularly audit CI/CD pipelines.
- Continuously monitor the software supply chain for anomalies.

Supply chain security should be treated as an end-to-end process rather than a single security control.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A SaaS provider hosts hundreds of customer-facing applications on Amazon EKS.

An attacker compromises a third-party dependency and attempts to inject malicious code into the organization's build pipeline.

Because the CI/CD platform implements SLSA practices and uses in-toto metadata:

- The unauthorized dependency change is detected.
- Provenance validation fails.
- The generated container image is never signed.
- Admission policies reject the deployment.
- Security teams investigate the incident using detailed provenance and audit records.

The malicious software never reaches production, preserving customer trust and business continuity.

Learning Objectives

Section titled “Learning Objectives”

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Learn why supply chain frameworks are necessary

Why This Matters

Section titled “Why This Matters”

Modern applications are built using numerous tools and services.

A typical build pipeline includes:

  • Source code repositories
  • CI/CD platforms
  • Package managers
  • Build servers
  • Container registries
  • Deployment pipelines
  • Kubernetes clusters

If any stage of this pipeline is compromised, attackers can inject malicious software into production.

Recent attacks on software supply chains have demonstrated that compromising the build process can impact thousands of organizations simultaneously.

Supply chain security frameworks help establish trust across the entire software development lifecycle.

What is Software Supply Chain Security?

Section titled “What is Software Supply Chain Security?”

Software Supply Chain Security ensures that every component involved in creating and deploying software is trustworthy.

Every stage must be protected against tampering.

What is SLSA?

Section titled “What is SLSA?”

SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) is a security framework developed to improve software build integrity and reduce supply chain attacks.

Its objectives include:

  • Prevent build tampering
  • Improve build integrity
  • Generate provenance
  • Secure CI/CD pipelines
  • Verify software authenticity
  • Establish deployment trust

SLSA provides a maturity model that organizations can progressively adopt.

SLSA Goals

Section titled “SLSA Goals”

SLSA focuses on four key goals.

Together, these controls reduce the likelihood of malicious software entering production.

SLSA Levels

Section titled “SLSA Levels”

SLSA defines increasing levels of security maturity.

Level Description
Level 1 Basic build process and provenance generation
Level 2 Hosted build services with authenticated source control
Level 3 Hardened build platform with stronger isolation
Level 4 Highest assurance with reproducible and verifiable builds

Higher levels provide stronger protection against sophisticated supply chain attacks.

What is Provenance?

Section titled “What is Provenance?”

Provenance is a verifiable record describing how software was produced.

It answers questions such as:

  • Who built the software?
  • Which source code was used?
  • Which build system created it?
  • Which dependencies were included?
  • Which compiler version was used?
  • Which security checks were performed?

Provenance creates an auditable history for every software artifact.

Provenance Example

Section titled “Provenance Example”

Every step is recorded and can be verified.

What is in-toto?

Section titled “What is in-toto?”

in-toto is an open-source framework that protects software supply chains by recording and verifying every step in the build pipeline.

It creates cryptographically signed metadata describing:

  • Build steps
  • Developers
  • Build systems
  • Artifacts
  • Dependencies
  • Validation checks

This metadata helps ensure no unauthorized modifications occur during the software lifecycle.

How in-toto Works

Section titled “How in-toto Works”

Each stage signs its work, creating a verifiable chain of trust.

Chain of Trust

Section titled “Chain of Trust”

A secure software supply chain establishes a continuous chain of trust.

Breaking the chain results in deployment failure.

Supply Chain Attack Example

Section titled “Supply Chain Attack Example”

Without supply chain protection:

The malicious software reaches production unnoticed.

Protected Build Pipeline

Section titled “Protected Build Pipeline”

With SLSA and in-toto:

Unauthorized changes are detected before deployment.

Enterprise CI/CD Architecture

Section titled “Enterprise CI/CD Architecture”

Every stage contributes to software trust.

SLSA + SBOM + Image Signing

Section titled “SLSA + SBOM + Image Signing”

Modern supply chain security combines several technologies.

Technology Purpose
SBOM Software inventory
Image Scanning Vulnerability detection
Image Signing Authenticity verification
Provenance Build history
SLSA Secure build framework
in-toto Pipeline integrity verification

Together, these controls provide defense in depth.

Enterprise Example

Section titled “Enterprise Example”

A global financial institution builds over 5,000 container images every month.

To secure its software supply chain, the organization implements:

  • Git commit signing
  • Protected source repositories
  • SLSA-compliant build pipelines
  • Automated SBOM generation
  • Continuous vulnerability scanning
  • Cosign image signing
  • in-toto build metadata
  • Admission controller verification
  • Private Amazon ECR repositories

When an attacker attempts to modify an artifact during the build process, the generated provenance no longer matches the expected metadata.

The deployment is automatically rejected, and the security team receives an alert before the image reaches Amazon EKS.

Common Supply Chain Risks

Section titled “Common Supply Chain Risks”

Cloud Security Engineers frequently encounter:

  • Unverified source code
  • Manual build processes
  • Shared CI/CD credentials
  • Missing provenance
  • Unsigned artifacts
  • Untrusted dependencies
  • Weak build server security
  • Incomplete audit trails
  • Missing artifact verification
  • Public dependency confusion attacks

These weaknesses increase the risk of software compromise.

Enterprise Monitoring

Section titled “Enterprise Monitoring”

Security teams should monitor:

  • Build pipeline integrity
  • Provenance generation
  • Build failures
  • Artifact verification failures
  • Admission controller denials
  • Unauthorized source code changes
  • Image signing events
  • Dependency updates
  • SBOM generation status
  • CI/CD audit logs

Monitoring provides visibility into the health of the software supply chain.

Enterprise Implementation Strategy

Section titled “Enterprise Implementation Strategy”

A recommended roadmap:

This layered approach provides end-to-end software supply chain protection.

SLSA vs in-toto

Section titled “SLSA vs in-toto”
SLSA in-toto
Security framework Security implementation framework
Defines maturity levels Records build steps
Focuses on build integrity Focuses on artifact verification
Provides best practices Generates signed metadata
Guides enterprise adoption Enables cryptographic verification

They complement each other rather than compete.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

  • Protect source code repositories with strong authentication.
  • Automate builds using trusted CI/CD systems.
  • Generate provenance for every build.
  • Produce SBOMs for all production images.
  • Scan images before deployment.
  • Sign images using trusted signing keys.
  • Verify signatures and provenance during deployment.
  • Implement admission policies that enforce trusted artifacts.
  • Regularly audit CI/CD pipelines.
  • Continuously monitor the software supply chain for anomalies.

Supply chain security should be treated as an end-to-end process rather than a single security control.

Real-World Scenario

Section titled “Real-World Scenario”

A SaaS provider hosts hundreds of customer-facing applications on Amazon EKS.

An attacker compromises a third-party dependency and attempts to inject malicious code into the organization’s build pipeline.

Because the CI/CD platform implements SLSA practices and uses in-toto metadata:

  • The unauthorized dependency change is detected.
  • Provenance validation fails.
  • The generated container image is never signed.
  • Admission policies reject the deployment.
  • Security teams investigate the incident using detailed provenance and audit records.

The malicious software never reaches production, preserving customer trust and business continuity.

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

Combined with SBOMs, vulnerability scanning, image signing and admission policies, they provide a comprehensive defense against modern software supply chain attacks.

# Lesson 09 — Enterprise Container Registry Security

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand the role of container registries
- Learn why container registry security is critical
- Explore Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR)
- Secure image storage and access
- Implement enterprise repository governance
- Protect container images using encryption and IAM
- Apply enterprise best practices for Amazon EKS

---

# Why This Matters

A container registry is the **central repository** where container images are stored before deployment.

Every Kubernetes workload begins by pulling an image from a registry.

If an attacker compromises the registry, they may:

- Replace trusted images
- Upload malicious images
- Delete production images
- Steal proprietary software
- Deploy backdoored applications

Because every workload depends on the registry, securing it is a critical part of software supply chain security.

---

# What is a Container Registry?

A container registry stores container images and related artifacts.

Typical contents include:

- Container images
- Image tags
- Image digests
- Digital signatures
- SBOMs
- Image metadata

```text
Developer

↓

Container Registry

↓

Amazon EKS

↓

Running Container
```

The registry acts as the trusted source for production deployments.

---

# Public vs Private Registries

Organizations can use both public and private registries.

| Public Registry | Private Registry |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Internet accessible | Restricted access |
| Community images | Enterprise images |
| Higher supply chain risk | Greater control |
| Limited governance | Centralized governance |
| Public software | Internal production workloads |

Enterprise production workloads should primarily use private registries.

---

# Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR)

Amazon ECR is AWS's managed private container registry.

Key capabilities include:

- Private repositories
- Public repositories
- IAM integration
- Encryption at rest
- Vulnerability scanning
- Image lifecycle policies
- Cross-region replication
- Repository policies
- CloudTrail auditing

Amazon ECR integrates natively with Amazon EKS.

---

# Enterprise Registry Architecture

```text
Developer

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Image Build

↓

Image Scan

↓

Image Signing

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon EKS
```

Images should never bypass the enterprise registry.

---

# Repository Structure

Large organizations typically organize repositories by application, environment, or business unit.

Example:

```text
Amazon ECR

├── finance-api

├── payment-service

├── customer-portal

├── inventory-service

└── shared-base-images
```

This improves governance and simplifies access management.

---

# IAM-Based Access Control

Amazon ECR integrates with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).

Typical permissions include:

- Pull images
- Push images
- Delete images
- Create repositories
- Update repository policies
- Configure lifecycle policies

Access should follow the Principle of Least Privilege.

---

# Example Access Model

```text
Developers

↓

Push Images

----------------

Amazon EKS Nodes

↓

Pull Images

----------------

Security Team

↓

Manage Registry Policies
```

Each role receives only the permissions required for its responsibilities.

---

# Repository Policies

Repository policies provide fine-grained access control.

Policies can:

- Restrict image uploads
- Restrict image downloads
- Limit cross-account access
- Control repository administrators
- Prevent unauthorized deletion

Repository policies complement IAM permissions.

---

# Encryption at Rest

Amazon ECR encrypts stored images.

Supported options include:

- AWS-managed encryption keys
- Customer-managed AWS KMS keys

```text
Container Image

↓

Encryption

↓

Amazon ECR Storage
```

Encryption protects images against unauthorized storage access.

---

# Encryption in Transit

All communication with Amazon ECR uses TLS.

```text
Developer

↓

TLS Encryption

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

TLS Encryption

↓

Amazon EKS
```

This protects image uploads and downloads from interception.

---

# Image Immutability

Image tags should be immutable.

Bad practice:

```text
v1.0

↓

Overwrite

↓

Different Image
```

Recommended:

```text
v1.0

↓

Locked

↓

Cannot Modify
```

Immutable tags ensure deployment consistency and prevent accidental or malicious replacement.

---

# Vulnerability Scanning

Amazon ECR integrates with:

- Amazon Inspector
- Enhanced Scanning
- CVE databases

Every image should be scanned before deployment.

```text
Image

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

Amazon Inspector

↓

Security Findings
```

---

# Image Lifecycle Policies

Old images should not remain indefinitely.

Lifecycle policies automatically:

- Delete unused images
- Remove old versions
- Retain approved releases
- Reduce storage costs

Example:

```text
Version 1

↓

Version 2

↓

Version 3

↓

Delete Older Images Automatically
```

Lifecycle management keeps repositories organized and reduces operational overhead.

---

# Cross-Region Replication

Global organizations replicate repositories.

```text
Primary Region

↓

Replication

↓

Secondary Region

↓

Disaster Recovery
```

Benefits include:

- High availability
- Lower deployment latency
- Disaster recovery
- Regional resilience

---

# Registry Auditing

Every registry action should be logged.

Common events include:

- Image push
- Image pull
- Repository creation
- Repository deletion
- Permission changes
- Lifecycle policy updates
- Scan results
- Replication events

AWS CloudTrail provides detailed audit logs for Amazon ECR activities.

---

# Enterprise Governance

Enterprise registry governance includes:

- Approved repositories
- Approved base images
- Repository naming standards
- Image signing requirements
- Mandatory vulnerability scanning
- Repository ownership
- Lifecycle policies
- Audit logging
- Compliance reporting
- Regular access reviews

Governance ensures consistency across development teams.

---

# Enterprise Example

A multinational banking organization maintains over **15,000 production container images** in Amazon ECR.

The organization enforces the following controls:

- Private repositories only
- IAM least-privilege access
- Mandatory image signing
- Enhanced vulnerability scanning
- Customer-managed KMS encryption
- Immutable image tags
- Cross-region replication
- CloudTrail auditing
- Automated lifecycle policies

When a developer attempts to overwrite a production image tag, the operation is rejected because immutable tags are enforced.

The deployment pipeline requires a new versioned image instead, preserving traceability and deployment integrity.

---

# Common Registry Security Risks

Cloud Security Engineers frequently identify:

- Public repositories used for production
- Excessive IAM permissions
- Mutable image tags
- Missing vulnerability scanning
- Disabled encryption
- Weak repository policies
- Orphaned repositories
- Missing lifecycle policies
- Unrestricted cross-account access
- No audit logging

These weaknesses expose organizations to supply chain attacks and operational risk.

---

# Enterprise Monitoring

Security teams should monitor:

- Repository access
- Image uploads
- Image downloads
- Failed authentication attempts
- Vulnerability findings
- Image signing status
- Lifecycle policy execution
- Cross-region replication health
- CloudTrail audit events
- Unauthorized permission changes

Continuous monitoring helps detect malicious or accidental changes to the registry.

---

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

A recommended rollout:

```text
Step 1

↓

Create Private Amazon ECR Repositories

↓

Step 2

↓

Implement IAM Least Privilege

↓

Step 3

↓

Enable Encryption

↓

Step 4

↓

Enable Enhanced Vulnerability Scanning

↓

Step 5

↓

Require Image Signing

↓

Step 6

↓

Enable Immutable Tags

↓

Step 7

↓

Configure Lifecycle Policies

↓

Step 8

↓

Enable Cross-Region Replication

↓

Step 9

↓

Monitor with CloudTrail & Amazon Inspector
```

This layered approach provides a secure and resilient container registry.

---

# Enterprise Registry Security Architecture

```text
Developer

↓

Git Repository

↓

CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Build Image

↓

Generate SBOM

↓

Image Scan

↓

Image Sign

↓

Amazon ECR

↓

IAM Authorization

↓

Amazon Inspector

↓

AWS CloudTrail

↓

Amazon EKS
```

This architecture integrates identity, vulnerability management, auditing, and deployment controls into a unified software supply chain.

---

# Best Practices

As a Kubernetes Security Engineer:

- Use private Amazon ECR repositories for production workloads.
- Enforce IAM least-privilege access for users, services and automation.
- Enable immutable image tags to prevent image replacement.
- Encrypt repositories using AWS KMS.
- Enable Enhanced Scanning with Amazon Inspector.
- Require digital signatures for production images.
- Configure lifecycle policies to manage image retention.
- Enable CloudTrail logging for all registry operations.
- Replicate critical repositories across AWS Regions.
- Regularly review repository permissions and unused images.

A secure registry forms the trusted distribution point for enterprise container workloads.

---

# Real-World Scenario

A global retail company hosts all production container images in Amazon ECR.

During a security review, analysts discover that one development repository allows unrestricted image deletion.

An attacker who gains temporary access could remove production-ready images, disrupting deployments.

The security team responds by:

- Restricting repository permissions using IAM.
- Applying repository policies.
- Enabling immutable image tags.
- Activating CloudTrail monitoring.
- Enforcing mandatory image signing and vulnerability scanning.

The registry now supports secure, auditable and resilient software delivery across all Amazon EKS clusters.

---

# Key Takeaways

After completing this lesson, you should understand:

- The role of container registries in Kubernetes
- Amazon ECR architecture and capabilities
- Registry access control using IAM and repository policies
- Encryption at rest and in transit
- Image immutability
- Vulnerability scanning with Amazon Inspector
- Lifecycle policies and cross-region replication
- Enterprise registry governance for Amazon EKS

Enterprise Container Registry Security is a critical layer of Kubernetes software supply chain protection. By securing Amazon ECR with strong identity controls, encryption, vulnerability scanning, immutable image tags, auditing and governance, organizations ensure that only trusted container images are stored, distributed and deployed into production Amazon EKS environments.
