# Why This Matters

Kubernetes gives development teams tremendous flexibility.

That flexibility can also introduce risk.

Without enforceable policies, teams may deploy:

- Privileged containers
- Root containers
- Workloads from untrusted registries
- Pods without resource limits
- Containers with writable root filesystems
- Workloads that use excessive Service Account permissions
- Applications without Network Policies
- Services exposed directly to the internet
- Images with mutable tags
- Pods that mount sensitive host paths

Security guidance alone does not prevent these deployments.

A documented standard may say:

> Production containers must not run as root.

But unless that requirement is enforced, a developer can still deploy a root container.

Kubernetes policies convert security requirements into technical controls that can:

- Warn
- Audit
- Reject
- Mutate
- Report
- Remediate

For Cloud Security Engineers, policies are essential for creating secure and consistent Amazon EKS environments at scale.

# What is a Kubernetes Policy?

A Kubernetes policy is a rule that defines what is allowed, required or prohibited within a cluster.

A policy may apply to:

- Pods
- Deployments
- Services
- Namespaces
- ConfigMaps
- Secrets
- Ingress resources
- RBAC objects
- Service Accounts
- Custom resources

Examples include:

- Containers must run as non-root.
- Privileged containers are prohibited.
- Images must come from an approved registry.
- Every production workload must define resource limits.
- Host networking is prohibited.
- Default Service Accounts cannot be used.
- Network Policies are required.
- Every resource must include ownership labels.
- LoadBalancer Services require approval.

# Policy as a Security Boundary

Policies create a controlled boundary between development flexibility and enterprise security requirements.

```text
Developer Manifest

↓

Kubernetes API Request

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorisation

↓

Policy Evaluation

↓

Allowed, Warned, Mutated or Denied

↓

Cluster Resource Created
```

Without policy enforcement, insecure configurations may reach production unnoticed.

# Governance Policy Versus Technical Policy

A governance policy is a written organisational requirement.

A technical policy is an enforceable implementation of that requirement.

Example:

| Governance Requirement | Technical Enforcement |
|---|---|
| Containers must not run as root | Pod Security Admission, Gatekeeper or Kyverno |
| Only approved images may be deployed | Admission policy |
| Secrets must not be stored in manifests | CI/CD scanning and admission validation |
| Production workloads require resource limits | Policy engine |
| Public services require approval | Admission policy and change workflow |
| Every namespace requires ownership | Namespace label policy |

```text
Enterprise Security Standard

↓

Kubernetes Policy Definition

↓

Admission Enforcement

↓

Compliance Evidence

↓

Governance Reporting
```

A strong programme connects written standards to technical enforcement.

# Policy Enforcement Layers

Kubernetes policies can be enforced at several stages.

```text
Source Code

↓

CI/CD Validation

↓

Admission Control

↓

Cluster Configuration

↓

Runtime Monitoring

↓

Continuous Compliance
```

Each layer provides a different type of protection.

# Pre-Deployment Policy Enforcement

Policies should be evaluated before workloads reach the cluster.

Pre-deployment controls may include:

- YAML validation
- Helm chart testing
- Infrastructure as Code scanning
- Container image scanning
- Secret detection
- Policy-as-code checks
- Signed image verification

```text
Developer Commit

↓

CI Pipeline

↓

Security Policy Checks

↓

Approved or Rejected

↓

Deployment
```

This gives developers early feedback and reduces failed production deployments.

# Admission-Time Policy Enforcement

Admission control evaluates resources when they are submitted to the Kubernetes API.

```text
kubectl apply

↓

API Server

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorisation

↓

Admission Controllers

↓

Resource Stored or Rejected
```

Admission control is one of the strongest policy enforcement points because it can prevent insecure configurations from entering the cluster.

# Runtime Policy Enforcement

Admission policies evaluate configuration, but they do not observe everything that happens after deployment.

Runtime controls detect behaviours such as:

- Shell execution
- Unexpected process creation
- Sensitive file access
- Network connections
- Privilege escalation attempts
- Cryptocurrency mining
- Container escape activity

Runtime tools such as Falco complement configuration policies.

```text
Admission Policy

Prevents insecure configuration

+

Runtime Security

Detects malicious behaviour

↓

Defence in Depth
```

# Continuous Compliance

Policies must also be evaluated after deployment.

A resource may become non-compliant because of:

- Manual changes
- New policy versions
- Cluster upgrades
- Application updates
- Configuration drift
- Changed business requirements

Continuous compliance tools scan existing resources and identify policy violations.

# Policy Types

Kubernetes policies can be grouped into several categories.

| Policy Category | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Workload Security | Restrict container privileges and unsafe configurations |
| Identity | Control Service Accounts, RBAC and authentication |
| Network | Restrict ingress, egress and service exposure |
| Supply Chain | Control image sources, signatures and versions |
| Resource Governance | Enforce requests, limits and quotas |
| Data Protection | Restrict Secret handling and sensitive volumes |
| Metadata | Require labels, annotations and ownership |
| Operational | Enforce probes, disruption budgets and resilience |
| Compliance | Map resources to organisational and regulatory standards |

# Workload Security Policies

Workload security policies protect Pods and containers.

Common requirements include:

- Run as non-root
- Deny privileged containers
- Disable privilege escalation
- Require read-only root filesystems
- Drop Linux capabilities
- Apply seccomp
- Restrict host namespaces
- Restrict hostPath
- Restrict device access
- Require resource limits

# Example Secure Workload Requirements

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

  capabilities:
    drop:
      - ALL

  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

Policies can require these settings before a workload is admitted.

# Deny Privileged Containers

A privileged container has broad access to worker node resources.

Unsafe configuration:

```yaml
securityContext:
  privileged: true
```

Enterprise policy:

```text
Privileged containers are prohibited in production.

Exceptions require:

- Security approval
- Business justification
- Dedicated namespace
- Dedicated node group
- Additional monitoring
- Expiry date
```

# Require Non-Root Execution

Policy requirement:

```text
All application containers must run as a non-root user.
```

Compliant configuration:

```yaml
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
```

This reduces the impact of application compromise.

# Deny Host Namespace Access

High-risk fields include:

```yaml
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostIPC: true
```

Policies should deny these settings unless explicitly approved.

# Restrict HostPath Volumes

Unsafe configuration:

```yaml
volumes:
  - name: host-root
    hostPath:
      path: /
```

A policy can:

- Deny all hostPath volumes
- Allow only approved paths
- Require read-only mounts
- Restrict usage to specific namespaces
- Require an approved exception

# Require Resource Requests and Limits

Resource policies improve both availability and security.

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 128Mi

  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi
```

Benefits include:

- Reduced resource exhaustion
- Improved scheduling
- Better capacity planning
- Lower risk of denial-of-service conditions
- Improved monitoring accuracy

# Pod Security Standards

Kubernetes Pod Security Standards define three policy levels.

| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| Privileged | Unrestricted workload permissions |
| Baseline | Prevents common privilege escalation |
| Restricted | Strong workload hardening |

The `restricted` profile is the preferred production target where application compatibility permits.

# Pod Security Admission

Pod Security Admission is a built-in Kubernetes admission controller that enforces Pod Security Standards at namespace level.

It supports three modes:

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Enforce | Rejects non-compliant workloads |
| Audit | Records policy violations |
| Warn | Displays warnings to users |

# Pod Security Admission Labels

Example production namespace configuration:

```bash
kubectl label namespace production \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version=latest \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version=latest
```

This configuration:

- Rejects workloads that violate the Restricted profile
- Generates audit events
- Warns users during deployment

# Pod Security Admission Rollout Strategy

A staged rollout reduces application disruption.

```text
Inventory Existing Workloads

↓

Enable Warn Mode

↓

Review Violations

↓

Enable Audit Mode

↓

Remediate Applications

↓

Enable Enforce Mode

↓

Monitor Continuously
```

Moving directly to enforcement may break workloads.

# Pod Security Admission Strengths

Pod Security Admission provides:

- Native Kubernetes integration
- Simple namespace-level controls
- Standardised security profiles
- Low operational complexity
- Strong baseline workload protection

# Pod Security Admission Limitations

It does not provide highly customised policies for requirements such as:

- Approved image registries
- Required labels
- Mandatory resource limits
- Naming conventions
- Custom Secret restrictions
- Service exposure rules
- Business-specific controls

For these requirements, organisations commonly use policy engines.

# OPA Gatekeeper

OPA Gatekeeper is a Kubernetes-native policy engine built around the Open Policy Agent.

It uses:

- ConstraintTemplates
- Constraints
- Rego policy language
- Admission control
- Audit functionality

```text
Kubernetes Resource

↓

Gatekeeper Admission Webhook

↓

Constraint Evaluation

↓

Allow or Deny
```

Gatekeeper is useful for complex and reusable enterprise policies.

# Gatekeeper Architecture

```text
Policy Author

↓

ConstraintTemplate

↓

Constraint

↓

Admission Webhook

↓

Kubernetes API Requests

↓

Policy Decision
```

A ConstraintTemplate defines policy logic.

A Constraint applies the policy to specific resources.

# Example Gatekeeper Policy Use Cases

Gatekeeper can enforce:

- Approved image registries
- Required labels
- Non-root execution
- Resource limits
- Restricted Service types
- Allowed volume types
- Approved Ingress hosts
- Namespace naming standards
- Required security annotations
- Restricted RBAC permissions

# Example Gatekeeper Constraint

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: require-enterprise-labels
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups:
          - ""

        kinds:
          - Namespace

  parameters:
    labels:
      - key: owner
      - key: environment
      - key: cost-centre
```

This example requires every Namespace to include defined enterprise metadata.

# Kyverno

Kyverno is a Kubernetes-native policy engine that uses YAML-based policies.

It can:

- Validate resources
- Mutate resources
- Generate resources
- Verify container images
- Scan existing resources
- Produce policy reports

```text
Kubernetes Resource

↓

Kyverno Policy Engine

↓

Validate, Mutate, Generate or Verify

↓

Allow, Modify or Deny
```

Kyverno is often easier for Kubernetes teams because policies are written in YAML rather than a separate policy language.

# Kyverno Policy Types

| Policy Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Validate | Accept or deny resources |
| Mutate | Modify resources automatically |
| Generate | Create related resources |
| Verify Images | Validate image signatures and attestations |
| Cleanup | Remove resources based on policy |
| Policy Report | Record compliance status |

# Example Kyverno Validate Policy

```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce

  rules:
    - name: check-non-root
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Pod

      validate:
        message: Containers must run as non-root.

        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: true
```

This policy rejects Pods that do not explicitly run as non-root.

# Example Kyverno Mutation

A mutation policy can add a secure default.

```text
Incoming Pod

↓

Policy Detects Missing Setting

↓

Policy Adds Secure Configuration

↓

Modified Pod Admitted
```

For example, a policy may add:

- Default labels
- Seccomp profile
- Read-only root filesystem
- Approved annotations
- Image pull policies

Mutation should be used carefully because it changes submitted resources.

# Gatekeeper and Kyverno Comparison

| Capability | Gatekeeper | Kyverno |
|---|---|---|
| Policy Language | Rego | YAML |
| Validation | Yes | Yes |
| Mutation | Limited or external patterns | Yes |
| Resource Generation | No native equivalent | Yes |
| Image Verification | Requires integration | Native capability |
| Audit Existing Resources | Yes | Yes |
| Kubernetes-Native Authoring | Moderate | Strong |
| Learning Curve | Higher | Lower for YAML users |

The correct choice depends on:

- Team skills
- Existing platforms
- Policy complexity
- Governance model
- Integration requirements

# ValidatingAdmissionPolicy

Kubernetes also supports native admission policies using the Common Expression Language.

This capability can enforce certain policies without deploying an external webhook.

A native policy approach may reduce:

- Operational overhead
- External dependencies
- Webhook failure risks
- Additional platform components

However, policy engines may still be preferred for:

- Rich reporting
- Image verification
- Mutation
- Complex policy libraries
- Enterprise dashboards
- Cross-resource logic

# Identity Policies

Policies should also control identities and permissions.

Examples include:

- Prohibit use of the default Service Account
- Require dedicated Service Accounts
- Disable automatic token mounting
- Restrict cluster-admin bindings
- Deny wildcard permissions
- Restrict Secret access
- Require approved EKS access entries
- Enforce namespace-level roles

# Service Account Policy

Enterprise requirement:

```text
Every application must use a dedicated Service Account.
```

Compliant Pod:

```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: payment-api-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
```

The token should only be mounted when Kubernetes API access is required.

# RBAC Policy

High-risk RBAC configurations include:

```yaml
verbs:
  - "*"

resources:
  - "*"
```

Policies and review processes should identify:

- Wildcard permissions
- cluster-admin assignments
- Secret access
- RoleBinding creation
- ClusterRoleBinding creation
- Pod execution permissions
- Token creation permissions
- Impersonation permissions

RBAC policies often require both automated checks and human review.

# Privilege Escalation Through RBAC

A user may not have direct administrative permissions but may be able to create a privileged workload.

```text
User Can Create Pods

↓

Creates Privileged Pod

↓

Mounts Host Filesystem

↓

Accesses Node Credentials

↓

Escalates Privileges
```

Policy assessment must consider effective attack paths, not only Role names.

# Network Policies

Kubernetes Network Policies control traffic between Pods and network destinations.

They can enforce:

- Ingress restrictions
- Egress restrictions
- Namespace isolation
- Application communication paths
- Default-deny behaviour

# Default-Deny Policy

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}

  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
```

This policy denies traffic unless another policy explicitly allows it.

# Network Policy Enforcement Requirements

Network Policies require a compatible networking implementation.

In Amazon EKS, engineers must confirm that the selected CNI and configuration support the required policy behaviour.

A policy document without effective enforcement provides false confidence.

# Network Governance Policies

Enterprise requirements may include:

- Every production namespace must use default-deny.
- Databases may only accept traffic from approved applications.
- Internet egress must pass through approved controls.
- Development namespaces cannot communicate with production.
- Metadata service access must be restricted.
- Public ingress must use approved controllers.
- Internal applications must not use public LoadBalancers.

# Service Exposure Policies

Unsafe configuration:

```yaml
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
```

An admission policy can require:

- Approved namespaces
- Security team approval
- Required annotations
- Internal load balancer configuration
- Approved ingress architecture
- TLS settings
- Ownership metadata

This prevents accidental public exposure.

# Ingress Policies

Ingress policies may require:

- TLS
- Approved hostnames
- Approved IngressClass
- Approved certificates
- Web Application Firewall integration
- Restricted annotations
- No wildcard hosts
- Required ownership labels

Example requirement:

```text
All production Ingress resources must use TLS and an approved IngressClass.
```

# Supply Chain Policies

Supply chain policies help ensure only trusted software enters the cluster.

Examples include:

- Approved registries only
- Signed images only
- Immutable image references
- No `latest` tags
- Required vulnerability scan status
- Required SBOM
- Required provenance attestation
- Restricted image pull policies

# Approved Registry Policy

Allowed:

```yaml
image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/payment-api:v2.1.0
```

Denied:

```yaml
image: unknown-public-registry.example/payment-api:latest
```

This reduces exposure to untrusted container images.

# Immutable Image Policy

Avoid:

```yaml
image: company/app:latest
```

Prefer:

```yaml
image: company/app:v2.1.0
```

For stronger assurance:

```yaml
image: company/app@sha256:exampledigest
```

Policies can deny mutable tags in production.

# Image Signature Verification

An enterprise policy may verify that an image:

- Was built by an approved pipeline
- Has a valid cryptographic signature
- Includes required attestations
- Comes from an approved registry
- Passed vulnerability scanning

```text
Container Image

↓

Signature and Attestation Verification

↓

Admission Policy

↓

Approved Deployment
```

Policies should discourage patterns such as:

```yaml

  - name: DATABASE_PASSWORD
    value: plaintext-password
```

Preferred approaches include:

- Kubernetes Secrets with restricted RBAC
- AWS Secrets Manager
- AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store

Metadata improves accountability and operations.

Required labels may include:

- `owner`

    owner: payments-team
    environment: production

# Policy Failure Modes

Admission policies are part of the control plane request path.

A policy engine failure can affect cluster availability.

Webhook configurations commonly define:

- `failurePolicy: Fail`
- `failurePolicy: Ignore`

# Fail Closed

```text
Policy Engine Unavailable

↓

Request Rejected
```

Advantages:

- Prevents policy bypass
- Maintains security enforcement

Risks:

- May block deployments
- Can affect production availability

# Fail Open

```text
Policy Engine Unavailable

↓

Request Allowed
```

Advantages:

- Maintains deployment availability

Risks:

- Insecure resources may be admitted
- Creates a policy bypass window

The correct choice depends on policy criticality and business requirements.

# Common Security Risks

## Policy Not Enforced

A policy exists in documentation but is not technically enforced.

**Risk:** Insecure workloads can still be deployed.

**Control:** Implement admission and CI/CD policy checks.

## Policies Applied Only to Production

Development environments remain unrestricted.

**Risk:** Insecure configurations reach production late in the lifecycle.

**Control:** Apply policies throughout development, with appropriate enforcement levels.

## Excessive Exceptions

Teams bypass policies through broad exclusions.

**Risk:** Security controls become ineffective.

**Control:** Require narrow, time-limited and reviewed exceptions.

## Untested Policies

A new policy unexpectedly blocks system workloads.

**Risk:** Cluster or application disruption.

**Control:** Use audit mode, test cases and staged rollout.

## Policy Engine Failure

Admission webhooks become unavailable.

**Risk:** Deployments fail or policy enforcement is bypassed.

**Control:** Design for high availability and define appropriate failure behaviour.

## Inconsistent Cluster Policies

Different clusters enforce different standards.

**Risk:** Security posture varies across the enterprise.

**Control:** Use central policy repositories and automated deployment.

## No Runtime Monitoring

Admission policies validate configuration only.

**Risk:** Malicious behaviour after deployment remains undetected.

**Control:** Combine policy enforcement with runtime detection.

# Enterprise Implementation Strategy

## Phase 1 — Define Policy Standards

- Review enterprise security requirements
- Map CIS, NSA and NIST guidance
- Define mandatory workload controls
- Define identity and network requirements
- Establish exception governance
- Assign policy ownership

## Phase 2 — Assess Current Workloads

- Inventory clusters and namespaces
- Identify privileged workloads
- Identify root containers
- Review Service Account usage
- Review image sources
- Review resource limits
- Review Network Policy coverage
- Identify legacy exceptions

## Phase 3 — Select Enforcement Tools

- Use Pod Security Admission for baseline controls
- Evaluate Gatekeeper for complex Rego-based policies
- Evaluate Kyverno for YAML-native policies and image verification
- Evaluate native admission policies
- Define CI/CD integrations
- Define monitoring requirements

## Phase 4 — Build the Policy Library

Create policies for:

- Non-root execution
- Privileged container denial
- Capability restrictions
- Approved registries
- Resource limits
- Required labels
- Service Account governance
- Network protection
- Ingress security
- Image verification

## Phase 5 — Test and Roll Out

- Test policies in development
- Use warn and audit modes
- Review existing violations
- Remediate workloads
- Approve narrow exceptions
- Enable production enforcement
- Monitor deployment impact

## Phase 6 — Establish Continuous Governance

- Store policies in Git
- Automate policy testing
- Monitor policy engine health
- Track violations
- Review exceptions
- Report compliance
- Update policies as threats evolve

# Enterprise Best Practices

As a Cloud Security Engineer:

- Translate written security standards into enforceable policies.
- Apply policy checks early in CI/CD.
- Use admission control to prevent insecure deployments.
- Use Pod Security Admission as a minimum workload baseline.
- Apply the Restricted profile to production where possible.
- Use Gatekeeper, Kyverno or native admission policies for custom controls.
- Deny privileged containers by default.
- Require non-root execution and restricted capabilities.
- Enforce approved image registries and immutable image references.
- Require resource requests and limits.
- Apply default-deny Network Policies.
- Require dedicated Service Accounts.
- Restrict wildcard RBAC permissions.
- Store policies in version control.
- Test every policy before enforcement.
- Use audit mode during rollout.
- Design policy engines for high availability.
- Monitor violations and policy engine health.
- Manage exceptions through a time-limited approval process.
- Combine admission policies with runtime detection.

# Real-World Scenario

A global financial organisation allows hundreds of development teams to deploy applications to Amazon EKS.

A security assessment identifies several issues:

- Root containers in production
- Privileged workloads
- Images from public registries
- Missing resource limits
- Default Service Accounts
- Public LoadBalancer Services
- Missing Network Policies
- Inconsistent ownership labels

The Cloud Security team establishes an enterprise policy programme.

The organisation:

1. Enables Pod Security Admission in warn and audit modes.
2. Remediates workloads that violate the Restricted profile.
3. Enables enforcement for production namespaces.
4. Deploys Kyverno to require approved registries, resource limits and ownership labels.
5. Uses image verification to require signed production images.
6. Applies policies that restrict public LoadBalancer Services.
7. Introduces default-deny Network Policies.
8. Creates a formal exception process for security agents and infrastructure components.
9. Sends policy violations to the SIEM.
10. Publishes compliance metrics through Grafana dashboards.

The result is a consistent and measurable Kubernetes security baseline across the enterprise.

# Key Takeaways

- Kubernetes policies convert security requirements into enforceable controls.
- Policy enforcement should occur in CI/CD, admission control and continuous compliance.
- Pod Security Admission provides a strong native workload baseline.
- Gatekeeper supports flexible Rego-based enterprise policies.
- Kyverno provides Kubernetes-native YAML policies, mutation, generation and image verification.
- Policies should protect workloads, identities, networking, software supply chains and operations.
- Audit mode and staged rollout reduce deployment disruption.
- Policy engines must be highly available and continuously monitored.
- Exceptions must be narrow, approved and time-limited.
- Runtime monitoring remains necessary because configuration policies cannot detect all malicious behaviour.

# Knowledge Check

## 1. What is the primary purpose of a Kubernetes security policy?

**Answer:** To define and enforce what configurations and actions are allowed, required or prohibited within a Kubernetes environment.

## 2. What are the three modes supported by Pod Security Admission?

**Answer:**

- Enforce
- Audit
- Warn

## 3. Why should policies be introduced in audit mode before enforcement?

**Answer:** Audit mode identifies existing violations and application impact without immediately blocking deployments.

## 4. What is one major difference between Gatekeeper and Kyverno?

**Answer:** Gatekeeper primarily uses Rego-based policies, while Kyverno uses Kubernetes-style YAML and supports validation, mutation, resource generation and image verification.

## 5. Why are runtime security tools still needed after admission policies are deployed?

**Answer:** Admission policies validate configurations at deployment time, while runtime tools detect malicious behaviour that occurs after a workload starts.

Why This Matters

Section titled “Why This Matters”

Kubernetes gives development teams tremendous flexibility.

That flexibility can also introduce risk.

Without enforceable policies, teams may deploy:

  • Privileged containers
  • Root containers
  • Workloads from untrusted registries
  • Pods without resource limits
  • Containers with writable root filesystems
  • Workloads that use excessive Service Account permissions
  • Applications without Network Policies
  • Services exposed directly to the internet
  • Images with mutable tags
  • Pods that mount sensitive host paths

Security guidance alone does not prevent these deployments.

A documented standard may say:

Production containers must not run as root.

But unless that requirement is enforced, a developer can still deploy a root container.

Kubernetes policies convert security requirements into technical controls that can:

  • Warn
  • Audit
  • Reject
  • Mutate
  • Report
  • Remediate

For Cloud Security Engineers, policies are essential for creating secure and consistent Amazon EKS environments at scale.

What is a Kubernetes Policy?

Section titled “What is a Kubernetes Policy?”

A Kubernetes policy is a rule that defines what is allowed, required or prohibited within a cluster.

A policy may apply to:

  • Pods
  • Deployments
  • Services
  • Namespaces
  • ConfigMaps
  • Secrets
  • Ingress resources
  • RBAC objects
  • Service Accounts
  • Custom resources

Examples include:

  • Containers must run as non-root.
  • Privileged containers are prohibited.
  • Images must come from an approved registry.
  • Every production workload must define resource limits.
  • Host networking is prohibited.
  • Default Service Accounts cannot be used.
  • Network Policies are required.
  • Every resource must include ownership labels.
  • LoadBalancer Services require approval.

Policy as a Security Boundary

Section titled “Policy as a Security Boundary”

Policies create a controlled boundary between development flexibility and enterprise security requirements.

Without policy enforcement, insecure configurations may reach production unnoticed.

Governance Policy Versus Technical Policy

Section titled “Governance Policy Versus Technical Policy”

A governance policy is a written organisational requirement.

A technical policy is an enforceable implementation of that requirement.

Example:

Governance Requirement Technical Enforcement
Containers must not run as root Pod Security Admission, Gatekeeper or Kyverno
Only approved images may be deployed Admission policy
Secrets must not be stored in manifests CI/CD scanning and admission validation
Production workloads require resource limits Policy engine
Public services require approval Admission policy and change workflow
Every namespace requires ownership Namespace label policy

A strong programme connects written standards to technical enforcement.

Policy Enforcement Layers

Section titled “Policy Enforcement Layers”

Kubernetes policies can be enforced at several stages.

Each layer provides a different type of protection.

Pre-Deployment Policy Enforcement

Section titled “Pre-Deployment Policy Enforcement”

Policies should be evaluated before workloads reach the cluster.

Pre-deployment controls may include:

  • YAML validation
  • Helm chart testing
  • Infrastructure as Code scanning
  • Container image scanning
  • Secret detection
  • Policy-as-code checks
  • Signed image verification

This gives developers early feedback and reduces failed production deployments.

Admission-Time Policy Enforcement

Section titled “Admission-Time Policy Enforcement”

Admission control evaluates resources when they are submitted to the Kubernetes API.

Admission control is one of the strongest policy enforcement points because it can prevent insecure configurations from entering the cluster.

Runtime Policy Enforcement

Section titled “Runtime Policy Enforcement”

Admission policies evaluate configuration, but they do not observe everything that happens after deployment.

Runtime controls detect behaviours such as:

  • Shell execution
  • Unexpected process creation
  • Sensitive file access
  • Network connections
  • Privilege escalation attempts
  • Cryptocurrency mining
  • Container escape activity

Runtime tools such as Falco complement configuration policies.

Continuous Compliance

Section titled “Continuous Compliance”

Policies must also be evaluated after deployment.

A resource may become non-compliant because of:

  • Manual changes
  • New policy versions
  • Cluster upgrades
  • Application updates
  • Configuration drift
  • Changed business requirements

Continuous compliance tools scan existing resources and identify policy violations.

  1. Enables Pod Security Admission in warn and audit modes.
  2. Remediates workloads that violate the Restricted profile.
  3. Enables enforcement for production namespaces.
  4. Deploys Kyverno to require approved registries, resource limits and ownership labels.
  5. Uses image verification to require signed production images.
  6. Applies policies that restrict public LoadBalancer Services.
  7. Introduces default-deny Network Policies.
  8. Creates a formal exception process for security agents and infrastructure components.
  9. Sends policy violations to the SIEM.
  10. Publishes compliance metrics through Grafana dashboards.

The result is a consistent and measurable Kubernetes security baseline across the enterprise.

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”
  • Kubernetes policies convert security requirements into enforceable controls.
  • Policy enforcement should occur in CI/CD, admission control and continuous compliance.
  • Pod Security Admission provides a strong native workload baseline.
  • Gatekeeper supports flexible Rego-based enterprise policies.
  • Kyverno provides Kubernetes-native YAML policies, mutation, generation and image verification.
  • Policies should protect workloads, identities, networking, software supply chains and operations.
  • Audit mode and staged rollout reduce deployment disruption.
  • Policy engines must be highly available and continuously monitored.
  • Exceptions must be narrow, approved and time-limited.
  • Runtime monitoring remains necessary because configuration policies cannot detect all malicious behaviour.

# Why This Matters

Kubernetes allows development teams to create infrastructure and deploy applications quickly.

However, without central policy enforcement, teams may deploy resources that violate enterprise security standards.

Examples include:

- Privileged containers
- Containers running as root
- Images from untrusted registries
- Workloads without resource limits
- Pods using host networking
- Containers mounting sensitive host paths
- Resources without ownership labels
- Public LoadBalancer Services
- Excessive Linux capabilities
- Workloads without approved security controls

Security teams may document that these configurations are prohibited.

Documentation alone does not prevent them.

OPA Gatekeeper converts enterprise security requirements into enforceable Kubernetes policies.

It evaluates Kubernetes API requests and can reject configurations that violate approved standards.

```text
Enterprise Security Requirement

↓

Gatekeeper Policy

↓

Kubernetes Admission Request

↓

Policy Evaluation

↓

Allow, Warn or Deny
```

Gatekeeper therefore creates a technical enforcement point between developer activity and the Kubernetes cluster.

# What is Open Policy Agent?

Open Policy Agent, commonly called OPA, is a general-purpose policy engine.

OPA allows organisations to separate policy decisions from application and infrastructure code.

Instead of embedding security decisions directly inside every system, administrators define central policies that determine whether an action should be allowed.

OPA can be used for:

- Kubernetes admission control
- API authorisation
- Infrastructure validation
- CI/CD policy checks
- Service-mesh authorisation
- Application-level decisions
- Cloud configuration validation
- Compliance enforcement

OPA policies are written using the **Rego** policy language.

# Policy Decision Model

OPA evaluates structured input against defined policy logic.

```text
Structured Input

+

Policy Rules

+

Policy Data

↓

OPA Evaluation

↓

Decision
```

The decision may be:

- Allow
- Deny
- Return a violation
- Return supporting information
- Require additional review

# What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a Kubernetes-native policy controller built using Open Policy Agent.

It integrates OPA with Kubernetes admission control and provides resources for:

- Defining reusable policy templates
- Applying policies to selected resources
- Rejecting non-compliant requests
- Auditing existing resources
- Reporting policy violations
- Managing policy parameters
- Supporting policy testing
- Applying selected resource mutations
- Integrating external data into policy decisions

Gatekeeper extends Kubernetes using Custom Resource Definitions.

The primary validation resources are:

- `ConstraintTemplate`
- `Constraint`

# Gatekeeper Architecture

```text
Developer

↓

kubectl, Helm or CI/CD Pipeline

↓

Kubernetes API Server

↓

Authentication

↓

Authorisation

↓

Gatekeeper Admission Webhook

↓

OPA Policy Evaluation

↓

Allow or Deny

↓

Resource Stored in etcd
```

Gatekeeper operates during the admission stage.

It does not replace:

- Kubernetes authentication
- Kubernetes RBAC
- Pod Security Admission
- Network Policies
- Runtime detection
- Container image scanning

It complements these controls.

# Kubernetes Request Lifecycle

A simplified Kubernetes request follows this sequence:

```text
API Request

↓

Authentication

Who is making the request?

↓

Authorisation

What is the identity permitted to do?

↓

Admission Control

Does the requested configuration comply with policy?

↓

Resource Validation

↓

Resource Persisted
```

Gatekeeper works primarily in the admission-control stage.

# Authentication, Authorisation and Admission

These controls answer different security questions.

| Security Layer | Security Question | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication | Who are you? | AWS IAM identity |
| Authorisation | What can you do? | Kubernetes RBAC |
| Admission Control | Is this configuration permitted? | Gatekeeper policy |
| Runtime Detection | What is the workload doing? | Falco alert |

A user may be authorised to create Pods but should still be prevented from creating privileged Pods.

```text
Developer Has Permission to Create Pods

↓

Developer Submits Privileged Pod

↓

RBAC Allows the Create Operation

↓

Gatekeeper Evaluates Pod Configuration

↓

Privileged Pod Denied
```

This demonstrates why RBAC alone is insufficient.

# Gatekeeper Components

A typical Gatekeeper deployment includes several components.

```text
Gatekeeper System

├── Admission Webhook
├── Audit Controller
├── ConstraintTemplates
├── Constraints
├── OPA Policy Engine
├── Custom Resource Definitions
├── Mutation Resources
└── Metrics Endpoint
```

# Admission Webhook

The admission webhook evaluates new and updated Kubernetes resources.

It can inspect resources such as:

- Pods
- Deployments
- StatefulSets
- DaemonSets
- Jobs
- CronJobs
- Services
- Ingresses
- Namespaces
- Roles
- RoleBindings
- ClusterRoles
- ClusterRoleBindings

When a request violates a Constraint, Gatekeeper can reject it.

# Audit Controller

The audit controller evaluates resources that already exist in the cluster.

This is important because a resource may:

- Have existed before a policy was created
- Have been admitted while enforcement was disabled
- Become non-compliant after a policy update
- Exist in a namespace that was previously excluded
- Have been created during a policy-engine outage

```text
Existing Cluster Resources

↓

Gatekeeper Audit Controller

↓

Evaluate Against Constraints

↓

Record Violations

↓

Compliance Reporting
```

Admission enforcement prevents new violations.

Audit identifies existing violations.

# ConstraintTemplates

A `ConstraintTemplate` defines reusable policy logic.

It normally specifies:

- The name and type of the future Constraint
- The schema for policy parameters
- The target system
- The policy logic
- Violation messages

Think of a ConstraintTemplate as a reusable policy definition.

```text
ConstraintTemplate

Defines:

- Policy Logic
- Expected Parameters
- Constraint Type
- Violation Output
```

A ConstraintTemplate does not normally determine the exact namespaces or workloads to which the rule applies.

That is configured through a Constraint.

# Constraints

A `Constraint` activates a policy defined by a ConstraintTemplate.

It specifies:

- Which resources are evaluated
- Which namespaces are included
- Which namespaces are excluded
- What parameters are passed to the policy
- Which enforcement action is used

```text
ConstraintTemplate

Defines the reusable rule

↓

Constraint

Applies the rule to selected resources
```

# ConstraintTemplate and Constraint Relationship

```text
ConstraintTemplate

K8sRequiredLabels

↓

Constraint 1

Require owner label on Namespaces

↓

Constraint 2

Require owner label on Deployments

↓

Constraint 3

Require owner label in production
```

One template can support multiple Constraints with different parameters and scopes.

# Example Policy Requirement

Consider the following enterprise requirement:

> Every Kubernetes Namespace must contain an `owner` label.

This requirement can be implemented using:

1. A ConstraintTemplate that defines how required labels are evaluated.
2. A Constraint that requires the `owner` label on Namespace resources.

# Example ConstraintTemplate

```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredlabels
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredLabels

      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object

          properties:
            labels:
              type: array

              items:
                type: string

  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh

      rego: |
        package k8srequiredlabels

        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          required_label := input.parameters.labels[_]
          not input.review.object.metadata.labels[required_label]

          msg := sprintf(
            "Resource must contain the required label: %v",
            [required_label]
          )
        }
```

This template creates a new Constraint type named:

```text
K8sRequiredLabels
```

# Understanding the ConstraintTemplate

The template contains several important sections.

| Section | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `metadata.name` | Identifies the ConstraintTemplate |
| `crd.spec.names.kind` | Defines the new Constraint kind |
| `validation` | Defines accepted policy parameters |
| `targets` | Identifies the evaluation target |
| `rego` | Contains the policy logic |
| `violation` | Returns policy violations |

# Example Constraint

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: namespaces-must-have-owner
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny

  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups:
          - ""

        kinds:
          - Namespace

  parameters:
    labels:
      - owner
```

This Constraint applies the reusable label policy to Namespace resources.

# Testing the Policy

Attempt to create a namespace without the required label.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payment-production
```

Apply the manifest.

```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
```

Expected result:

```text
Error from server:

Admission webhook denied the request.

Resource must contain the required label: owner
```

# Creating a Compliant Resource

Add the required label.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payment-production

  labels:
    owner: payments-team
```

Apply the manifest again.

```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
```

Expected result:

```text
namespace/payment-production created
```

The resource is admitted because it complies with policy.

# Rego Policy Language

Gatekeeper validation policies commonly use Rego.

Rego is a declarative policy language designed for evaluating structured data.

A Gatekeeper policy can access the submitted Kubernetes object through:

```text
input.review.object
```

For example:

```rego
input.review.object.metadata.name
```

This retrieves the resource name.

```rego
input.review.object.metadata.namespace
```

This retrieves the namespace.

```rego
input.review.object.spec.containers
```

This retrieves the container list from a Pod.

# Example Rego Logic

```rego
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  container.securityContext.privileged == true

  msg := sprintf(
    "Privileged container %v is not permitted",
    [container.name]
  )
}
```

This rule:

1. Iterates through each container.
2. Checks whether `privileged` is set to `true`.
3. Returns a violation message.

# Rego Evaluation Model

Rego describes conditions that must be true for a rule to produce a result.

```text
Kubernetes Object Submitted

↓

Rego Reads Object Fields

↓

Policy Conditions Evaluated

↓

Violation Generated or No Violation
```

A violation result causes enforcement according to the Constraint configuration.

# Matching Resources

Constraints use the `match` section to determine which resources are evaluated.

Policy scope may include:

- Resource kinds
- API groups
- Namespaces
- Namespace selectors
- Object labels
- Cluster-scoped resources
- Namespaced resources

# Matching Resource Kinds

Example:

```yaml
match:
  kinds:
    - apiGroups:
        - apps

      kinds:
        - Deployment
        - StatefulSet
```

This policy applies only to Deployments and StatefulSets in the `apps` API group.

# Matching Namespaces

```yaml
match:
  namespaces:
    - production
    - payments
```

This applies the policy only to the listed namespaces.

# Excluding Namespaces

```yaml
match:
  excludedNamespaces:
    - kube-system
    - gatekeeper-system
```

Namespace exclusions should be used carefully.

Broad exclusions may create policy bypasses.

# Namespace Selectors

A policy can target namespaces based on labels.

Example enterprise namespace labels:

```yaml
metadata:
  labels:
    environment: production
    policy-tier: restricted
```

A Constraint can then target namespaces using a selector.

```yaml
match:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      policy-tier: restricted
```

This enables scalable policy assignment.

# Enforcement Actions

Gatekeeper Constraints can use enforcement actions to control policy behaviour.

Common actions include:

- `deny`
- `warn`
- `dryrun`

# Deny

```yaml
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
```

The request is rejected when it violates policy.

Use `deny` for mature and tested policies.

Examples include:

- Privileged containers
- Unapproved registries
- Host filesystem access
- Missing mandatory security settings

# Warn

```yaml
spec:
  enforcementAction: warn
```

The API request may continue, but the user receives a warning.

Warn mode is useful for:

- Developer education
- Policy rollout
- Non-critical requirements
- Upcoming enforcement changes

# Dry Run

```yaml
spec:
  enforcementAction: dryrun
```

The request is admitted, but violations are recorded through Gatekeeper audit.

Dry run is useful for:

- Assessing potential impact
- Discovering existing violations
- Testing new policies
- Planning remediation
- Measuring policy readiness

# Enforcement Rollout Strategy

```text
Policy Designed

↓

Policy Tested Locally

↓

Dry-Run Mode

↓

Review Violations

↓

Remediate Workloads

↓

Warn Mode

↓

Notify Application Teams

↓

Deny Mode

↓

Continuous Monitoring
```

This staged approach reduces business disruption.

# Example Policy — Deny Privileged Containers

The following conceptual template evaluates privileged containers.

```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sblockprivileged
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sBlockPrivileged

  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh

      rego: |
        package k8sblockprivileged

        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          container.securityContext.privileged == true

          msg := sprintf(
            "Privileged container %v is prohibited",
            [container.name]
          )
        }
```

Apply the corresponding Constraint.

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sBlockPrivileged
metadata:
  name: block-privileged-containers
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny

  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups:
          - ""

        kinds:
          - Pod

    excludedNamespaces:
      - kube-system
      - gatekeeper-system
```

# Important Workload Coverage Consideration

Developers commonly create Deployments rather than individual Pods.

A Deployment creates Pods through a ReplicaSet.

Admission policies must be designed to evaluate the correct object structures.

Enterprise teams should test policies against:

- Pods
- Deployments
- StatefulSets
- DaemonSets
- Jobs
- CronJobs
- ReplicaSets
- Ephemeral containers

A policy that only checks direct Pod creation may not provide the intended coverage.

# Example Policy — Require Resource Limits

Enterprise requirement:

> Every application container must define CPU and memory limits.

Conceptual Constraint:

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredResources
metadata:
  name: containers-must-have-limits
spec:
  enforcementAction: dryrun

  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups:
          - apps

        kinds:
          - Deployment
          - StatefulSet
          - DaemonSet

  parameters:
    limits:
      - cpu
      - memory
```

The policy should initially run in `dryrun` mode to identify application impact.

# Example Policy — Approved Registries

Enterprise requirement:

> Production workloads may only use images from approved Amazon ECR registries.

Example approved registry:

```text
123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com
```

Conceptual Constraint:

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sAllowedRepositories
metadata:
  name: production-approved-registries
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny

  match:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        environment: production

    kinds:
      - apiGroups:
          - apps

        kinds:
          - Deployment
          - StatefulSet
          - DaemonSet

  parameters:
    repos:
      - 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/
```

This reduces the risk of deploying images from untrusted sources.

# Example Policy — Restrict LoadBalancer Services

Enterprise requirement:

> Only approved namespaces may create LoadBalancer Services.

A policy can inspect:

```yaml
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
```

Possible enforcement logic:

```text
Service Type Is LoadBalancer

AND

Namespace Is Not Approved

↓

Deny Request
```

This helps prevent accidental public exposure.

# Example Policy — Restrict HostPath

Enterprise requirement:

> Application workloads must not mount worker-node file paths.

A policy can inspect Pod volumes for:

```yaml
hostPath:
  path: /
```

Approved infrastructure components may require narrowly scoped exceptions.

# Gatekeeper Policy Library

Organisations do not always need to create every policy from the beginning.

Gatekeeper policy libraries can provide reusable templates for common requirements such as:

- Required labels
- Allowed repositories
- Container limits
- Host namespace restrictions
- Privileged container restrictions
- Service type restrictions
- Volume restrictions
- Replica requirements
- Ingress restrictions

Enterprise teams must still:

- Review the policy logic
- Test it
- Approve it
- Version it
- Adapt it to internal standards
- Monitor its effect

Using an existing template does not remove the need for governance.

# Gatekeeper Audit

Gatekeeper audit periodically evaluates existing Kubernetes resources against configured Constraints.

Audit results can be viewed in Constraint status.

List Constraints.

```bash
kubectl get constraints
```

Inspect a specific Constraint.

```bash
kubectl describe \
k8srequiredlabels namespaces-must-have-owner
```

The status may include violations such as:

- Resource kind
- Resource name
- Namespace
- Violation message
- Enforcement action

# Example Audit Result

```yaml
status:
  totalViolations: 2

  violations:
    - kind: Namespace
      name: legacy-application
      message: Resource must contain the required label owner

    - kind: Namespace
      name: temporary-test
      message: Resource must contain the required label owner
```

These resources may have existed before enforcement was enabled.

# Admission Versus Audit

| Capability | Admission | Audit |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluates new requests | Yes | No |
| Evaluates existing resources | No | Yes |
| Can block creation | Yes | No |
| Supports compliance discovery | Limited | Yes |
| Helps identify historical drift | No | Yes |

Both capabilities are necessary for continuous governance.

# Mutation

Gatekeeper also supports mutation capabilities through dedicated mutation resources.

Mutation can modify resources before admission.

Potential uses include:

- Adding default labels
- Adding annotations
- Applying secure defaults
- Setting approved configuration values
- Assigning standard runtime classes

```text
Incoming Resource

↓

Gatekeeper Mutation

↓

Resource Modified

↓

Validation Policies

↓

Resource Admitted
```

Mutation should be used carefully.

Developers should understand when their submitted resources are being changed.

# Risks of Mutation

Mutation may introduce:

- Unexpected application behaviour
- Conflict with GitOps desired state
- Difficulty troubleshooting manifests
- Differences between submitted and stored resources
- Policy-ordering complexity
- Upgrade compatibility concerns

For security-critical settings, explicit configuration and validation may be easier to audit than silent mutation.

# External Data

Some policy decisions require information that does not exist inside the Kubernetes resource.

Examples include:

- Container vulnerability status
- Image-signing status
- Approved software inventory
- External identity attributes
- Risk classification
- Registry reputation
- Change-ticket approval

External-data integration can allow Gatekeeper policies to consult approved providers.

```text
Kubernetes Admission Request

↓

Gatekeeper Policy

↓

External Data Provider

↓

Security or Compliance Decision

↓

Allow or Deny
```

External dependencies introduce availability and latency considerations.

# External Data Risks

External policy decisions may be affected by:

- Provider availability
- Network latency
- Stale data
- Authentication failures
- Provider compromise
- Timeout behaviour
- Caching behaviour

Enterprise designs must define what happens when an external provider is unavailable.

# Failure Policy

The Kubernetes admission webhook configuration defines behaviour when the Gatekeeper webhook cannot respond.

Common strategies are:

- Fail closed
- Fail open

# Fail Closed

```text
Gatekeeper Unavailable

↓

Admission Request Rejected
```

Benefits:

- Policy cannot be bypassed
- Security remains enforced

Risks:

- Deployments may stop
- Emergency changes may be blocked
- Cluster operations may be affected

# Fail Open

```text
Gatekeeper Unavailable

↓

Admission Request Allowed
```

Benefits:

- Application deployments can continue
- Availability impact is reduced

Risks:

- Insecure resources may enter the cluster
- Creates a temporary enforcement gap
- Requires retrospective audit and remediation

# Choosing Failure Behaviour

The decision should consider:

- Policy criticality
- Business-service availability
- Cluster function
- Emergency access requirements
- Gatekeeper architecture
- Monitoring capability
- Recovery procedures
- Regulatory obligations

A critical policy preventing privileged containers may warrant fail-closed behaviour.

A non-critical metadata policy may allow a different approach.

# Gatekeeper Availability

Because Gatekeeper participates in the admission path, it must be operated as critical platform infrastructure.

Production controls should include:

- Multiple controller replicas
- Pod anti-affinity
- PodDisruptionBudgets
- Resource requests and limits
- Health probes
- Metrics collection
- Alerting
- Controlled certificate management
- Tested upgrades
- Tested failure scenarios
- Documented recovery procedures

# Enterprise Gatekeeper Architecture

```text
Amazon EKS API Server

↓

Gatekeeper Validating Webhook Service

↓

Multiple Controller Replicas

↓

OPA Policy Evaluation

↓

ConstraintTemplates and Constraints

Meanwhile:

Gatekeeper Audit Controller

↓

Existing Kubernetes Resources

↓

Violation Reports

↓

Prometheus and SIEM
```

Policies should be maintained in a controlled repository.

```text
gatekeeper-policies/

├── templates/
│   ├── required-labels.yaml
│   ├── block-privileged.yaml
│   ├── allowed-registries.yaml
│   └── required-resources.yaml
│
├── constraints/
│   ├── development/
│   ├── testing/
│   └── production/
│
├── tests/
│   ├── compliant/
│   └── non-compliant/
│
├── exceptions/
├── documentation/
└── README.md
```

This separates reusable templates from environment-specific Constraints.

# Policy Testing

Gatekeeper policies should be tested before they reach production.

Testing should cover:

- Known compliant resources
- Known non-compliant resources
- Missing fields
- Empty fields
- Init containers
- Ephemeral containers
- Multiple containers
- Namespaced resources
- Cluster-scoped resources
- Excluded namespaces
- Helm-generated manifests
- System workloads

# Example Test Cases

| Test | Expected Result |
|---|---|
| Non-root container | Pass |
| Root container | Deny |
| Approved ECR image | Pass |
| Public unapproved image | Deny |
| Workload with CPU and memory limits | Pass |
| Workload without limits | Violation |
| Approved system namespace | Excluded |

# Safe Exception Design

Prefer narrow exceptions based on:

- Exact service account

# Common Gatekeeper Challenges

## Rego Learning Curve

Rego may be unfamiliar to Kubernetes engineers.

**Impact:** Policies may be difficult to develop or review.

**Response:**

- Start with approved policy libraries.
- Provide Rego training.
- Create reusable templates.
- Require peer review.
- Maintain automated tests.

## Policy Breaks Applications

Strict policies may reject existing application configurations.

**Impact:** Deployment failures and business disruption.

**Response:**

- Begin with dry-run mode.
- Review audit violations.
- Remediate workloads.
- Enable enforcement gradually.

## Incorrect Resource Coverage

A policy may inspect Pods but not controller templates.

**Impact:** Insecure workload controllers may bypass expected checks.

**Response:**

- Test Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs.
- Use tested templates.
- Validate resource schemas.

## Excessive Namespace Exclusions

Teams may request broad policy exclusions.

**Impact:** Security controls become ineffective.

**Response:**

- Approve narrow exceptions.
- Require expiry dates.
- Apply compensating controls.
- Monitor excluded workloads.

## Admission Latency

Complex policies may slow Kubernetes API requests.

**Impact:** Deployment and cluster-operation delays.

**Response:**

- Optimise Rego.
- Reduce unnecessary policy scope.
- Monitor admission latency.
- Load-test policy changes.

## Gatekeeper Availability

Webhook outages may block requests or permit bypasses.

**Impact:** Availability or security risk.

**Response:**

- Use multiple replicas.
- Configure disruption budgets.
- Monitor health.
- Test failure behaviour.

## Policy Drift

Clusters may run different policy versions.

**Impact:** Inconsistent enterprise security.

**Response:**

- Use GitOps.
- Maintain a central policy repository.
- Monitor deployed policy versions.
- Automate drift detection.

## False Positives

A policy may reject legitimate configurations.

**Impact:** Reduced developer trust and policy bypass pressure.

**Response:**

- Improve test coverage.
- Use representative application manifests.
- Tune parameters.
- Document policy rationale.

# Enterprise Best Practices

As a Cloud Security Engineer:

- Use Gatekeeper as part of defence in depth.
- Begin with a small set of high-value policies.

- Use Constraints for environment-specific enforcement.
- Test policies against real application manifests.
- Begin new policies in dry-run mode.
- Remediate workloads before enabling denial.
- Store policies and tests in Git.

- Deploy Gatekeeper with multiple replicas.

# Real-World Scenario

A global financial organisation operates more than 300 Amazon EKS clusters.

During an internal security assessment, the Cloud Security team identifies:

- Privileged containers in production
- Workloads using public container registries
- Missing CPU and memory limits
- Public LoadBalancer Services
- Namespaces without ownership labels
- HostPath mounts on application Pods
- Inconsistent security controls across clusters

The organisation deploys OPA Gatekeeper as its central Kubernetes policy engine.

The implementation follows a phased strategy.

First, the security team creates ConstraintTemplates for:

- Privileged container restrictions
- Approved image repositories
- Required resource limits
- Required ownership labels
- Restricted Service types
- Restricted host volumes

The team deploys corresponding Constraints using `dryrun`.

Gatekeeper audit identifies hundreds of existing violations without blocking application deployments.

The findings are assigned to application owners and tracked through remediation tickets.

After the highest-risk violations are resolved, the organisation enables `deny` enforcement for production clusters.

Policies are stored in Git, tested through CI/CD and distributed using GitOps.

Gatekeeper metrics are collected by Prometheus, policy dashboards are displayed in Grafana and high-risk admission violations are forwarded to the SIEM.

The result is a measurable and consistently enforced Kubernetes security baseline across the enterprise.

# Key Takeaways

- OPA is a general-purpose policy engine that uses Rego.
- Gatekeeper integrates OPA with Kubernetes admission control.
- ConstraintTemplates define reusable policy logic.
- Constraints apply that logic to selected Kubernetes resources.
- Admission enforcement prevents new non-compliant resources.
- Gatekeeper audit identifies violations in existing resources.
- Dry-run mode supports safe policy assessment and rollout.
- Policies must be tested against Pods and workload controllers.
- Gatekeeper should be deployed as highly available infrastructure.
- Policy violations should be monitored and integrated with enterprise security operations.
- Exceptions should be narrow, approved and time-limited.
- Gatekeeper complements Pod Security Admission, RBAC, Network Policies and runtime detection.
- Enterprise success requires policy ownership, version control, testing and continuous governance.

# Knowledge Check

## 1. What is the primary purpose of OPA Gatekeeper?

**Answer:** To enforce policy-as-code against Kubernetes resources during admission and audit existing resources for compliance violations.

## 2. What is the difference between a ConstraintTemplate and a Constraint?

**Answer:** A ConstraintTemplate defines reusable policy logic and parameters, while a Constraint applies that policy to selected resources with a specific scope and enforcement action.

## 3. Why should new Gatekeeper policies begin in dry-run mode?

**Answer:** Dry-run mode identifies existing violations and potential application impact without blocking deployments.

## 4. What is the purpose of the Gatekeeper audit controller?

**Answer:** It evaluates existing Kubernetes resources against configured Constraints and reports resources that violate policy.

## 5. Why must Gatekeeper be designed for high availability?

**Answer:** Gatekeeper participates in the Kubernetes admission request path, so an outage may block API operations or create a policy-enforcement gap depending on the configured failure behaviour.

Why This Matters

Section titled “Why This Matters”

Kubernetes allows development teams to create infrastructure and deploy applications quickly.

However, without central policy enforcement, teams may deploy resources that violate enterprise security standards.

Examples include:

  • Privileged containers
  • Containers running as root
  • Images from untrusted registries
  • Workloads without resource limits
  • Pods using host networking
  • Containers mounting sensitive host paths
  • Resources without ownership labels
  • Public LoadBalancer Services
  • Excessive Linux capabilities
  • Workloads without approved security controls

Security teams may document that these configurations are prohibited.

Documentation alone does not prevent them.

OPA Gatekeeper converts enterprise security requirements into enforceable Kubernetes policies.

It evaluates Kubernetes API requests and can reject configurations that violate approved standards.

Gatekeeper therefore creates a technical enforcement point between developer activity and the Kubernetes cluster.

What is Open Policy Agent?

Section titled “What is Open Policy Agent?”

Open Policy Agent, commonly called OPA, is a general-purpose policy engine.

OPA allows organisations to separate policy decisions from application and infrastructure code.

Instead of embedding security decisions directly inside every system, administrators define central policies that determine whether an action should be allowed.

OPA can be used for:

  • Kubernetes admission control
  • API authorisation
  • Infrastructure validation
  • CI/CD policy checks
  • Service-mesh authorisation
  • Application-level decisions
  • Cloud configuration validation
  • Compliance enforcement

OPA policies are written using the Rego policy language.

Policy Decision Model

Section titled “Policy Decision Model”

OPA evaluates structured input against defined policy logic.

The decision may be:

  • Allow
  • Deny
  • Return a violation
  • Return supporting information
  • Require additional review

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

Section titled “What is OPA Gatekeeper?”

OPA Gatekeeper is a Kubernetes-native policy controller built using Open Policy Agent.

It integrates OPA with Kubernetes admission control and provides resources for:

  • Defining reusable policy templates
  • Applying policies to selected resources
  • Rejecting non-compliant requests
  • Auditing existing resources
  • Reporting policy violations
  • Managing policy parameters
  • Supporting policy testing
  • Applying selected resource mutations
  • Integrating external data into policy decisions

Gatekeeper extends Kubernetes using Custom Resource Definitions.

The primary validation resources are:

  • ConstraintTemplate
  • Constraint

Gatekeeper Architecture

Section titled “Gatekeeper Architecture”

Gatekeeper operates during the admission stage.

It does not replace:

  • Kubernetes authentication
  • Kubernetes RBAC
  • Pod Security Admission
  • Network Policies
  • Runtime detection
  • Container image scanning

It complements these controls.

Real-World Scenario

Section titled “Real-World Scenario”

A global financial organisation operates more than 300 Amazon EKS clusters.

During an internal security assessment, the Cloud Security team identifies:

  • Privileged containers in production
  • Workloads using public container registries
  • Missing CPU and memory limits
  • Public LoadBalancer Services
  • Namespaces without ownership labels
  • HostPath mounts on application Pods
  • Inconsistent security controls across clusters

The organisation deploys OPA Gatekeeper as its central Kubernetes policy engine.

The implementation follows a phased strategy.

First, the security team creates ConstraintTemplates for:

  • Privileged container restrictions
  • Approved image repositories
  • Required resource limits
  • Required ownership labels
  • Restricted Service types
  • Restricted host volumes

The team deploys corresponding Constraints using dryrun.

Gatekeeper audit identifies hundreds of existing violations without blocking application deployments.

The findings are assigned to application owners and tracked through remediation tickets.

After the highest-risk violations are resolved, the organisation enables deny enforcement for production clusters.

Policies are stored in Git, tested through CI/CD and distributed using GitOps.

Gatekeeper metrics are collected by Prometheus, policy dashboards are displayed in Grafana and high-risk admission violations are forwarded to the SIEM.

The result is a measurable and consistently enforced Kubernetes security baseline across the enterprise.

  • Policy violations should be monitored and integrated with enterprise security operations.
  • Exceptions should be narrow, approved and time-limited.
